en: (B1) Śrīḥ! The Bhāṭṭadīpikā, accompanied by its commentary, the Prabhāvalī.
Therein begins the first quarter of the third chapter. (First Topic:
Now, therefore, follows the definition of the subsidiary (śeṣa). Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.1.

Thus, having defined the sixfold classification of ritual acts (*karmabheda*), we now define "subsidiariness" (*aṅgatva*), which is synonymous with "subservience" (*śeṣatva*) as determined by that which is primary (*śeṣin*). For this [subsidiariness] is possible only between distinct things, not between non-distinct ones; thus, its definition serves as the logical ground for that [classification]. Furthermore, although the previously mentioned definition does not serve as the ground for the mutual relationship of principal and subsidiary (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) between a substance and an action;

Nevertheless, since the logical connection (*saṅgati*) is established by taking the causality as being co-located with the status of being a subordinate member (*aṅgatva*), there is no contradiction even if that [causality] does not exist under the delimitation of the delimitor (*avacchedaka*).
It should also be understood that causality resides only in one part, while its investigation in the other part is undertaken to avoid the contingency of such [unrestricted] causality.
The status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) alone is the explicit meaning of the scriptural passage, whereas the status of being the principal (*aṅgitva*) follows by implication.
Furthermore, that [status of being an auxiliary] is established by the six means of proof beginning with direct statement (*śruti*),
because here we do not investigate that which is established by the means of proof consisting of extended application (*atideśa*).
And that [auxiliary status] is examined in its various forms:

the definition of auxiliary status (*aṅgatva*), the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the denotable capacity (*śakyatva*) of the word *śeṣa* (subordinate), and the delimitors of both the subordinate (*aṅga*) and the principal (*aṅgin*).
The six means of proof—direct statement and the rest—are the authorities regarding the status of being an auxiliary;
[this treatise discusses] their relative strength and weakness when there is a conflict, as well as where such a conflict exists and where it does not, and so forth. // 3 // 1 //
Thus ends the first section, concerning the proposition.
I bow to the beautiful and great splendor whose form is Śrī, which destroys the darkness of ignorance, illuminates the knowledge of reality, and bestows all that is desired. (1)

I bow to my father Bālakṛṣṇa, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of the Vedas and Śāstras, who is exceedingly skillful in the performance of rituals such as sacrifices, and whose mind is purified by the worship of Sadāśiva. // 2 //

Having prostrated before the venerable Śrī Khaṇḍadeva, my true guru, who is the sun to the lotus-like hearts of Mīmāṃsakas, I compose this commentary, the *Prabhāvalī*, upon his work which treats its categories in an extremely concise manner. (3)

Even though I am merely bringing to light some inconsistency here that has already been pointed out by the Guru, this is not an act of partiality on my part, for I am skilled in promoting [the truth].

Rather, it is my hope that those ornaments of the earth, whose intellects are as sharp as kusa-grass and who are devoted to the established tenets, will set aside my words and instead grace the work composed by him. (4)

Although the word *atha* has three meanings— immediacy (*ānantarya*), dependence on what precedes (*pūrvaprakṛtāpekṣitva*), and introduction (*adhikāra*)— nevertheless, since the rule regarding what precedes applies only to that which is explicitly indicated by the word itself in the *Jijñāsā-sūtra*,

and since study (*adhyayana*) has not been explicitly indicated by a word prior [to this sūtra], it is untenable for the word to mean dependence on what precedes. Furthermore, because the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is dependent upon the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Since there is an absence of being achievable through human effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), since eligibility (*adhikāra*) is impossible by way of the operation of the word (*śabdavyāpāra*), and since there is a lack of evidence for the word "atha" indicating the commencement of inquiry (*vicāra-lakṣaṇā*), it was accepted that the word "atha" signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*) alone, rather than having those two meanings. However, in the present case, because the operation of the word directed toward the determination of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) is possible, its meaning as eligibility (*adhikāra*) is appropriate; and of that...

Since immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is established by the very fact that [the subsequent topic] is being treated immediately after the definition of difference (*bhedalakṣaṇa*), and since dependence on what was previously discussed (*pūrvaprakṛtāpekṣatva*) is established by the force of the context itself— given that the latter depends upon the former— it is unnecessary to assume that [the particle *atha*] has the purpose of expressing those two meanings as well.

As it is stated in the Vārttika: "Thus, when two meanings have been described for the word *atha*, the connection between the chapters has been stated; or rather, that [connection] is established by implication."

"Therefore, because it is not redundant, the purpose of the word 'atha' (now/then) will be stated as being for the sake of indicating a new topic, having as its scope the meaning that is about to be explained."

Thus, indicating the meaning of the word "atha" (now/then), he makes a formal declaration regarding the subject matter already treated and that which is about to be treated, for the sake of easy comprehension: "tadevam" (thus, therefore).

The phrase "now" (*saṃprati*) is stated to indicate the occasion for the statement made in the *Vārttika*: "In this context, the qualification belongs only to the subordinate element (*śeṣa*), and not to anything else; for the cognitions of the characteristics of other [elements] depend upon the establishment of the cognition of the subordinate.
Although, due to their mutual relationship, it is necessary to investigate both the subordinate and the principal (*śeṣin*) for the sake of understanding both, [the text proceeds as follows].

On the contrary, since the subordinate (*śeṣa*) is primary, it is more appropriate to define the principal (*śeṣin*); thus, the objection that the statement in the Sūtra "the definition of the subordinate" (*śeṣalakṣaṇam*) is improper is raised. To dispel this doubt, it is stated: "defined by the principal," and so forth. Since the term "subordinate" implies possession (*matvartha*), when the specific definition of the principal is to be made, it is necessary to define the subordinate as its qualifier. Furthermore, once the subordinate is defined, the definition of the principal is established by implication alone; such is the case with the means of knowledge, such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

And since the operation [of the relationship] occurs only when there is subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*), and because the relative strength or weakness (*balābala*) is possible only in the subsidiary itself—given that it is not contradictory for such strength or weakness to reside in the principal (*śeṣin*)—the author intends that the definition of the subsidiary alone must necessarily be performed; thus, the mere proposition regarding that [subsidiary] is stated in the Sūtra.

Furthermore, in this context, the nature of being a principal (*śeṣitva*)—defined as possessing the status of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatā*) which constitutes the "limb-ness" (*aṅgatva*) whose definition will be stated later—is established by implication (*arthāt*) alone, so there is no contradiction.

By this, the intention is that Somanātha’s statement— that even though he has established that the knowledge of being a subordinate (*śeṣitva*) is necessarily concomitant (*nāntarīyasiddhika*), the definition of it constitutes the subject matter of the chapter— is rejected, as it contradicts the Vārttika.

Intending the meaning of the sūtra—which indicates that in the remaining words of the sūtra there is a predominance of the abstract state (bhāvapradhānatva) and an absence of the necessity for endless ellipses or other implied meanings, and by which "remainder" (śeṣa) is characterized as "subsidiarity" (aṅgatva)—he says: "In regard to subsidiarity... (śeṣatve). We shall explain that [subsidiarity] by means of this chapter.

The author of the Sautrānta [commentary], having established the word, demonstrates the logical connection (*saṃgati*) of cause and effect between the determination of the subject matter of the preceding and succeeding chapters by means of the phrase "of distinct [entities]" and "of substance and action."

The meaning is that there is a relationship of mutual principal and subordinate (aṅgāṅgibhāva) between substances such as curd and so forth, as well as among actions, which possess distinctions established in the world but whose specific differences were not determined in the second [chapter].

Since the determination of the mutual relationship of principal and subordinate among actions depends upon the determination of the distinctions established in the second chapter, he resolves this by establishing the connection through coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya), saying "nevertheless" (tathāpi).
To avoid the consequence of inconsistency regarding the determination of the subordination of substances and so forth under this view, he states another position: "only a part" (aṃśa eva).
The phrase beginning with "because the definition of mere subsidiarity (śeṣatva) constitutes the subject matter of the chapter" and so forth.

Avoiding the objection regarding the connection of the chapter that is about to be composed—which deals with the definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—he says: "And that [cognition] is manifold."

Therefore, by the very proposition defining *śeṣatva* (subservience), all the various investigations to be undertaken regarding its relations are also included within the subject matter of this chapter; thus, there is no lack of coherence for that [proposition].

In this regard, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) will here explain such matters as: "What is the subordinate (*śeṣa*)? By what reason is it subordinate? And how is it applied (*viniyujyate*)?"—namely, the grounds for application—and the relative strength and weakness of those [grounds].
By means of this primary intent (*tātparya*), it has been shown that there are multiple modes [of definition], such as through incidental introduction (*upodghāta*) and so forth.

In that regard, in the subsequent sūtra—"The remainder [is *arthavāda*] because it is for the sake of another" (*śeṣaḥ parārthatvāt*)—the definition previously stated is understood to be expressed verbally (*śābda*) by way of the employment of a reason in the ablative case.

Consequently, with the intention that the essential nature (*svarūpa*), though established by implication (*artha-siddha*), is considered non-verbal (*ārthika*), even for that which is intended to state the essential nature...
Indicating that the Bhāṣya conveys an implicit intention, he shows the explanation as being directed toward the definition [of subsidiarity]:
"the definition of the status of being a subsidiary (aṅgatva)."

Intending that the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*)— the cause by which the word "subsidiary" (*śeṣa*) is employed in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth— is precisely the delimiting factor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of that word "subsidiary," he states the meaning of the subsequent portion of the second proposition's commentary, beginning with the words "the word 'subsidiary'."

The intended meaning of the subsequent commentary— which concerns the third proposition— that "the threshing and so forth, being enjoined by means of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and other criteria, are applied to all [grains] either by subverting the objective reference (*uddeśyatā*) as delimited by the form heard in the text, or else by the absence thereof," is shown in the phrase:
"between the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*aṅgin*)."

He states another proposition indicated by the Bhāṣya—namely, that "there is contradiction"—which, while having this as its primary intent, also includes other points through incidental introduction (*upodghāta*).

By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), there is an inclusion of the investigation that will be undertaken through incidental discussion following the primary analysis of contradiction and non-contradiction.
Thus ends the first section, concerning the thesis.
(B1) (Section 2) (Topic 2):
"The subsidiary exists because it is for the sake of another" (Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.2).
Here, the first two types [of relationship] are being examined.
For that which constitutes the definition of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is precisely the delimitor of the denotable meaning of the word "subordinate" (*śeṣa*), and nothing else.
In this context, being an auxiliary means being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*).
And that [being for the sake of another] consists in being that which is enjoined as a factor of action (*kāraka*) proceeding toward a specific objective; that is what constitutes being an auxiliary.

Furthermore, because the person acting for the sake of heaven (svarga) connects with the injunction as a causal factor (*kāraka*) in the effort conducive to the sacrifice (*yāga*), the definition [of being a subsidiary] applies to the sacrifice. Likewise, because the *prayāja* and other such rites connect with the injunction as causal factors in the person’s effort directed toward the primary rite and conducive to the *prayāja*, the same [definition] applies to the *prayāja* and others as well.

And in the case of substances, qualities, time, agents, place, and so forth, since they are enjoined as causal factors—such as instrumentality, agency, or locus—in the effort conducive to the sacrifice which has the sacrifice itself as its objective, there is no contradiction in their being subsidiaries of the sacrifice.

Furthermore, even though the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expresses a general relationship, it ultimately resolves into the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action); thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).
Moreover, since a causal condition (*nimitta*), although connected with the action, lacks the status of a *kāraka*, it does not incur the status of being a subordinate member (*aṅga*).

And because a causal condition, despite having the status of a "purpose" (*uddeśyatva*) known as "that which causes performance," lacks the status of a "purpose" known as "that which is intended to be reached" (*ripsitatva*), the sacrifice does not have the causal condition as its subordinate member.
Because in the definition, it is precisely such a *uddeśyatā* (status of being the intended object) that is intended;

and since the status of being a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) in the form of the *karman* (object) is already obtained through the term *uddeśyatā* itself, the word *kāraka* refers to something other than that.

Since even acts such as plowing (*kṛṣi*) could result in the undesired consequence of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) due to being a *kāraka* of the performance of a sacrifice (*yāga*), the phrase ending in "being that which is to be enjoined" (*vidheyatva*) is added.
And just as there is no instance of under-extension (avyāpti) or over-extension (ativyāpti) in this regard, so it is explained in detail in the *Kaustubha*.
And thus, where this definition does not apply—
such as in the case of sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like with respect to productive activity (*bhāvanā*) and so forth— [the definition fails].
In that regard, the designation of "subsidiary status" (*aṅgatva*) in the treatise is figurative (*bhākta*).
For although such subsidiary status is not established by the means of proof such as direct Vedic statement (*śruti*),
because the instrumental case-ending and so forth denote merely the state of being a factor (*kārakatva*).
Nevertheless, while the object denoted by the word "heaven" and so forth is [understood] from the word "heaven" and so on through a relation such as being the objective,
the effort is [understood] from the verbal suffix (ākhyāta).

The status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action) belongs to the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth; the connection with the injunction (*vidhi*) arises from its co-occurrence with the word expressing the injunction.

For an injunction, while enjoining a qualified productive activity (*bhāvanā*), enjoins the qualifiers by implication as well; thus, all [elements] are connected to the injunction either as the object of reference (*uddeśya*) or as that which is enjoined (*vidheya*).

Therefore, even though other constituent elements that form part of the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) may be established by other means of knowledge, because their status as a causal factor (*kārakatva*)—which constitutes that auxiliary nature—is understood through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and so forth, there is the conventional usage of "authority regarding their status as auxiliaries.
Thus ends the second section concerning the definition of the auxiliary (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇa-adhikaraṇa*).

(B2) Since, in the inference regarding the status of being denoted by the word *śeṣa* (subsidiary) in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, "being for the sake of another" (*parārthatva*) is stated as the reason by means of the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*), that alone is the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word *śeṣa*. And since it also serves to define its own nature by implication, it is also its definition (*lakṣaṇa*). With this intention, he says: "For that which indeed... (*yadeva hi*).

Regarding that which Bādari describes as *śeṣatva* (subsidiarity) being the state of being helpful, and that which others describe as subsidiarity based on the cause of inseparable connection— namely, that when one thing does not exist without another, the former, such as a seed, is the subsidiary of the latter, such as a sprout— it was in order to refute these views that Jaimini stated in the sūtra "The subsidiary is that which exists for the sake of another" (*śeṣaḥ parārthatvāt*) that subsidiarity consists in the form of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*).
He explains that [point] with the words: "In that regard" (tatra).

The definition of "subsidiary" (aṅga) as "that which provides assistance" is incorrect, because even items such as the *prayāja* offerings or the *godohana* vessel—which are themselves subsidiary to the animal sacrifice—would then result in being subsidiaries to the *puroḍāśa* cake and the water-carrying (*praṇayana*), since they too provide some form of assistance.

Likewise, the definition as "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*) is also incorrect, because it would lead to the mutual subsidiarity of the *āgneya* and other primary sacrifices due to their inseparability from one another;
rather, the meaning is that subsidiarity consists solely in "being for the sake of another" (*pārārthya*).
Now, what indeed is this so-called "being for the sake of another" (*parārthatva*)?

If it means being the inherent substrate (*samavāyitva*) of an activity (*kṛti*) directed toward another's purpose, then there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in the case of sacrifices and the like, which are insentient.
If, however, it means being that which is to be accomplished by such an activity, then there is an over-narrow definition in the case of place, time, the agent, and so forth.

By this, the definition of *pārārthya* (being for the sake of another) stated in the *Nyāyaprakāśa*—namely, that it is "subsidiariness" (*aṅgatva*), which is synonymous with being pervaded by an activity directed toward another—is refuted.

If, however, [subsidiariness] were defined as "the state of being connected to the aforementioned activity," then there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of a *nimitta* (a conditional cause).
Therefore, since even *pārārthya* cannot withstand a valid definition, it is impossible for it to serve as a defining characteristic; thus, he says: "In that regard... (*tatra*).
It is being an auxiliary part of that.

The meaning is that [the sacrifice] possesses the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅga*) as defined by that objective (*uddeśya*). This is because of its connection with the injunction (*vidhi*) by way of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action).

Since there is a connection with the injunction in respect to an effort (*kṛti*) qualified by that [objective], through the cause of being a *kāraka*, the injunction enters into the sacrifice which serves as the qualifier; thus, by virtue of this connection with the injunction, the sacrifice is "enjoined. Such is the application of the definition.
This is the meaning.

In the first [section] of the seventh [book], after refuting the doubt that the *prayāja* and other rites are enjoined with heaven as their purpose, the status of being "pariplava" (floating/intermittent) will be refuted; keeping that in mind, he demonstrates the application of the definition [of *pariplava*] with the words: "pradhānoddeśa... (with reference to the primary rite).

Since a substance is enjoined as a factor (*kāraka*) by way of bringing about an action, and a quality is enjoined as a factor by way of delimiting the substance, [the quality] is construed there as an instrument (*karaṇa*); he shows that [quality] is also construed therein [as an instrument].
And this is also an indication of sequence (*krama*), because sequence too is enjoined as a factor by way of delimiting the meaning of the word (*padārtha*).
"The sixth."

The meaning is as follows: although the injunction formulated by the designation (*samākhyā*) "as in the case of the *adhvaryu*" conveys through the genitive case merely a relationship with the *adhvaryu*, it culminates in [establishing] his status as an agent; therefore, he does not possess subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) toward those respective ritual acts by virtue of being an agent.

To refute the subsidiarity of the occasion (*nimitta*), [the author] states "of the occasion" (*nimittasya*), because the occasion is construed as the objective (*uddeśyatva*) that prompts performance, and since the quality of being enjoined as a causal factor (*kāraka*) for the activity initiated by aiming at the occasion exists in the sacrifice, [the author speaks thus] to exclude its being a subsidiary of the occasion.
And as it is for him...

Although the *prayāja* and other such elements are prescribed by extension (*atideśa*) as being the causal factors (*kāraka*) for the volitional activity (*kṛti*) directed toward the animal sacrifice, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). This is because, in the case of the *paśupuroḍāśa*, while only the assistance (*upakāra*) is implied by extension, no extension is postulated regarding the constituent parts (*padārtha*); thus, they are not prescribed as being the causal factors for the volitional activity directed toward that [animal sacrifice].

Thus, even though the *godohana* vessel assists in the act of fetching water (*praṇayana*), there is no over-extension [of the definition], because it lacks the status of being a factor (*kāraka*) in an action directed toward that [fetching] as its primary purpose.

In this context, if one were to state merely that "the status of being a factor of volition (*kṛti-kārakatva*) [constitutes being subsidiary]" then, since the fruit (*phala*) also possesses the status of being a factor of volition by virtue of its connection with the object (*karman*), it would follow that the fruit is subsidiary to the rite.
Therefore, the qualification of volition—"that which is directed toward an objective" (*yad-uddeśa-pravṛtta*)—is intended to convey the meaning "directed toward another.

Since there is no "otherness" (*paratva*) with respect to the fruit itself, even though the fruit might be subsidiary to the enjoyer (*bhoktr*) through its connection with the injunction (*vidhi*) as the object of the person's volition directed toward the fruit, there is no possibility of the fruit being subsidiary to the rite.
It is with this very intention that it was stated, "by the term 'intended object' (uddeśyatā) alone," and so forth.

The meaning is that even for the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), its status as an auxiliary to the fruit is established because it is connected as an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the effort (*kṛti*) directed toward the attainment of the fruit; the details of this should be seen in the *Kaustubha*.

Even though, since threshing and other such acts are subordinate elements (aṅga), there is no effort directed toward them for the sake of the rice and other materials already established in the world, nevertheless, there is no deficiency because an effort directed toward them is possible by way of their being means to the *apūrva*.

The meaning is that the designation of "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) and so forth for the action (*kṛti*) is figurative, because there is no other action [apart from itself]; likewise, the sacrificial act (*yāga*) is [figuratively called] cultivation with respect to the cultivation, that [cultivation] is [figuratively called] cultivation with respect to the fruit,

the verbal cultivation (*śabdabhāvanā*) is [figuratively called] cultivation with respect to the objective cultivation (*arthabhāvanā*), the animal and so forth are [figuratively called] cultivation with respect to the factor (*kāraka*), and the status of being a factor is [figuratively called] cultivation with respect to the action— the conventional usage of "subsidiarity" (*aṅgatva*) is thus metaphorical.

As for what the authors of the *Prakāśa* have stated— that once the primary status of the conventional usage regarding the *bhāvanā* being a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the result is established, its being a subordinate element with respect to each of its own desired [ends] consists in its being prompted by an instigation (*pravartanā*) directed toward a desired object;
and that "being prompted" (*prayojyatva*) applies both to the action itself and to its effects—

[namely], that the effect of the instigation is the activity (*pravṛtti*), and the effect of that is the sacrifice, the result, and so forth, which are subordinate elements with respect to each of their respective desired ends.

Since the substance, place, time, agent, and so forth would also result in being "limbs" (aṅga) because they are produced by the instigation (*pravartanā*) through the mediation of their respective functions as instrument, locus, agent, and so on, it remains difficult to establish that the verbal productive energy (*śābdabhāvanā*) is an "limb" of the objective productive energy (*ārthabhāvanā*) even under such circumstances; thus, [the opponent's position] is incorrect,
as is clearly stated in the Kaustubha.

As for what was stated by the author of the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra*—namely, that "that which, when there is an inconsistency regarding the object of the effort associated with an injunction, is resolved by being the objective (*uddeśya*) of that [effort], is its subsidiary (*aṅga*), and is for its sake"—that is not correct. For, in a sentence expressing a connection with time, since it is impossible to resolve the inconsistency regarding the object of the effort residing in the time (and so forth) even by making the ritual action the objective, one must instead accept that the ritual action itself is the object of the effort with respect to the time. Consequently, this would result in the ritual action being a subsidiary of the time, rather than the time being [a subsidiary] of the action.

Because it would not follow that [the action] is a constituent part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*). In our view, however, since prescriptiveness (*vidheyatva*)—which is the general rule—is co-located with the state of being something to be undertaken (*upādeyatva*), which consists in being the object of volitional effort (*kṛti*), then in the presence of evidence such as proximity (*sannidhi*) that causes recognition, that [general] prescriptiveness is sublated; thus, when prescriptiveness cannot coexist with the state of being something to be undertaken, [the action is not a constituent part].
Even so, its status as something to be enjoined is not untenable, because it makes known that its locus is otherwise unknown.

And here, because the *kārakas* (factors of action) differ according to the difference in their operations (*vyāpāra*), it is understood that the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*)—which is constituted by those *kārakas*—also differs for each individual object.

Therefore, in order to indicate that the property of being a *prayāja* and so forth serves as the delimiting factor (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) for each respective auxiliary status, the words "yat" and "tat" are employed in the definition.

It should be noted that since the state of being for another’s sake (*pārārthya*)—defined as being connected with an injunction by way of being a *kāraka* of an action (*kṛti*)—cannot be stated without the means of proof such as direct assertion (*śruti*) and the rest, these [means of proof] are also implicitly introduced here.
Thus ends the second section concerning the definition of the remainder (śeṣalakṣaṇa).
(B1) (Section 3 / [A.3 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 3]) Bādari [holds that] subsidiariness resides in substances, qualities, and purificatory acts. Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.3:
Even though subsidiariness consists in being for the sake of another, nevertheless, sacrifice and the like are not what is indicated [as the primary object].

Because, by virtue of the co-occurrence in the same word (*samānapadaśruti*), it is the sacrifice and so forth alone that are the objects to be produced (*bhāvya*) by the productive operation (*bhāvanā*); therefore, that [sacrifice] is not enjoined with heaven as its purpose.

Furthermore, since the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is the injunction (*vidhi*) in its capacity as a formal suitability (*svarūpayogyatva*) alone, it does not imply the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).

Even if it were to imply it, since the cognition of being a means to a desired end—which is common to both error and valid knowledge—is the cause [of action], there is no evidence for establishing that [the sacrifice] is actually a means to a desired end.

However, since the term *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven) can be explained as referring to the agent—as in the expression "one desiring a wife should perform an expiation"—there is no necessity for it to refer to the end to be achieved (*bhāvya*).
Therefore, the sacrifice and so forth are not to be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
In reality, however, being an auxiliary (*śeṣatva*) consists precisely in being a factor of assistance.
For even that which is harmful toward that end lacks the designation of being a "subsidiary" (śeṣa).
And that [means of establishing subsidiarity] consists of exactly three types of evidence: direct statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), and syntactical connection (vākya).

For this very reason, substances such as rice, qualities such as redness, and purificatory acts such as threshing are considered subsidiaries because they are observed to be beneficial to the primary purpose.

As for the consecratory rites such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), although their status as subsidiaries (*aṅgatva*) cannot be established through indicative mark (*liṅga*), their subsidiarity is understood through direct statement (*śruti*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*); therefore, by the force of those very [scriptural means], their status as auxiliaries (*śeṣatva*) is justified through the postulation of a benefit (*upakāra*). Thus, it is argued that these [rites] alone are what are to be characterized [as auxiliaries]. To this, we reply: subsidiarity is not defined merely by being a benefactor (*upakārakatva*), for if it were, then even the *godohana* vessel and the bringing of curds (*dadhyānayana*) would result in being subsidiaries to the act of carrying water (*praṇayana*) and the sacrifice of whey (*vājinayāga*) respectively.
Rather, it is solely the state of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*).

In the case of one who causes harm, however, the objectivity (*uddeśyatā*) belongs to that very act of harming because it is what is desired, and not to the person themselves; thus, even regarding such a harmful agent, there is no conventional usage of the term "subsidiary" (*śeṣatva*).
Furthermore, it will be explained that this [subsidiarity] is also cognizable through the six means of proof, beginning with direct verbal testimony (*śruti*).

And for this reason, even the sacrifice is a subsidiary element with respect to the fruit. To explain: although the optative suffix conveys that the injunction possesses a suitability for action by its very nature, nevertheless, since the injunction would otherwise be rendered purposeless if no activity ever occurred, it must necessarily be the case that such activity occurs at some time.

At that time, since that [cognition] is impossible without the knowledge that it is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), and since it cannot be an error in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), the fact that sacrifice is a means to a desired end is first understood through the force of the injunction;

furthermore, its being a means to a specific desired end is understood from the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*). Thus, the status of sacrifice as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of heaven is established.
In the same way, the fruit also possesses the status of being a subordinate element of the person who enjoys it.

And the enjoyer is, by default, none other than the agent itself—due to the force of the injunction, the force of desire, and the force of the ātmanepada suffix; however, when there is evidence [to the contrary], it is another.
It should be noted that in this case, the conventional usage of "subsidiary" (aṅga) is figurative.

Furthermore, since the person (puruṣa) is an instrumental factor (kāraka) for the volitional effort directed toward sacrifices and the like by virtue of his agency and so forth, it is beyond dispute that he is a subsidiary element (aṅga) of the rite solely on the basis of the scriptural statement itself. // 3 //
Thus concludes the third section concerning the status of the sacrifice, its fruit, and the person as subordinate elements to heaven, the person, and so forth.
(B2) Intending to state that this section will determine what the "remainder" is by way of demonstrating the objects of the definition already mentioned here, he says: "Even though... and so forth.

Now, one might object: since the optative suffix (*liṅ*) denotes an instigation (*pravartanā*) consisting of an activity conducive to an inclination toward a result, and since such an inclination cannot arise without a cognition of the means as being a source of what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*), it follows that this must necessarily be implied. Consequently, because the sacrifice and so forth can be enjoined as a means for the sake of a desired end, why should they not be the objects of indication (*lakṣya*)? To this, he says: "Of the injunction" (*vidheḥ*).
The meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is simply an operation conducive to activity by virtue of its fitness (*yogyatā*), and not an conduciveness to activity as qualified by a result,
which would imply that the sacrifice and so forth— the objects of the activity— are the instrumental factors (*kāraka*) for an effort directed toward a desired end.
The meaning is this: even when there is a desire for a ritual action (*kāmya-karma*) and one has heard hundreds of injunctions (*vidhi*), activity may sometimes fail to arise.

Therefore, since an injunction—which is merely capable of generating activity—does not necessitate that its own object be the instrumental cause (*kāraka*) of an effort directed toward a desired end, the subservience (*pārārthya*) of the sacrifice and so forth is not established.

[Objection: "But surely, once it is understood from the term *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven) that heaven is the objective (*uddeśya*), then—since it is impossible for the sacrifice to fall into the role of the end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) by implication—it must be enjoined as the instrument (*karaṇa*) itself; thus there is no inconsistency. To this, he says:
*svargakāma iti*.

And thus, since the sacrifice itself is that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*) and the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) is connected as its agent, there is no fruit [of the sacrifice]; therefore, the sacrifice is not a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the fruit, nor is the fruit a subordinate part of the person.
However, because the person is connected as the agent, he is a subordinate part of the sacrifice. With this intention, he concludes: "Therefore... (*ataḥ*).
"Even for that purpose," [it is said].

The meaning is as follows: although smoke intended for the purpose of warding off flies possesses a "parārthatva" (being for the sake of another) insofar as there is the cognition that "this smoke is for the sake of the flies," the conventional usage of the term "śeṣatva" (subsidiarity) does not apply to it. Therefore, subsidiarity is simply the state of being a benefactor (upakārakatva) as distinguished from being a source of harm. And since this [subsidiarity] is possible only where it is apprehended through perception and other means of knowledge, sacrificial acts and the like do not fall under the definition of "lakṣya" (the object to be defined).
"By means of the mark."
The meaning is: "even though assistance is impossible," as if it were determined by implication (*sāmarthyena*).
[This refers to] the word "śruti" (scriptural statement).

The meaning is as follows: "vrīhīn" (rice grains) is the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) in the accusative case; the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of that word with the term ending in "-antam" (the object of sprinkling) in the expression "prokṣati" (he sprinkles) constitutes the syntactical connection (*vākya*); and "tābhyām" (by those two) refers to these two means of proof.
The phrase "teṣām eva" (of those very [grains]) [is used].

By the word "eva" (only), it is indicated that neither the sacrifice nor the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) and so forth are the objects of definition (*alakṣyatva*), because their status as contributing factors (*upakārakatva*) is not perceived through direct perception or from the second-case (*dvitīyā*) words in the scriptural injunctions.
And for this reason, from the statement [it follows].

It is stated "from the sentence" because there is an absence of the instrumental case-ending and so forth which would indicate instrumentality; furthermore, "context" is also implied for the sake of establishing the subsidiary status of the *prayāja* offerings and others.
[The phrase] "to a specific desired [result]"...

Therefore, the word *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven), which conveys the specific desired object required [by the injunction], refers by implication (*lakṣaṇā*) to the "heaven" that is the goal to be accomplished (*bhāvya*), and not to the agent;

the reason it is conveyed by that word—which at first sight appears to refer to the agent—is in order to conform to the fact that the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) is intransitive (i.e., lacks an external object). This is the meaning.
"But if there were valid means of cognition," however.

Just as in the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice, where the meaning is "son" because there exists the authoritative evidence of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) in the concluding statement, "He indeed becomes purified and radiant," so too [the term] is figurative (*bhākta*).

With respect to the experiencing subject—the active person—there is an absence of "otherness," and since there is no hearing of a connection with an injunction by way of being the object of reference (uddeśya), it is impossible for there to be primary subsidiarity (aṅgatva) consisting in being the object of the volitional effort (kṛti) directed toward that reference; therefore, [the status of being subsidiary] is merely figurative, such as through the state of being the agent (kartṛtva).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the status of instrument (*karaṇatā*) as a means in cases such as the honoring of the *audumbarī* post is intended.

Since even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) Bādari accepts the subsidiary status (*śeṣatva*) of substances, there is no dispute between the two regarding the person’s being a subsidiary by virtue of being a substance; thus, the point that "the person [is subsidiary] because he exists for the sake of the ritual" would render the subsequent formulation of the sūtra redundant, as it would involve no dispute at all—this is what is indicated by the phrase "it is indeed undisputed."

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since there is an absence of means of proof such as *prakaraṇa* (context) for the status of the *prayāja* offerings and others as subsidiaries (*aṅga*), they would not be extended [to other rites] because they would be primary (*pradhāna*) due to the assumption that heaven mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is their fruit.
In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, the word "that" [referring to the extension] has been stated [in the sūtra], and thus it is not explicitly mentioned here as it is clear.
Thus ends the third section concerning the status of the sacrifice, its fruit, and the person as being subordinate to heaven, the person, and so forth.
(B1) (Section 4 / [A.3 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 4]) Of those...

Thus, having established the nature of subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*), it was stated that there are six means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for subsidiarity, beginning with direct statement (*śruti*). Among these, "direct statement" (*śruti*) refers to a word that primarily denotes either the objecthood (*uddeśyatā*) or the status of being a factor of action (*kārakatva*)— both of which constitute subsidiarity—
and this [word] takes the form of case-endings such as the accusative or instrumental.

The term "primarily" (*prādhānyena*) is used for the purpose of excluding [words] such as those ending in *kṛt* suffixes, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), or those ending in *tṛc* and so forth;
for these, because they denote a substance qualified by its status as a *kāraka*, they do not primarily denote the *kāraka* status itself.
For this very reason, [in the injunction]: "One threshes with the two mortars and pestles that have been sprinkled,"...
In passages such as "The elephant is for the sacrificial rite," the application (*viniyoga*) is purely syntactical (*vākyīya*), not scriptural (*śrauta*).
In that case, the accusative case ending, signifying the status of being the objective (*uddeśyatva*), is the reason for the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth being subordinate (*aṅga*) elements.

However, in reality, since the status of being the objective—known as the state of being most desired (*īpsitatva*)—is not denotable by the accusative case ending, which expresses merely the state of being a goal to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*), even there the primary scriptural indication (*mukhyā śrutiḥ*) does not apply.
Rather, the usage of the Veda is indeed figurative (bhakta),

because a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) is accepted regarding the aspect of being "most desired" (īpsitatva). Therefore, even the term "status of being the object of reference" (uddeśyatāpada) need not be included in the definition.

Thus, even in the case of the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and others, because they lack the capacity for being a *kāraka*, the designation "based on direct statement" (*śruti*) is merely figurative. Likewise, wherever another *kāraka* is indicated by a case-ending through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there too the application (*viniyoga*) is based solely on syntactical connection (*vākya*), not on direct statement.
The same should be understood regarding [the application of] words that are identical in form (*samānapada*) and so forth.

Thus, since the applicatory power of direct statement (*śruti*) is already established by the *tadbhūta* section (PMS 1.1.24), we now undertake an investigation into the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the relationship between the subordinate (*aṅga*) and the principal (*aṅgin*), which is useful for the application of direct statement common to both the primary and the secondary senses:
"In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one threshes the rice-grains (*vrīhi*)."

The purifying of the clarified butter (*ājya*), the milking of the cow, and so forth— these preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) related to the clarified butter, the vegetable offerings, and the *sānnāyya* are prescribed in the scriptures. Regarding these, is the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) common to all of them as it is in the injunction for threshing (*avaghāta*), or is it distinct from each, excluding the clarified butter and the others?
The investigation [concerning] other cases is likewise:
in that regard, first of all, the genus *vrīhitva* (rice-ness) and so forth cannot be the delimiting factor of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*),
because that would result in redundancy (*ānarthakya*).

Since [the result] arises even apart from acts such as threshing and sprinkling— because [the result] occurs in respect to that which is delimited by "rice-ness" (*vrīhitva*) and so forth, and because it would not apply to barley— it is necessary, according to the principle of the ninth section (*adhikaraṇa*), to disregard the specific mention of "rice-ness" and instead employ an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on being a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*). Therefore, in that case...

Because it is proximate to the fruit, because it is unitary, and because it possesses an established capacity as an instigator among the indirectly contributing factors (*ārādupakāraka*), the supreme apūrva alone is indicated by way of the relationship of being a constituent of the offering material (*pradeya*) as its means of accomplishment.
And the Āgneya and other sacrifices possess that status of being a means toward it as well.
For this very reason, the principle of the restriction of speech (*vāṅniyamanyāya*) does not apply either.

Consequently, since the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) is common to all [grains], there would be a confusion (*saṅkara*) of threshing and other such operations even with respect to clarified butter (*ājya*) and the like.
Nor can a fixed rule be established on the basis of specific designation (*pratiniyatanirdeśa*).

If that were the case, since the intention to denote "rice-ness" (*vrīhitva*) and so forth would be necessary, it would follow that [the rule] would not apply to *nīvāra* grass and other substitutes; such being the prima facie view (*prāpta*), we reply: even if the injunction were to operate without distinction, it would nevertheless be restricted to specific cases in accordance with the requirement for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) and the parsimony of restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi-lāghava*).
How much more so when that injunction itself operates specifically?

In the case of words such as *vrīhi* (rice), by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it is precisely the status of being a means to the *utpattyapūrva* (originative apūrva) of the *āgneya* sacrifice that is indicated (*lakṣya*). Since that [status] also has an unascertained mode of operation, it is capable of being the motivator (*prayojaka*) of dharma; thus, because there is no lack of purpose (*ānarthakya*), there is no reason to bypass it, especially since it possesses fruitfulness through a mediated succession (*paraṃparā*).

Therefore, by the word *vrīhi* (rice), what is intended as the delimitor of the scope of the injunction (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) is precisely the state of being a substratum for a general instrumentality consisting of a mediating operation in the form of rice-grains— which are the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the substance to be offered— and which is defined by an effect-ness residing in the sacrifice and so forth, where that effect-ness is in turn defined by an object-ness (*kāryatā*) residing in those *apūrva*s (unseen potencies) produced by the originative injunctions of the Āgneya, Agnīṣomīya, and Aindrāgna sacrifices. Because this is what is intended,
there is no over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to clarified butter (*ājya*) and other such substances.
And here, although there is no single unifying factor for the three unprecedented [results], there is no syntactical split (avākyabheda) because they are presented within a single word.
Furthermore, it is only their status as means possessing those respective operations that is intended to be expressed, and not even the delimiters of that means-status and so forth.
Therefore, there is no deficiency even in the absence of the nature of sacrifice (yāgatva), the nature of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśatva), the nature of rice (vrīhitva), and the like.
And just as there is a commonality regarding barley despite the difference in the causal nature of rice and barley—
as is explained in detail in the *Kaustubha*— so too will it be established in various places, such as in the ninth chapter and elsewhere. // 3 // 4 //
Thus concludes the fourth section concerning the fixed scope of the *nirvāpa* (offering) and other rites.

(B2) Here, intending that the subject matter of the first quarter [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*] consists in the investigation of what is useful for the application of the primary Vedic injunction (*śruti*), [the author], after first investigating the matters falling under the scope of the third [quarter’s] proposition, states the definition of *śruti* at the outset:
"In that regard... (*tatra*).

Therefore, regarding the phrase "by means of the two sprinkled [objects]," because the past passive participle suffix in "prokṣitābhyām" denotes a substance in the form of the mortar and pestle qualified by the status of being the object (*karman*), it does not directly indicate— by way of primary importance— that the sprinkling has that [substance] as its objective; thus, the connection of the sprinkling is not through direct statement (*śruti*),
but rather through syntactical connection (*vākya*).

The meaning is that even in the case of the term *vāraṇa*, by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that by which one acts" (*avacaryate* / *anuṣṭhīyate*), there is the communication of its being an instrument for sacrifice (*yajñasādhanatva*).

Regarding the determination of subservience (*pārārthya*)—which consists in being a causal factor (*kāraka*) of an activity directed toward another—the object of reference (*uddeśya*) is primary; therefore, first he establishes that the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā-śruti*) expressing that [object] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that subservience, in order to deliberate upon the distinction between what is established and what is not established as subservient. Thus [he says]: "In that regard... (*tatra*).

While case endings beginning with the third (instrumental) indicate that the meaning of their respective stem is subordinate to another by establishing its status as a *kāraka*, the accusative (*dvitīyā*) does not indicate the subordination of its own stem-meaning to another; rather, by means of indicating the status of its own stem-meaning as the objective (*uddeśyatā*),

it brings about the status of the other meaning as the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), thereby indicating— through the intention of [the latter's] instrumentality— that the meaning of the other is subordinate to the meaning of its own stem.
He establishes its validity through a distinction, stating: "being intent upon that which is to be designated."
It should not be given at all as a characteristic mark.

[Objection: "But surely, even if the definition were merely 'that which primarily denotes the fruit of the effort (kṛti-kāraka),' it would still be logical for the accusative case-ending, which expresses the status of being an object (*karmatva*), to possess the status of primary direct statement (*mukhya-śruti*);
let its mode of application simply differ from what was stated previously. [Reply: No;

because in the definition of subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*), the term "subject matter" (*uddeśya*) is included, and it is precisely as something distinct from that [subject matter] that the status of being a factor of effort (*kṛti-kārakatva*) is intended. Therefore, it is not possible for that [accusative ending] to serve as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for that [subsidiarity].

For this very reason, the phrase "constituting the nature of being an auxiliary" (*aṅgatvaghaṭakībhūta*) has also been included [in the definition]. And this is logical: for that [action] such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), whose status as an auxiliary to the rice (*vrīhi*) is understood through its being an instrument (*karaṇa*), the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) is not the means of proof; because that [case-ending] only indicates the state of being the intended object (*uddeśyatā*) residing in the meaning of its own base noun (*svaprakṛtyartha*).

Therefore, in that case, the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅgatva*) is understood solely through the sentence (*vākya*), which consists of the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of words ending in the [sixth] case-ending. As for the conventional designation of the words ending in the second case as "direct statement" (*śruti*)—which was previously described as the means of application (*viniyojaka*)—that is merely figurative (*bhākta*). This is because, even though they possess the nature of a sentence consisting in the proximity of heard words, they lack the capacity to prompt the assumption of words expressive of the objective (*uddeśyatā*) or the kāraka-role that constitutes the essence of subsidiarity.
And its purpose is the establishment of the superiority of direct statement (*śruti*) over indicative mark (*liṅga*) by not postulating [an intermediate] indicative mark or direct statement.

Therefore, in this view, the intention is that even though there is a syntactical application (*vākyīya-viniyoga*) in the passage "With this he takes the horse's halter," the sublation of the indicative mark by direct statement is logically justified.
Thus, it is also in whatever case [this applies].

Just as in the case of the expression "with the remnant of the *prayāja*," the second and third case endings (*dvitīyā* and *tṛtīyā*) indicate through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that the oblations (*havis*) are the substratum and thus constitute subordinate elements (*aṅga*), so too the meaning here is that the act of sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) has the remnant of the *prayāja* as its subordinate element.
Thus it is said.

As for that which is stated in the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra*: "The definition of direct statement (*śruti*) is this: when two things intended as the primary (*śeṣin*) and the subordinate (*śeṣa*), presented in their respective forms, have their relationship produced by the cognition of the word 'yat' without depending on any mediation—that is direct statement. Having thus formulated the definition of direct statement, it continues: "And as for the relationship—whether it be perceived as the nature of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*), as the nature of being a means (*sādhanatva*), or simply as a relationship—no specific distinction among these is required."
It has been stated that by this [definition], the inclusion of word-hearings (*padaśruti*) involving the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*), the third case, and the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is achieved; however,
if therein the intended meaning is the absence of an intervention caused by a delay in the presentation of the genitive sense,

then there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) regarding the word-hearing that enjoins the sacrifice, because that [enjoining] depends on an intervention caused by the delay in the presentation of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) in relation to the connection between the sacrifice and heaven.
If, however, the intended meaning is the absence [of direct denotation] caused by the delay in the cognition of the object presented by another word, then this is incorrect;

for in that case, there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) regarding the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) that assigns the status of being an auxiliary to the purchase (*kraya*), because redness (*āruṇya*) depends on an intervention mediated by the determination of the form of the cow presented by another word, namely the term *ekahāyanī*.
Therefore, even when such an intervention exists, wherever there is the status of a factor of action (*kārakatva*) by virtue of its own expressive power (*śakti*), [it remains an auxiliary].

In this regard, the intention of the Venerable Master is as follows: by accepting that where there is direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), there is no figurative scriptural statement (*gauṇa-śruti*), the status of redness (*āruṇya*) and other such qualities as being subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the purchase is established through direct scriptural statement, whereas the fact that the sacrifice is for the sake of heaven is established through figurative scriptural statement; such is the general direction of his thought.
Thus, it is so because of the Śruti.
The meaning is: of the primary *śruti* characterized by such marks and of the secondary (*gauṇa*) *śruti*.
[Regarding the term] "tadbhūta":...

The meaning is that since the *Tarkapāda* establishes— in the sūtra "tadbhūtānāṃ kriyārthatvena samāmnāyaḥ"— the syntactic connection of the meanings of words denoting case-factors (*kāraka*) contained within a sentence with the action, the status of being a case-factor as defined by the action is established by implication through direct statement (*śruti*); thus, the fact that direct statement is the means of application (*viniyojaka*) is proven.
Regarding the relationship between the members and the whole:
Although from this point onward only the delimitors of the status of the principal (*aṅgin*) will be investigated, and not the delimitors of the status of the subordinate (*aṅga*);

nevertheless, once the delimitors of the status of the principal have been defined, it follows by implication that the very nature of being a causal factor (*kāraka*) for an activity directed toward an object delimited by such a delimitor of the objective reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) is itself the delimitor of the status of the subordinate relative to that [principal].
The presentation of both [theories] is made with a view toward establishing the proof;
such are the [arguments].
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is an inclusion of the ritual details of the *sānnāyya* offering, such as milking, curdling, and so forth.
The same applies elsewhere as well.
The meaning is: "even in the case of rituals such as the pressing [of Soma], which belong to the section concerning Soma."

Regarding the question "How is it applied?", having proposed the thesis that it is applied by means of an objective reference (uddeśa) delimited by a form distinct from the clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth— thereby rendering the requirement satisfied according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*)— the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) as its opposite,
beginning with the word "tatra."

[Objection: Since there is an injunction of substances and so forth with reference to a sacrifice characterized by a specific generic quality (*vaijātya*) established by its capacity to produce a result, and since there is no evidence that such a sacrifice—characterized by that specific generic quality—can arise without a refinement (*saṃskāra*) applied to that substance, there is no risk of futility (*anarthakya*) even if [the injunction] is for the sake of the rice-grains (*vrīhi*). To this, he says:
"Therefore, [this is discussed] in the ninth [book]."

In order to establish the status of the injunctions regarding substances such as *vrīhi* rice as restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*), it must first be shown that there is a possibility of their application. Since even distinct instances of sacrifices of a different class (*vijātīya-yāga*) are included within the category of "sacrifice" (*yāgatva*) which pervades them all, and since there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) preventing the production of a sacrifice of a different class even without another substance, the production of such a sacrifice must necessarily be admitted. Consequently, when such a sacrifice is produced, there is an even greater requirement for its refinement (*saṃskāra*).
Since the lack of purpose remains in the same state due to the absence of any other means of knowledge (*māna*), the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being a means to the *apūrva* is necessary.

At that time, because it is understood from the word-meaning that [the substance] produces [the result] with respect to the *apūrva* which serves as its qualifier, and since there is no evidence for the production of that *apūrva*, which is of the nature of an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), without the prescribed purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), the avoidance of pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) is impossible; therefore, such a status of being a means to the *apūrva* constitutes a component of the offering substance (*pradeya*).
Since the nature that is to be characterized exists in barley as well as in clarified butter and so forth, the meaning is that *dharmas* pertain to all things.

[Objection: But even if there is a figurative indication (*lak�śaṇā*) based on being a means to the *apūrva*, since it is more appropriate to indicate precisely that which is a means to the intermediate *apūrva* of the Āgneya sacrifice—due to its proximity by virtue of being produced from rice (*vrīhi*)—then [the rule] would not apply to clarified butter (*ājya*) and the like, which are not means to that [intermediate *apūrva*]. To this, he says: "In that case, [it is] the result... etc.

The meaning is as follows: because proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is common to both the *āgnīṣomīya* and *aindrāgna* sacrifices—just as it is to the *āgneya* sacrifice—their status as means to that same *apūrva* must also be indicated by implication (*lakṣaṇīyatva*).

Since there is no single property (*dharma*) inherent in all three that could serve as a basis for activity, it is impossible to indicate them through a specific qualification as means to a subordinate *apūrva*.

Therefore, because they are equally proximate to the fruit, the confusion of ritual properties (*dharmasaṃkara*) is unavoidable, as they must be indicated by implication solely as means to the *apūrva* of the final fruit which is common to all.

Since the restriction of speech (*vāṅniyama*) prescribed with reference to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice lacks the status of being a means to the *apūrva* of the Jyotiṣṭoma, it cannot be indicated by the word *dīkṣaṇīyā*. Therefore, because this would result in a "metaphor of the metaphorized" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*)— whereby the word *dīkṣaṇīyā* would first indicate its own produced *apūrva* as a means, and then indicate [through that] the status of being a means to the Jyotiṣṭoma *apūrva* produced by it— it is not accepted that the restriction has that [Jyotiṣṭoma *apūrva*] as its purpose.
Moreover, [the use of *vrīhi*] is indeed for the sake of the intermediate *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice;

however, in the case of the archetype (*prakṛti*), since the quality of being produced by a sacrifice made of *vrīhi* grains exists even in the ultimate *apūrva*, it is appropriate to understand the term *vrīhi* as a mere indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of that [ultimate *apūrva*]. Intending to state this difference—that it is not for the sake of the intermediate *apūrva*—he says:
"For this very reason."
Regarding the phrase "because its object is perceived":
Even though threshing has the transcendental (*apūrva*) as its purpose, it serves that purpose only by means of a visible purpose residing in the rice-grains which are its instrument;

thus, while it has the rice-grains as its object, it has the visible purpose of dehusking (*vaituṣya*) as its objective in one part and the invisible purpose in another part such as the clarified butter (*ājya*), resulting in this dual nature (*vairūpya*).

Likewise, if it were for the sake of dehusking, the injunction for threshing would be a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*); however, if it were for the sake of the invisible purpose, it would be an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).

The meaning is as follows: since there would be the fault of inconsistency (*vairūpya*), and because it is more parsimonious to rely on uniformity (*ekarūpya*) in order to avoid that fault, and in accordance with the principle that a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) must have a visible purpose, it is proper to characterize [the property] as belonging to the substance itself—namely, the medicinal substance—as being the means for producing the *apūrva*.
Thus, it is logical that it possesses those very properties.

[Objection: Is it not the case that accepting a diversity of forms (*vairūpya*) in accordance with an injunction that applies without distinction is not a fault, just as accepting an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) is accepted everywhere? To this, he says: "How much more so..."—by way of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), because the referent denoted by the word *vrīhi* (rice), such as rice-grains and the like, first accomplishes the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) through the production of rice-grains, and thus serves as the means for the *utpattyapūrva* (the originative apūrva); therefore, since there is no reason to bypass that, whatever apūrva is to be accomplished by rice and the like [is what is meant].
The meaning is that only its being a means to that [result] is the object of indication (*lakṣya*) by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*).

If, somehow, the avoidance of purposelessness (*ānarthakya*) could not be achieved through the indication of its being a means to that, then, as a last resort, one would have to abandon that and indicate the state of being a means to the ultimate transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*), even though it is remote (*viprakṛṣṭa*).
This is not the case;
for since that [word] also has its specific mode of application unknown, it is possible to avoid its pointlessness even when it serves that purpose. Thus he says: "tasyāpi" (of that too).

For this very reason, in cases where— in the archetype (prakṛti)— the accomplishment of the *apūrva* is determined to be independent of the seventeen-cubit length and so forth, such as in the case of the animal-sacrifice *apūrva*, it is accepted that even by transgressing those [measurements], there is an indirect (*paramparayā*) status of being the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the *vājapeya-apūrva*.

However, since that is absent in the present case (the *vrīhi* rule), the sense is that— out of parsimony (*lāghava*) and in accordance with proximity and possible connection— the definition is simply "being the substratum of the instrumentality consisting in the operation whose nature is the production of rice-grains that constitute the offering-material (*pradeya*), which is related to the means of accomplishing the *utpattyapūrva* of the Āgneya sacrifice, and which is co-locative (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the state of being *vrīhi*."
He demonstrates a type of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) by incorporating the status of being a means for various intermediate operations; this is indicated by the words "ataḥ" (hence).

The phrase "consisting of the material to be offered" (*pradeyaprakṛtibhūta*) is stated in order to exclude the operation [of the verb] upon the form of the flour; for that [flour], being something to be offered, lacks the status of being the material cause (*prakṛti*) of that [offering].
For just as *āmikṣā* is not a different substance from the milk, [so too the flour is not distinct from the offering].
But it is merely milk that has reached a state of thickening,
or just as a ball of barley meal is merely barley meal itself and not a different entity.
The contact with water and so forth is merely an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) for the state of being a lump;
likewise, although the contact with water, fire, and so on is an instrumental cause with respect to the lump, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is not a different entity from the flour,
but is merely the state of being a lump.
Therefore, since it has rice (*taṇḍula*) as its material cause (*prakṛti*), flour (*piṣṭa*) does not intervene in the process.

For this very reason, even though in the *caru* oblation—which takes the place of the *puroḍāśa* cake—there is an absence of flour as the material cause, there is no obstruction to the application of the ritual rules (*dharma*) precisely because it has rice as its material cause.
Although where flour itself is the substance to be offered, the application of the rules by virtue of having rice as the material cause would be unavoidable; [yet such is not the case here].

Nevertheless, although there is the possibility of taking already prepared sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and the like everywhere according to the principle of the *anovāsa* (the [unprepared] vessel) case, since it is necessary to produce them in the middle of the performance— because otherwise the injunction for cooking within the performance would be inexplicable— and because the rule for the specific materials is prescribed only when those materials are taken up right there, the ritual properties (*dharma*) are enjoined only with respect to such materials that are thus being restricted.

However, in cases where the material to be offered—such as a lump of rice—is not subject to cooking (*śrapaṇa*), since the cooking that brings about the cooked lump denoted by terms such as *puroḍāśa* is absent, it is appropriate to omit it (just as grinding is omitted). Consequently, one employs ordinary flour or rice, like [ordinary] firewood or cloth;

thus, just as with the rice grains themselves, there is no taking up of rice grains during the course of the ritual performance, nor is there a restriction regarding rice as the raw material (*prakṛti*). Therefore, the properties of that [rice] do not apply.

Therefore, the meaning of the sentence "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*) is that these are injunctions of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra-vidhi*) solely for the purpose of the sacrifice which is the means to the *apūrva*, by way of the operation of the rice-grains (*taṇḍula*) which constitute the material substance of what is to be offered.
More on this should be seen in the *Kaustubha*.

Now, one might object: "If the instrumentalities (*sādhanatā*) qualified by specific operations such as being *āgneya* or being *vrīhi* are what are introduced [into the definition], then since those instrumentalities qualified by those respective properties do not exist in the *saurya* sacrifice and others, how can there be the attainment of a property in the substrata of instrumentalities qualified by a different property? To this, he says: "tadvyāpāraka... (qualified by that operation).
To the extent that something must be included because without it the avoidance of meaninglessness cannot be achieved, that much may be included by necessity.

However, since the avoidance of that [meaninglessness] can be accomplished here simply by including the mere status of being a means (*sādhanatāmātra*), there is no inclusion of its delimiters such as *vrīhitva* (the nature of rice), due to the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*).
Nor does this lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Since this much alone is possible even for the *vāraṇa* [rice], the meaning is that in the case of the *naivāra* sacrificial porridge and in the case of *yava* [barley], the application of the ritual properties (*dharma*) occurs without deficiency.

Now, one might object: since rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*) differ in their causal status due to being distinct words or having different qualities, how can the ritual properties (*dharma*) apply to barley when it lacks the status of being a substratum for the instrumentality that effects the production of rice-grains? For this very reason, even though in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) wild rice (*nīvāra*) acquires the properties through extension (*atideśa*)—because its instrumental role takes over the function of the original material (*prakṛta*)—such acquisition of properties would be impossible in the case of the primary sacrifice (*prakṛti*), where that [instrumentality] is absent.
To explain how that is attained, he says: "And just as... (yathāca).

Just as, when the avoidance of meaninglessness is achieved by intending to express merely the state of being a means (*sādhanatā*), there is no intention to express the delimitant of that state of being a means due to the resulting complexity (*gaurava*); so too, since the avoidance of that [meaninglessness] is equally possible by intending the general state of being a means, there is likewise no intention to express a specific state of being a means— whether it has entered [the definition] as a "capable relation" (*śakyasambandha*)— in either the delimitant of the indicated object (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) or the delimitant of the subject of the enunciation (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*).

Alternatively, the inclusion [of barley] due to its gravity is justified by the intention to express that it serves as a substratum for the general property of being a means [to the sacrifice]; thus, the attainment of ritual properties (dharma) applies to barley but not to clarified butter and the like—this is the meaning, as explained in detail in the Kaustubha.
Thus ends the fourth section concerning the fixed scope of the offerings and other rites.
(B1) (Section 5 / ) (A.3 Pā.1 Adh.5) Substance.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, after enumerating ten substances— namely, "the wooden sword (sphya) and the potsherds (kapālāni)"— by means of the scriptural statement, "These indeed are the ten sacrificial implements (yajñāyudhāni)," all ten substances are enjoined as instruments for the sacrifice; consequently, by virtue of being enjoined at the very origin (utpatti-śiṣṭa), they exclude the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) and other such items.

And since it is impossible for [the substance] to be a direct means of accomplishing the sacrifice, [the injunctions] apply to the subsidiaries; therefore, substances are enjoined with reference to those actions that are capable of being performed and which require a substance as a means for accomplishing the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the context. As for specific applications such as "he digs with a wooden shovel" (*sphyenoddhanti*), these are restatements by way of partial extraction (*avayutya-anuvāda*). This being the position reached—by that and that...

Since the implements such as the *sphya* are specifically enjoined by a perceptible injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*) assisted by a third-person scriptural statement (*tṛtīyāśruti*), the sentence concerning the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudhavākya*) alone is that which lacks an explicit injunction;
it is merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*) connected with the word "verily" (*vai*),
because multiple restatements would otherwise be purposeless.

And because the statement "and its sacrificial implements come into being" possesses purpose as an explanatory supplement (arthavāda) to an injunction, the word *uddhanana* (digging up) indicates, by way of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), the status of being a means for the primary transcendental result (*apūrva*) produced by the operation consisting solely of digging up; and it is with reference to that very [result] that the injunction of the wooden sword (*sphya*) and other implements is established. // 3 // 5 //
Thus ends the fifth section concerning the application [of mantras] based on Vedic injunction.

(B2) Having commenced from the previous section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*), and having— within three sections— the mode of application (*viniyoga*) to be determined by defining the delimiters of the objective status (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) of purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*), substances (*dravya*), and qualities (*guṇa*), [the author] first defined, in the previous section, the mode of application effected by the hearing of the accusative case (*dvitīyāśruti*), because it is primary as it conveys the objective status that constitutes "being for the sake of another" (*pārārthya*). Now,
in order to define the mode of application effected by the hearing of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyāśruti*) regarding substances, he provides an illustration.
—Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

In order to restrict [the application] to all materials suitable for the context and to indicate the status of being a means to the *apūrva* (unprecedented result), the phrase "of the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsayoḥ*) was stated.

By means of the particle *iti*, which has the sense of "beginning with," there is an inclusion of everything up to the passage: "The *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle, the winnowing basket, the black antelope skin, the *śamyā* peg, the mortar, the pestle, the grinding stone, and the lower millstone.

Thus, even though implements such as the wooden sword (*sphya*) are enjoined by rules such as "he digs with the wooden sword" (*sphyenoddhanti*) and are consequently assigned to tasks like digging, this serves to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the previously mentioned definition.

Intending to begin again with the aim of dispelling the specific doubt that— even though there is no evidence for [the primary sense]— there is no obstacle to a metaphorical sense characterized as the instrumentality of an operation produced by mere rice, since the statement regarding the "sacrificial implements" exists here as a factor determining the intended meaning (tātparya)— he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): "Of all ten as well..."

Although this [word *eva*] is connected with the particle *vai*, because its meaning is not already established, it is stated to be injunctive (*vidhāyaka*) with the intention that it functions as such by supplying a word expressing "that which is to be done" (*kartavyatā*).

Although the word *āyudha* denotes an instrument of war, because it conforms to the word *yajña*, it is stated to mean "as an instrument" (*sādhanatvena*) through a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) whose scope is limited to instruments in general.
Regarding the phrase "with the wooden sword he digs," etc., the word "etc. includes such passages as "he cooks on the potsherds" and "he pours out the oblations with the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle."
