This is a summary of the sequence ending with: "He sifts with a winnowing basket; he spreads the black antelope skin beneath the mortar; he places the wedge under the grinding stone; he threshes with the mortar and pestle; he grinds with the grinding stone and muller.
The rest is self-evident in meaning.

Since the universal applicability of the *sphya* and other implements has been refuted here, and they are again refuted in the fourth [section] after their status as things to be offered (*pradeya*) was raised, there is no contradiction.

One should understand that the statement regarding "in both cases" refers to the fact that the sentence concerning the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*) is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), as established in the *Audumbara* section; it is thus a restatement (*anuvāda*).
The practical purpose (*prayojana*) is not stated because it is obvious.
Thus ends the fifth section concerning the application [of mantras] based on direct Vedic injunction (śrauta-viniyoga).
(B1) (6th Adhikaraṇa /) (A.3 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 6) When there is unity of purpose.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "One purchases Soma with a red, one-year-old, yellow-eyed [cow].
In this context, the word *aruṇā* denotes either the quality of redness or the genus of redness, but it does not denote a specific individual [cow].
Furthermore, by means of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), the status of being an instrument is expressed only for that which is capable [of performing the action].
However, there is no indication of the substance (*dravya*) for that purpose [of expressing gender];
rather, the meaning of the feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* is also construed with that very same [substance] through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*),
and there is no indication of an individual (*vyakti*) even for the sake of that [gender].
Otherwise, the fault of non-comprehension would arise.

Furthermore, how the grammatical rule—"the gender and number of words denoting qualities (guṇavacana) follow those of their substratum" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.67)—is justified under this view should be seen in the Kaustubha.

As for words such as *ekahāyanī* ("one-year-old [cow]"), the ancients maintain that because they are *bahuvrīhi* compounds, their denotative power (*śakti*) resides solely in the substance (*dravya*), which consists of the external referent qualified by the meanings of its constituent parts.
Many, however, maintain that there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of both words in the sense of another word (*anyapadārtha*).
Nor should it be argued that—given that the substance can be enjoined by one word alone—it is impossible for it to be enjoined by the other, and thus the latter would be redundant;
for since both words function simultaneously, there is no instance of enjoining what has already been enjoined (*vihitavidhāna*).
Furthermore, it possesses purposefulness because it refers to another quality (*guṇāntara*).
Moreover, one can argue here as well that even indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not [necessary], according to the principle of the redness (*āruṇya-nyāya*);
for the grammatical rule governing compounds (*samāsa-anuśāsana*) is justifiable in the same way as the rules governing suffixes such as *matup*.

Furthermore, the establishment of the connection between a substance and its secondary qualities (*pārṣṭhaka-guṇa*) must be established by taking recourse to a substance cognized through another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Therefore, in this case, although redness (*āruṇya*) is capable [of connection], it cannot be connected to the substance and so forth mentioned in the sentence because its status as a factor of action (*kārakatva*) is not yet established;

and even if that were established, being incorporeal (*amūrta*), it cannot be connected to the action mentioned in the sentence. Consequently, being thus separated [from the sentence], it is [connected] by means of that which is produced from a part of the text—either directly heard or inferred—constructed through the context (*prakaraṇa*).

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, according to the principle of the *Ākara*—namely, "by means of the sentence, one should effect the delimitation of the substance that serves as the means for the *apūrva* under discussion"—redness (*āruṇya*) is an auxiliary to all substances mentioned in the context.

[Reply: This is not so. It is not the cognition of fitness (*yogyatā*) that is the cause of verbal comprehension; rather, it is merely that the ascertainment of unfitness (*ayogyatā-niścaya*) acts as an obstacle.
Therefore, since the absence of this obstructive factor exists, the comprehension of redness as being connected with the action is indeed possible.

Furthermore, since the subsequent search for compatibility establishes that redness (*āruṇya*) can indeed relate to the substance [of the purchase] as its secondary correlate (*pārṣṭika*), there is no fear of its being severed from it.

For this very reason, after the initial injunction of the *bhāvanā* qualified by all the factors (*kāraka*s) such as the purchase of Soma and redness, at the time when the purchase is connected with Soma, the triad beginning with redness is understood to be related to the purchase through the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*); subsequently, three separate injunctions of the qualifiers are postulated.

Once it has been understood that these two are auxiliary to the purchase (*kraya*), and subsequently there arises a requirement for a substance and other factors to serve as their delimiters, one should observe that the relationship between *aruṇā* (red) and *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) consists merely of a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) and a connection with a specific substance.
Consequently, it is logical that the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) finds its place only in the one-year-old cow that serves as the means of purchase.
But this does not apply to other substances for purchase, such as garments and the like;
nor is there any suspicion of their inclusion because they are equally substances for purchase used as means for obtaining Soma— as in the case of barley—
since those [other items] serve as materials for a different act of purchase.
In this case, the purchases are distinct on account of their qualities.
Furthermore, when there is an obstruction by a substance prescribed for the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa-dravya*), it is not possible for another substance to be introduced,
because the seller must be secured as one who is restricted to a single substance.
Otherwise, there would result the undesirable consequence that even the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) would be subject to sublation.
Nor can the statement "he buys with ten" alone be taken as indicating the intent for insertion [of the number];

for since that statement can also be explained as referring to the combination of purchases, it cannot serve to set aside the distinction established by the principle of subordinate elements (*guṇanyāya*).

Nor, even though there is a difference in the acts of purchase, can there be any suspicion that redness (*āruṇya*) might apply to the substance of another purchase, because there is no distinction in their common purpose of obtaining a single *soma* plant. This is because the qualifying injunction—which is inferred from the otherwise inexplicable nature of the injunction for a distinct type of purchase characterized by redness—must be postulated as having a posterior connection (*pārṣṭhikānvaya*) that does not lead to over-extension; thus, it applies only to the specific nature of that distinct type of purchase which produces the same non-distinct result.

Or rather, since there is no possibility of suspecting an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) on the grounds that [the term] is intended [to apply to all], and since this being the case, its application to a three-year-old steer (trivatsa) which has taken the place of all substances used for purchase is to be seen in the *Kaustubha*. // 3 // 6 //
Thus ends the sixth section concerning the dawn (aruṇādhikaraṇa).
(B2) Having previously examined the manner of application regarding substances, he now provides an illustration to examine that same matter regarding qualities: "The Jyotiṣṭoma."
As before, it was stated that "the Jyotiṣṭoma" is mentioned because it serves as the basis for establishing the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).

To refute the impossibility of the prima facie view—which would arise if the word *aruṇā* were taken to refer to a substance, since a substance could then logically connect with the verb "buys" (*krīṇāti*)—he establishes that it is an expression of a quality (*guṇavacana*), stating: "In that case... (*tatra*).

In that regard, according to the view that individual red things are distinct, the meaning is "denoting the quality of redness," and not "denoting a qualified individual"; this is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the application of the principle established in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*.

In this regard, the ancient teachers [hold that] since words such as *aruṇā* (red) denote only a quality, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—as in "the jar is red" (*aruṇo ghaṭaḥ*)—would be untenable, just as it is in the case of "Devadatta is white" (*śuklo devadattaḥ*). Furthermore, just as in the expression "the jar has color" (*rūpavān ghaṭaḥ*), coreferentiality would only be possible by means of a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*).

Therefore, according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, even words denoting qualities like *aruṇā* have reference to the substance (*dravya*) through conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*).

Therefore, it has been stated that there is no possibility of the application [of the suffix] because of the rule "the elision of *matup* is desired after words expressing qualities" (*guṇavacanebhyo matupo lugiṣṭa*);

however, that is not correct. Since the absence of usage makes a contemporary (or ad hoc) secondary signification (*sāṃpratikī lakṣaṇā*) untenable, a conventionalized secondary signification (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) is all the more untenable.
As it is said in the *Vārttika*: "Some [words] have conventionalized secondary significations by virtue of their capacity, like primary denotations."
"Currently, some [rites] are performed and some are not at all due to incapacity.
Thus [it is said].

Therefore, even if [words like *śukla*] denote a qualified substance, just as they denote that [substance] while words such as *rūpa* do not— because the latter are never used in that way— so too, even when they denote the quality alone, it is logical to restrict the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the substance to those very [words] and not to others. Thus, through indication with respect to the substance, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established, and there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

For this very reason, when [a word] denotes a quality (*guṇavacana*), it possesses the masculine gender; whereas when it denotes a substance (*dravyavacana*), it takes the gender and number of its substratum (*āśraya*). This is consistent with another grammatical rule which states: "The gender and number of words denoting qualities are determined by their substratum.

Furthermore, the term "denoting a quality" (*guṇavacanatva*) should be understood as referring to the fact that the quality is the primary object of denotation (*śakya*) by virtue of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Indicating that it is incorrect to state that the word *aruṇā* refers to a substance (*dravya*), [the author] demonstrates the lack of purpose in accepting that view by means of the instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyayā*).

The meaning is this: Is it because the connection with the status of being an instrument (karaṇatva) is untenable that [the word] must have substance as its referent, or is it because the connection with gender and number is untenable?

It is not the first; for, just as in the case of a universal (jāti), the connection is possible in the case of a quality (guṇa) as well—by means of delimiting the substance—and thus there is no such untenability.

Therefore, it has been stated in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* that the metaphorical application (*lakṣaṇā*) of those [terms] occurs only in cases where it is impossible for the status of being an object (*karmatva*)— defined as possessing a fruit produced by an action— and the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*)— defined as being the intended goal of that [action]— to reside in the rice or the Brahmin; but not in instances such as those involving words ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*).

Not the latter [alternative]; for, since that [instrumentality] can be accounted for either as a mere grammatical correctness (*sādhutvamātra*) or as residing in the substratum (*āśrayaniṣṭhatā*) according to the principle of the section on *pāśa* (Pāśādhikaraṇanyāya), there is no evidence for metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

For this very reason, since the cognition of the substance (*dravya*) is established even when those two [the stem and the suffix] function as instruments through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), or when they are construed with the meaning of the nominal stem itself—either as a mode of relation (*saṃsargavidhayā*) or as a subsequent state (*pārṣṭhikabhāva*)—there is no need for metaphorical indication here in the case of the third-case ending, whereas it would be necessary in cases such as the second case.

If such a case as this were also admitted to possess that definition [of *lakṣaṇā*], then, because the quality would have to be construed with the substance which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), that substance—being qualified by that quality—would be corporeal; consequently, like the "one-year-old cow" (*ekahāyanī*) and other examples, it could be logically included in the act of purchase itself through a relation of non-difference obtained via a subsequent connection (*pārṣṭhikānvaya*). On the contrary, this would require an excessive dependence upon the observation of the multiple words being compounded and their coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Because [the word *soma*] is a proper name (*vilambitatvāt*), it cannot be a prescription for a substance; rather, it follows that a prescription for a substance must occur through a word denoting a quality (*guṇaśabda*) alone. Consequently, while it would be logical for the substance to be introduced as the means of purchase, since a quality—being incorporeal (*amūrtatayā*)—cannot be introduced as the means of purchase, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the quality is merely introduced as any suitable factor of action (*kāraka*) within the context becomes untenable. Thus, the commencement of this section (*adhikaraṇa*) to resolve that difficulty, as well as the demonstration in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the quality itself serves as the instrument (*karaṇatva*) by way of delimiting the substance, would result in redundancy.

Likewise, if words such as "four" and so forth were also understood as referring to a handful qualified by a number, then even the least significant handful would become the primary element, resulting in the necessity of conforming to it;

consequently, the support of the number in the *caru* offering of seventeen *śarāva*-measures—which will be discussed later—would not be possible because of its primacy. Therefore, these words must refer solely to the quality [the number] itself.
Because it would otherwise result in the impossibility of linguistic derivation.

The meaning is that by abandoning the established grammatical usage (*vyutpanna*)— where gender, number, and so forth, are construed with the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), the case-role (*kāraka*), or the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) through the relation of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)— and instead accepting their construction with the substance (*dravya*), one would incur the fault of postulating a new linguistic rule (*vyutpattyantara*) for the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the substance.

[Objection: But if [words like *śukla*] denote only the quality (*guṇa*), how is the validity of the two grammatical rules established—namely, "the elision of the suffix *matup* is desired after words denoting qualities" and "for words denoting qualities, [the gender and number] depend on the substratum" (*guṇavacanānām āśrayato liṅgavacanāni*)?

For in that case, since the term "quality-denoting" (*guṇavacana*) must necessarily refer to those words such as *śukla* which express a quality while having the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) as their primary meaning, [the objection stands]. To this, he says: "And just as in this way...
This means that the first rule is intended for those cases where the application of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would otherwise be required.

In the second [interpretation], a word denoting a quality (*guṇa-pada*) is that which signifies a quality as the qualifier (*prakāra*) in a relation with an individual (*vyakti*), provided that such a relation is capable of being expressed through the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the word's own possible meaning. It is for this very reason that the term *guṇavacana* is employed in the grammatical rule. Thus, the justification for both grammatical injunctions is established. In this context, if one intended to include only the requirement of "capability" (*yogya*), then even in cases such as *ajāyāḥ śuklaḥ* ("the white [cloth] of the goat"), there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* and so forth.
Even though that [word] lacks denotative power (*lakṣakatva*) at that time, its fitness (*yogyatva*) exists—just like a staff standing in a forest;
therefore, the word "concomitance" (*anvaya*) is used to exclude that [fitness].

For this very reason, in that case, even when the gender residing in the substratum is absent, the masculine gender alone is prescribed for the sake of grammatical correctness by the rule: *agaṇe śuklādayaḥ puṃsi*.
In expressions such as "rūpam asti" (color exists), the first [type of quality] is [the one intended], because the substance does not enter into the relation as a qualifier (*prakāra*).
This is because, in that case, there is an absence of such fitness (*yogyatā*).
Consequently, even in the absence of a lakṣaṇā for the individual, the quality functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*) by means of delimiting the gender and substance.

The meaning is that since the suffix *ṭāp* and others arise precisely because [the word] refers to a female, it should be understood from the *Kaustubha* that the word *aruṇā* here denotes only a quality (*guṇa*).
Furthermore, this should be understood as having the sole purpose of refuting the distinction between the words *aruṇā* and *ekahāyanī* as stated by the ancient commentators.

In reality, however, in the case of "pacati" (he cooks), since the singularity [of the agent] is construed with the *bhāvanā* through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and because there arises a necessity for a cognition of the subject qualified by the property that delimits its locus— namely, the doubt as to whether the agent denoted by "pacati" is one or not— the venerable masters have stated that figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) applies there.
Similarly here as well, for the purpose of dispelling the doubt arising from the word *aruṇā*, a definition of substance (*dravya*) is indeed necessary.

Even with that much, since the substance is obtained [as the means] by virtue of being the instrument (*karaṇa*), it is necessary that the quality (*guṇa*), which is the qualifying portion, alone be the instrument.

Having thus established that the quality cannot be connected to the action because it is incorporeal (*amūrta*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) proceeds; and this is no different even in the case of the words *ekahāyanī* and so forth.
Thus it should be meditated upon.

As for what was stated in the Somanāthīya— that if the word *aruṇā* were intended to denote the universal (*jāti*) of redness, then although it could denote the quality through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) because a relation of inherence (*samavāya*) with that quality is possible, nevertheless, since such a relation is absent in the case of the substance, the indication of the individual would be untenable, and thus grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word denoting the substance would be impossible—
that is not convincing.

In the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "the blue pot," just as the word "blue" has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for the individual instance of the word "blue" through the relation of being conjoined with the substance that is the substratum of the blue color, so too here, since it is the same, the word denoting the universal (*jāti*) can also be justified by secondary signification through the relation of inherence in its own substratum.

For this very reason, since the universal "blue-ness" (nīlarūpatva-jāti), which exists through inherence (samavāya) in the cognition "this is a blue form," is accepted as the ground for the application [of the term], and since there is no obstacle to accepting that same universal in a jar and so forth through a mediated relation (paraṃparā-sambandha), the usage [of the term] is justified by its primary sense (mukhyayā vṛttyā); thus it has been established in the *Nakṣatravādāvalī* by the preeminent Mīmāṃsaka.
In that case, what fault is there in resorting to indication (*lakṣaṇā*) through a mediated connection? This is the general direction [of the argument].

In this sūtra, because of the inclusion of the phrase "due to the single function of substance and quality," it is necessary to establish that words such as *piṅgākṣī* (the tawny-eyed one) refer to the substance itself.

Just as with the possessive suffix (*matup*), since the intermediate relation is established through the denotation of the substance by the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself, and since [denoting the substance] is obtainable from another source, one does not postulate a separate expressive power (*śakti*) for it; rather, the reference to the substance is accepted for the *bahuvrīhi* just as it is for the possessive suffix.
As it has been stated in the *Vārttika*: "In all cases, it is the substance itself that is denoted by derivative (*yaugika*) words;
for it is not possible for the relation to be the expressed meaning, as that would entail excessive complexity (*atigaurava*).

Even in such instances as "the owner of brindled cows" (*citragu*), because the words *citra* and *go* denote meanings that are entirely distinct [from the possessor], [they require] words such as "Devadatta" [to express the connection].

Because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be impossible, and because even prior to [the application of] words such as "Devadatta," there is no possibility of the meaning of another word being the sentence-meaning—since it is already perceived—the word itself must have expressive power (*śakti*) with respect to the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*). In the view that this is based on indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since there is no difference between the *bahuvrīhi* compound and the word "red" (*aruṇa*) in their shared capacity to indirectly indicate the substance through an intervening factor, what would be the determining criterion (*vinigamaka*) for why the *bahuvrīhi* alone denotes the substance and not the word "red"? Therefore, there is expressive power in the meaning of another word.

Nor should it be asked: "How is it that [the objection] does not apply to the *indrapīta* word in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the defect of implying a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for another referent in a *bahuvrīhi* compound does not arise, and thus weakness relative to a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound is impossible? For although there is parity in both the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* and the *bahuvrīhi* regarding the connection of one [word] with the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) and with the meaning of the entire sentence, they differ in that in the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* there is the abandonment of only one [element], whereas in the *bahuvrīhi* there is the abandonment of both; thus, its weakness relative to the former is established.

By this, the following objection is also refuted: "If the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) were the primary denotation (*śakyatva*) in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, then—due to the parsimony resulting from the absence of the need for a separate application of Vedic knowledge—one would have to abandon the *karmadhāraya* interpretation of the term *niṣādasthapati* and instead resort to a *bahuvrīhi*.
For in a *karmadhāraya*, all the word-meanings as they are heard in the text are directly connected to the sentence-meaning.
Because weakness [of the *bahuvrīhi*] is established merely by the disparity that in a *bahuvrīhi*, each member is connected [to the head word] individually, therefore—
even though the analytical derivation (*vigraha*) "one whose cows are variegated" is well-known in common usage—

nevertheless, in the case of a genitive *tatpuruṣa* such as *rājapuruṣaḥ*, the status of being a subordinate element (*upasarjanatva*) belongs to the meaning expressed by the genitive-ending term with respect to the meaning expressed by the nominative-ending term.

He states the opinion of the ancients—that words such as *ekahāyanī* denote a substance (*dravya*)—on the grounds that if the analysis were "this belongs to the brindled cows" (*citrāṇāṃ gavām ayam*), it would result in the brindled cows themselves being the primary referent (as they are indicated by the nominative case), thereby destroying the perception of the primacy of the substance which constitutes the meaning of the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*). He says: "In the case of *ekahāyanī* and so forth... [The full argument is as follows: Just as in the case of [the word] *pradhāna*, if one were to analyze [the bahuvrīhi] as "this is of the brindled cows," the brindled cows—being indicated by the nominative case—would attain primacy. Consequently, there would be a collapse of the understanding of the primacy of the substance that constitutes the meaning of the other member of the compound. Therefore, because the power of the "other-member-meaning" (*anyapadārtha*) lies in the analysis "this belongs to the brindled cows," and because words such as *ekahāyanī* function as bahuvrīhis, they have the substance as their primary referent; this is the view of the ancients. Thus he says: "In the case of *ekahāyanī* and so forth..."

In cases such as compounds (kṛt) and secondary derivatives (taddhita), since one [element] establishes the implication of the other, the postulation of multiple powers is avoided; for in common worldly usage, it is observed that the subordinate element is implied by the principal one alone. Since a substance (dravya) capable of being connected with gender and number is what is denoted by the term "sattva" (being), the power resides in that [substance] alone by virtue of its primacy, and not in the relationship which has become a qualifier, because the manifestation of that [relationship] is established through implication alone.

Therefore, since the primacy of the genus (*jāti*) is observed in instances where it appears at the end of a third-case suffix, and the primacy of the individual (*vyakti*) is observed in instances where it appears at the end of a second-case suffix, and since there is no restrictive factor [to the contrary], the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* applies; thus, the genus alone is the denoted meaning (*vācyatva*), while the individual is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*).
Furthermore, verbal derivatives (*kṛdanta*) and the like do not have their expressive power (*śakti*) in the qualifier, but rather in the substance (*dravya*) itself.

Therefore, even the Vārttika stating "everywhere" (sarvatra) is intended to refute the expressive power of relations and so forth acting as qualifiers only in such contexts; it refers specifically to those cases where, in the realm of derivative (yaugika) words, there exists another denotative element such as a kṛt suffix.

However, in cases such as *bahuvrīhi* compounds where there exists another non-denotative element, since it is possible to account for the meaning through conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*)— as in the case of "Bring in the staff-bearers" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*), where the two words themselves indicate either the external referent qualified by their own meanings or the external referent alone— there is no evidence for postulating an additional denotative power (*śakti*);
for that which cannot be obtained otherwise is what constitutes the word-meaning.

Therefore, even in cases such as *udbhid* and *adhunā*, where there is elision (*lopa*) of both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), it is accepted that the remaining portion indicates that very meaning; however, no additional denotative power (*śakti*) is postulated.

Nor does it follow that, because a *bahuvrīhi* lacks the capacity to denote a meaning external to its constituent members (*anyapadārtha*), there would be no distinction from the word *aruṇā*, resulting in the untenability of the mention "of substance and quality" (*dravyaguṇayoḥ*) in the Sūtra;
for in our view, the distinction is established precisely by the presence or absence of conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*).
And thus, since metaphorical indication is accepted in both words, the weakness of the *bahuvrīhi*—and even more so its weakness compared to the *karmadhāraya*—is firmly established.

For this very reason, in the *Aindrāpītādhikaraṇa*, while demonstrating the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the necessity of resorting to an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) within a *bahuvrīhi* compound was shown;

yet, even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), without stating a resolution based on primary denotation (*śakti*), he states another view—highly favored by the Naiyāyikas and others—as a refutation of the prima facie position, which consists merely in pointing out the necessity of indicating a part of that [compound] by the word *indrapīta*, which denotes the aggregate of what has been offered and what has not been offered: "As for what was said by the authors of the *Prakāśa* regarding the 'meaning of another word'..."

Since, if there were a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the meaning of another word in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, that same [indication] would apply even to words such as *paṅkaja* ("lotus"), which would lead to the undesirable consequence of the destruction of the theory of "etymological-technical" (*yogarūḍhi*) power, it has been stated that here too there is indeed primary denotative power (*śakti*). The refutation of that [opposing view] is to be found in the *Kaustubha*.

In reality, however—just as in the case of the word *aruṇā* (red)—the words *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old female) and others also denote the qualifiers in the form of "one year old" and so forth, according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*; for even that [quality], like redness, can logically function as an instrument by means of delimiting the substance.

Therefore, in cases such as those where a word ending in the accusative occurs and that [instrumentality] is impossible, the rule for the *bahuvrīhi* compound—just like the rule for the *matup* suffix—is intended precisely for that purpose; thus, neither a primary denotative power (*śakti*) nor a secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) need be admitted with respect to the substance.

Intending to show that the word "substance" (*dravya*) found in the Sūtra is also logically tenable because it establishes a subsequent relationship with a substance already cognized by another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he states his own preferred alternative position, beginning with the words "But it is possible...
and "cognized by another means of valid knowledge."
The meaning is: "having taken the substance in the form of a cow, as understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, 'He buys it with a cow'."
And on this view, the sense is that since there is no distinction in their lack of corporeality, all [entities] without exception are objects of investigation.

Having thus established what is relevant to the present inquiry, [the author argues that] because the knowledge of semantic competency (*yogyatājñāna*) is a cause for [the arising of] verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) as delimited by the property of being a verbal cognition,

and because the incorporeal quality of redness (*āruṇya*) is unfit for connection with the productive urge of purchase (*krayabhāvanā*), it is not included therein. Consequently, setting aside the syntactic connection (*vākyīyānvaya*) on the grounds of such incompatibility,

the sūtra— "But that which is enjoined should be a property of all, because of the specific connection and because there is no distinction in the context"— is treated as the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) sūtra for the section concerning the purpose (*arthādhikaraṇa*).

Having relied upon the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that all substances are the primary meaning in the context of the *Prakaraṇa*, he refutes the possibility of a syntactic connection with a substance by way of its fitness, stating: "In that case... (*tadiha*).

In the sentence "wherein there is the *agnihotra-havaṇī*," although it is possible for the substance— which functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) as expressed by the suffix *-lyuṭ*— to be subordinate to the offering (*nirvāpa*) mentioned in its own sentence due to its suitability for that purpose, here [in the case of the *hiraṇya*], because the substance lacks form (*amūrta*) as a syntactic factor (*kāraka*), it cannot be construed either with the substance itself or with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of purchase; therefore, it does not possess subordination to that [purchase].

Moreover, when there is indifference between the direct statement (*śruti*) and the syntactical connection (*vākya*), the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice is presented through the context (*prakaraṇa*) known as "qualification" (*adhikāra*).

Then, by way of fitness (*yogyatā*), the injunctive sentence and the word denoting the substance are supplied as that which delimits the substance for that sacrifice; because it is enjoined thus, it possesses the status of being a fit factor (*kāraka*) for everything, and not merely the status of being a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) to the instrumental factor (*karaṇa-kāraka*) belonging to the specific context.
However, the meaning is that, by virtue of being common to those [two], it serves as a subordinate factor (aṅga) for the grammatical factors (kārakas) such as the agent (kartṛ) and so forth.

As for that which is stated in the Vārtika— having raised the objection that the already established quality of redness (*aruṇya*) cannot be grasped by the context— the instrumental case ending in *aruṇayā* refers back to the means of accomplishing the *jyotiṣṭoma* apūrva within the context, such as the Soma and other materials, and thereby prescribes the meaning of the nominal stem *aruṇa*.
"And thus, this very word is divided by the sentence in this manner."

That individual substance which is enjoined as an instrument for the accomplishment of the *apūrva* must always accomplish that [result] as qualified by redness; and if this is so, then even a house or the like, being a means to an action, would be "red."
Furthermore, regarding the statement: "As for other factors such as the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) which are prescribed [in the ritual],

this quality is not a subordinate part (*śeṣa*) of them, even though it has been determined to be for the sake of all," that is because, when the substance is acquired through the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there arises an indication specifically of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) through a mediated relationship (*paraṃparā-sambandha*).

"Because it is possible for the purchase mentioned in its own sentence to be connected [with the deity], and because it would result in the violation of the principle of 'single momentum' (ekaprasaratā), this is incorrect," as is clear in the Kaustubha.

By this [it is shown that]—since words such as *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) refer to a substance (*dravya*), and since the act of purchase (*kraya*) is already occupied by that [substance] directly expressed by the word, it is impossible for the word *aruṇā* (red) to enjoin a substance indicated by secondary signification (*lakṣya*)—this argument stated in the *Śāstradīpikā* is refuted.
This is because, despite the relative strength and weakness [of the words], there is in reality no contradiction due to their unity.
Therefore, the meaning is that, according to the previously stated method, [the quality of redness] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to all the case-factors (*kāraka*) with which it is compatible.
The cognition of semantic competency (*yogyatājñāna*) is not the cause for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) as delimited by the property of being a verbal comprehension;

for even in its absence, verbal comprehension arises in one who has grasped the conventional relation (*saṃketa*) between words and their referents, provided there is no certainty regarding semantic incoherence (*ayogyatāniścaya*).
Otherwise, since a verbal comprehension of the connection between a sacrifice and heaven would not arise [for such a person], the postulation of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) would be unnecessary.

However, since the ascertainment of unfitness (*ayogyatā*) acts as an obstacle, its absence serves as a causal factor; thus, even in the present case, it is logical for the *apūrva* to be connected with the efficient force of the purchase (*krayabhāvanā*) by that much alone.
With the intention that it is indeed a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that [purchase]’s substance, the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
"Not unfitness."
And "afterwards" means:

Since the redness (*āruṇya*) is first connected with the substance—because if it were connected with the action first, there would result a contradiction regarding its status as a *kāraka* (participant in an action)—even though its function of delimiting the substance is not yet perceived, it becomes related to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) by virtue of the aforementioned causal complex, just like other *kārakas* such as the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) or the purchase (*kraya*) and the Soma.

Thus, by means of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), the syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) caused by multiple things being enjoined is avoided; subsequently, at the stage where the purchase is understood to have the Soma as its instrument (*karaṇatva*), [the redness is understood as its qualifier].

Because it is proximate to the act of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), like the "one-year-old cow" (*ekahāyanī*), there is a connection with the purchase (*kraya*) through indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).

Even though there is no direct connection with the substance, since the status of the quality as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) cannot be established without its function of delimiting the substance, that function is understood by way of fitness.
Then, when there is a requirement for a specific substance, the cognition of the specific substance as the "one-year-old cow" is established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Furthermore, since there is mutual expectancy between both substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*), their restriction arises from their mutual association. Even though, under the view that [the word] denotes a quality alone, coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *ekahāyanī* is impossible— because words with different grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) cannot apply to a single referent— nevertheless, when the primary sense is impossible, the quality is construed as an instrument (*karaṇa*) by way of delimiting the substance, and thus its [connection to the action follows].

Since it is understood that [the quality] resides in the possessor of the quality, and since this is possible through the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the quality and its possessor, there is no inconsistency in their serving to delimit the substance—a one-year-old heifer (*ekahāyanī*)—which is the means for accomplishing that action, provided both are connected to a single action through mutual expectancy.

For this very reason, after establishing the subsequent syntactic connection (*pārṣṭhikānvaya*), the *Vārttika* states: "And thus, even the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) found within the sentence is established."
Therefore, even the coreferentiality with a substance-word in its form ending in the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is due to its status as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*),
and not because it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*).

Since that [coreferentiality] can be established as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) by assuming a qualifying injunction (*viśeṣaṇavidhi*) directed toward the purchase (*kraya*) itself, one should not resort to splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*) and, through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and other means, assume that it is an auxiliary to all substances mentioned in the context.
This is correct.
However, it does not follow from this alone that [the quality] is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the substance by virtue of being beneficial to it;
for otherwise, the reverse would also result, since the substance too is beneficial to the quality by virtue of being that which is delimited [by it].
Therefore, the sense is that here the direct Vedic statement (śruti) prevails over the syntactical connection (vākya), and thus redness is indeed an auxiliary to the act of purchase (*kraya*).

And so, since there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow), and a restriction is established by way of delimiting the substance of the *ekahāyanī*, there can be no application of redness to other substances used for purchase; thus he says: "And therefore... Now, one might raise this objection: "In the view where the purchase is a single act, since there is no difference in being the means for an activity conducive to obtaining a substance that serves as a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*), it would follow that redness applies even to items such as clothing. To address this doubt:
He rejects [this objection] with the words "and not" (na ca).
"For they are indeed distinct."

In the statement "He buys with a goat" (*ajāyā krīṇāti*), since multiple qualities are enjoined in the sentence concerning the redness (*aruṇā*) with reference to the purchase prescribed by that sentence, a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) would result.

Therefore, one must accept a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*). Since the origination of the act of purchase is thus necessary, and because a goat or other such items cannot be introduced into a purchase already restricted by a one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), there arises from each quality a distinct act of purchase extending as far as the substance itself.

The meaning is that, according to the view of Bhaṭṭa Someśvara, there is not a single purchase; therefore, the various capacities as means of performing those respective operations do not attain the status of being properties of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*).

Anticipating the argument that even for qualities prescribed by originative injunctions (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), there is no differentiating factor because their combination is possible— due to the lack of contradiction arising from the force of a single sacrifice— [the author] refutes it with the words "not so" (*na ca*) and "otherwise" (*anyathā*).
The sublation of the archetypal fees (*prākṛtadakṣiṇā*) by the modified fees (*vaikṛtadakṣiṇā*) through the principle of incidental application (*prasaṅga*) will be explained later.

In that case as well, since their combination would be possible on account of the necessity of hiring the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the meaning is that [the sublation] occurs because such a combination is impossible.

Nor should one raise the objection that even if there is a distinction between purchases based on the quality (guṇa), since substances are established within their respective distinct purchases by the very means of knowledge that apprehend them as subjects (dharmigrāhakapramāṇa), and because redness (āruṇya) possesses many other non-contradictory properties that serve as its motivators, its application to another substance cannot be prevented;
anticipating this, he refutes it with the words: "Nor even if there is a distinction between purchases..."

However, since other non-contradictory properties belong to different sentences, they are subsidiary to all acts of purchase by virtue of the intermediate context (avāntaraprakaraṇa); this is the meaning of the word "śeṣa" (subsidiary).

Now, one might object: since the three-year-old heifer (*trivatsā*) takes the place of all the items used for purchase, there is no possibility of the quality of "redness" (*āruṇya*) applying to it, because the form of the one-year-old heifer (*ekahāyanī*)—which serves as the door—is absent.
This is because, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), being mediated by the one-year-old heifer is intended to be significant.
For in that case, the one-year-old heifer is not the objective (*uddeśya*) [of the injunction], such that its mere essential form would not be intended on the grounds of fearing redundancy.

Because, by the third [reason], it is merely a means (*dvāra*) for its being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) with respect to the purchase (*kraya*); for there is no pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) in the nature of the means itself. Otherwise, if a ritual property were to apply merely through the existence of the object to be qualified (*uddeśya*) in the absence of a means, then the consequence would follow that threshing (*avaghāta*) must be performed even on *kṛṣṇala* grains. Therefore, he says: "And just as in this case... and so forth.

The meaning is this: even though the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) serves as a means [to the sacrifice], its status as a means does not derive from its being a "one-year-old cow," for that would result in it serving a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*);
rather, it is solely by virtue of being a substance that accomplishes the ritual action.

Therefore, even in the absence of the *puroḍāśa* cake, the status of rice grains as the material source (*prakṛti*) for the *caru* offering— which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice— is established. Furthermore, even in the case of the quality of redness (*āruṇya*), it does not function as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) by virtue of its own nature, but rather as a quality that serves as a means for the purchase at hand.

Therefore, even in a case where a purchase is to be accomplished through other qualities such as "white" and so forth, there is no contradiction in the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) serving as the delimiting factor; what then need be said when it is the door itself that serves as the door? Thus, the application of the ritual properties (*dharma*) therein is logical—this should be seen in the *Kaustubha*.
The practical purpose (*prayojana*) has not been stated because it is obvious.
Thus ends the sixth section concerning Aruṇā.
(B1) (Section 7 / Adhikaraṇa 7) That which is connected with singularity.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), and so forth.

In that context, does both the status of being a cup (*grahatva*) and oneness (*ekatva*) possess the property of being the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedakatā*) with respect to the cleansing and other such acts, or does only that [status of being a cup] possess it?
However, singularity is not intended [to be significant] because it is impossible for it to be connected with the injunction; this is the conclusion of the deliberation.

Just as in the case of the singularity of the animal (*paśu*), there is no reason to disregard the singularity of the cup (*graha*), and thus it functions as the delimiting factor of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedakatā*).

Therefore, since it follows that the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) applies to only one cup, [the following is said]: For where mutual connection (*parasparānvaya*) is grammatically established—as in the case of compounds and so forth, such as "the horse's bridle" or "anything smeared with Soma"—there indeed occurs a qualified objective (*viśiṣṭoddeśa*).

However, where such connection is not established, there can be no qualified objective; for if there were a qualified objective through mutual connection, it would result in the fallacy of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*) based on an unestablished syntactic relation.

For example, in the case of the rule "for whom both oblations (*havir*) should suffer damage, [he should perform] the *graha* sacrifice," there is no mutual syntactic connection between the two nominal stems (*subanta*), because it is a well-established linguistic principle that only the connection of nominal stems with the productive force (*bhāvanā*) is grammatically sanctioned, whereas their mutual connection with one another is not. Otherwise, even in the case of "the *ājya* chants are fifteen," there would result the undesirable consequence of it being a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).

However, in the case of number and so forth conveyed by the singular suffix and the like— which are already construed with the meaning of the suffix (such as instrumentality or objecthood) through the direct denotative power (*śruti*) of the same word— their connection with the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) via the direct denotative power of the word (*pada-śruti*) is simply not a recognized linguistic rule (*avyutpanna*).

Similarly, in instances such as "the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices] from all [people]," where after the cognition of multiple meanings from a single word, the notion of their collective unity (*sāhitya*) is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) directly from the nominal stem itself, even there the connection of that collective unity is with the meaning of the suffix alone, and not with the meaning of the nominal stem.
Thus it is clearly stated in the Kaustubha;
and for this reason, in such a case, the possibility of a qualified object of reference (viśiṣṭoddeśa) does not exist.

Now, even though a distinct specific purpose (*uddeśya*) is not possible, since both the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the meaning of the number (*vacana*) can connect with the meaning of the suffix—such as "objecthood" (*karmatva*)—it is logical that they connect with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) through that medium. Thus, there is no obstacle to the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*) being related to two subsequent purposes (*uddeśya*). Nor does a multiplicity of purposes result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); [for the connection is established through a single productive operation].

In the case of a meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there is no obstacle to its connection with multiple intended objects (*uddeśya*), just as there is none to its connection with multiple causal factors (*kāraka*).
Furthermore, there is no restrictive rule that it must have only a single delimitor of the intended object (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*);
for we observe even multiple such delimiters, such as "son-ness" and "cattle-ness," in injunctions like "the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices] are for all [desires]."

There is no defect whatsoever in the injunction simply because it has multiple intended objects. Nor is there a lack of eligibility for consecration on the grounds that there is no application [of the rite] to that which is delimited by singularity;

for just as blood and the like, though applied by way of being "animal" (*paśu*), are fit for consecration, so too it is logical that the cup (*graha*), though applied by way of being delimited by plurality, is fit for consecration by way of being delimited by singularity.

Nor should it be argued: "Even so, since there is no subordination to a single primary action for two distinct objects intended to be expressed (uddeśya), how can there be a rule of mutual syntactic connection? For this is possible even by means of the word-hearing (pada-śruti) itself, by postulating a mutual expectancy between the two primaries—even in accordance with a subordinate factor (guṇa)—just as in the case of modified (vaikṛta) subsidiaries. And this is accepted in cases where the elements reside in separate sentences, such as: "One divides the cake for Agni into four parts."

If it is argued that in cases such as "He divides the sacrificial cake into four parts," where there is a connection between two primary elements (the cake and the act of dividing) in accordance with a subordinate quality (the number four), and where— in a single syntactical unit— there is even more clearly a subordination of the primary elements to the action which serves as the principal qualificand in the verbal cognition,
and furthermore, that there is no fault in postulating such subordination rather than regarding the singularity as unintended; therefore,
it follows that even singularity and the like can validly function as delimiters of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) independently.

No; for since *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) is synonymous with "doing" (*karoti*), it is determined to have a single action as its object. If there were multiple intended objects, it would result in the fault of *vākyabheda* (sentence-splitting), which is caused by the breaking of that [unity]. Furthermore, having a single action as its object consists in possessing a property that serves as the delimitor of the substratum wherein the action-ness is fully resident within a single cognitive act.

In this regard, although in cases such as "The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices [are performed] for all [desires]," properties such as being a son or being cattle serve as the delimiters of the substratum wherein the action-ness is fully resident, [they do not constitute distinct actions].

Since all the factors (*dharma*) are understood simultaneously by a single word despite their diversity, there is no loss of the property of having a single action; this is the meaning from the beginning up to the end of the section on "object" (*viṣaya*).
However, the function of the term *paryāpti* (sufficiency) should be examined in the *Kaustubha*.

Consequently, it is clear that in the case of two results, two things to be refined (*saṃskārya*), or both results and things to be refined, there arises the contingency of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

Even in a case where there are two conditions (*nimitta*), one should observe that a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) results because, according to the principle of the *yāvajjīvādhikaraṇa*, each of the two conditions necessitates its own distinct result.
How it is not the case that a single result is necessitated by two conditions is clearly explained in the Kaustubha.

For this very reason, in cases involving a condition and a result, or a condition and something to be refined (*saṃskārya*), there is no syntactical split, as there is no disruption of the unity of the ritual act (*ekakarmakatva*).
Nor does that [single-sentence status] exist when there is a plurality of intended objects such as time and place;
and just as the concomitance of results and so forth cannot be the object of a single cognition, this is clearly explained in the *Kaustubha*.
Therefore, if one intends to express such concomitance, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is indeed difficult to avoid; the details of this and other points are elaborated elsewhere.
Now, even so, it is not that oneness and the rest are not intended to be expressed;
for it is logical that they are intended as subordinate qualities within the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of the cleansing.

Nor does it follow that there is a defect of dual form (*vairūpya*), nor a contradiction in having two simultaneous functions—because the accusative case indicates instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) with respect to the aspect of oneness, while it denotes predominance (*prādhānya*) with respect to the aspect of the cup (*graha*). Nor does it follow that there is a contradiction in having two simultaneous functions.

Since the accusative case has the power to denote merely the status of being an object—whether desired, undesired, or neutral—even when a specific distinction is understood from another means of knowledge, the syntactic connection of both [the singular number and the cup] is possible through a uniform application.

Nor does this imply that the singularity, which is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the cleansing (*saṃmārga*), cannot have the cup as its medium (*dvāra*) when it is not itself a subordinate element of the cup;
for even in the absence of subordinacy and so forth, the cup can serve as a medium just like heaven in the *āgneyī* mantra, by virtue of mere relatedness.
And if it is argued that "therefore, singularity is indeed intended," [we reply:

because it is improper to accept a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of instrumentality in the suffix in accordance with the subordinate singular ending, due to the contradiction of two simultaneous functions (*vṛtti-dvaya-virodha*), the lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*), and so forth;
therefore, it is better to assume mere figurative indication in that very [suffix] which is merely reiterative, according to the principle of the *pāśādhikaraṇa*.
Nor does the aforementioned defect follow merely from denoting a state of being an object common to both the desired and the undesired;
for if that were the case, the previously stated definition of having a single object would be violated, resulting in the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākya-bheda*).

Therefore, since resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to establish its status as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) would incur the aforementioned defects, the singular number—being intended to indicate plurality—is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of grammatical correctness and is not itself intended to be expressed.

And just as, when this is the case, there is an intention to express [the specific quality] such as "eight years of age" in passages like "one initiates a Brāhmaṇa who is eight years old," so too has this been established in the Kaustubha itself. // 3 // 7 //
Thus ends the seventh section concerning the singularity of the cup.

(B2) (Connected with Unity): Thus, having first examined in three sections the manner of application (*viniyoga*) of actions, substances, and qualities through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) in their respective order, the subsequent inquiry— though it would have been appropriate to perform immediately after the section on purpose (*arthādhikaraṇa*) due to its similarity in being an investigation into sanctification (*saṃskāra*) caused by *śruti*— is [now undertaken].

With the intention that, since a consideration of particulars depends upon a general consideration, a consideration of particulars is logically appropriate immediately after a consideration of the general, [the author] sets it aside for now; then, intending that it is proper to treat it now because the opportunity has arisen, he cites the sentence concerning the subject matter of the subsequent consideration: "The Jyotiṣṭoma... and so forth.

In both cases, by means of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), just as there is an inclusion of the sentence "he subsequently cuts the grasses" found in the *Agnihotra* context, as well as sentences such as "he carries fire around the sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśaṃ paryagnikaroti*) found in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* context, so too— accepting that the mention of "singularity" (*ekatva*) in the Sūtra is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*)— there is an inclusion of those sentences containing a subject (*uddeśya*) presented by words ending in dual or plural numbers, such as "for whom the two sacrificial cakes are destroyed" and "for whom all the oblations (*havīṃṣi*) should perish."
The summary has been indicated.

As for the passage from the *Vārttika* which cites, "He sprinkles the oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*," this appears inappropriate because, as will be explained in the fourth book, the sprinkling is intended as a disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *prayāja* remnant; thus, since the remnant of the *prayāja* would be the object (*uddeśya*) and the oblations would not be the objects, it seems ill-founded.
Nevertheless, the manner of its justification according to a different view will be demonstrated in that very place.

Regarding the phrase "he cleanses the vessel," although the word *daśāpavitra* is mentioned in the Bhāṣya as occurring before this [in the sūtra], its meaning there should be understood as either a cloth or a woolen blanket.

Regarding this, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* maintains that since the word *graha* denotes the Soma juice through an etymological derivation based on the action (*karma-vyutpatti*), the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the drops clinging to the outside at the time of drawing [the juice] occurs in a concealed form.

However, the authors of the *Prakāśa*, following Pārthasārathi, hold that based on the natural intent of the commentary on the subsequent section, the word *graha* refers to the vessels that serve as the receptacles for that [juice] through an etymological derivation based on the locus (*adhikaraṇa-vyutpatti*), and thus the consecration pertains to those vessels.
Regarding the property of being the delimiting factor of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedakatva*).

Although the application (*viniyoga*) of the act of cleansing is established, the specific mode of application must be stated: does it apply to the cup as qualified by singularity and so forth, or to the cup in general?

In this regard, even though the application occurs solely by way of its being a means to the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), nevertheless, the discussion concerns merely the role played by the capacity for a relationship that serves to define that [means], by way of whether it is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the objective (*uddeśyatā*) or not. This is the meaning.

Because there is no speaker for the Veda, it is impossible [to deny its authority] since that which is cognized through the authoritative Veda cannot be abandoned—whether in the form of desire or lack of desire to speak, or in the form of desire or lack of desire to act;

or, if one were to accept [the denial] in the form of cognition or non-cognition, it would be impossible because the oneness and so forth heard in the scripture have already been cognized and thus cannot be abandoned. In order to dispel this impossibility, [the author] establishes by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) the grounds for the possibility of desire and lack of desire to speak.
And it was stated [in the commentary] that this is "to indicate" [the distinction], because a connection with an injunction (*vidhi*) is impossible [in certain cases].

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: here, by the two terms "intended" (*vivakṣita*) and "not intended" (*avivakṣita*), what is actually intended are the contact with an injunction and the lack of contact with an injunction—respectively termed "that which is desired to be enjoined" (*vidhitsita*) and "that which is not desired to be enjoined" (*avidhitsita*)—which have as their cause the results consisting of performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) and non-performance (*ananuṣṭhāna*).
Having established this, the inquiry proceeds.
In that context, the meaning of the nominal stem *graha* is "cup-ness" (*grahatva*), the meaning of the verbal suffix is "oneness," and the meaning of the accusative case-ending is "objecthood.

Since it is impossible for the genus (*jāti*) to be directly construed with objecthood, a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the individual (*vyakti*) is necessary according to the previously stated method.

Thus, although the individual is the intended object (*uddeśya*) by virtue of its being the object, oneness is construed with that individual cup through the direct denotative power of the word (*padaśruti*) assisted by ownership and conventional designation; therefore, [the cup] is indeed qualified by oneness.

Just as the act of sprinkling (*saṃmārga*) does not apply to that which is not delimited by "cup-ness" (*grahatva*) when the cup and so forth are the object (*karman*), so too it does not apply to that which is not delimited by singularity (*ekatva*).
Although it is possible for singularity to be construed with the status of being the object through the direct statement of a common designation (*samānābhidhānaśruti*),
nevertheless, due to semantic incompatibility (*ayogyatva*) in that case, it is more appropriate for the construction to occur with the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) itself.
Nor is it impossible for a qualifier of the *kāraka* (the factor of action) to be connected with the injunction (*vidhi*).

Thus, even in cases such as "he whose [two] both... (*yasyobhayam*), where another word expressive of number is heard, since the connection occurs first with the word-base through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—that is, with the meaning of the secondary member (*upapada*)—it is possible for that qualified entity to be the object of reference (*uddeśya*). With this intention, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "just like the oneness of the animal" (*paśvaikatvavat*).

Because there is no connection with an injunction (*vidhi*), unity is not intended to be expressed. For what is the connection with the injunction? Is it by way of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*), or by way of being a subordinate quality (*guṇatva*)? Even in the former case, is it by way of referring to a qualified [object] or by way of referring to an independent [object]? It cannot be the first.

Intending to show that the specific qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is not yet understood prior to the connection with the action, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "For where... and so on, concluding with "it is certainly not understood."

Now, one might object: since the number and other properties conveyed by the singular suffix and so forth cannot be construed with the meaning of the base (prakṛti), there is no qualification; thus, when a qualified subject cannot be established—as in the case of the phrase "of all [of them]"—where the notion of conjunction is understood from the nominal stem itself, there would be no occasion for non-intentionality (avivakṣā), because it is possible for that which is delimited by conjunction to possess mutual qualification as understood through its inclusion within a single word.

Therefore, even when there is no intention to convey the connection (*anvaya*) of the conjunction (*sāhitya*) perceived through dual endings and so forth with the meaning of the suffix, there is no fault; hence he says: "In this way."

The meaning is as follows: since the cognition of "conjunction" (sāhitya) through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) occurs only after the nominal stem (prātipadika) has generated the cognition of its own primary denotation, simultaneous cognition is impossible;

furthermore, because that which is cognized subsequently constitutes the meaning of the entire nominal stem, and because the connection with the principal element is more highly esteemed, the grammatical connection (anvaya) is understood to occur only with the kāraka, just as it does with the primary denotation.
Thus, as stated clearly in the Kaustubha, there can be no possibility of a qualified objective (viśiṣṭoddeśa), because a qualification cannot apply to the meaning of the nominal stem itself.
He raises a second objection with "atha" (now/if),
[commenting on] the phrase "of the sweeping" (*saṃmārgasya*).

The meaning is that, just as the individuality characterized by "planethood" (grahatva) is connected to the efficient force (bhāvanā) through its status as the object of the action, so too the individuality characterized by "oneness" (ekatva) may be connected to the efficient force as the object; thus, even for the act of cleansing (saṃmārga), there is no inconsistency in its connection to two intended objects (uddeśya) by means of postulating two subsequent injunctive rules (viniyoga-vidhi).
There is no defect whatsoever.

Even if there were multiple things to be enjoined (*vidheya*), a split of the injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya-bheda*) would be logical because it would result in the destruction of the inherent nature of the fruit of an injunction— the making known of what was previously unknown— to have only a single object. However, when there are multiple things to be designated (*uddeśya*), since those [designata] are connected with the *bhāvanā* as heard in the text, and since the injunction— by enjoining a single *bhāvanā* qualified by all [the designata]— does not involve enjoining multiple [independent] things, it is possible to conceive of multiple injunctions regarding a single act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*) with respect to multiple designata, just as one conceives of multiple injunctions of various qualifiers with respect to a single action through implied injunctions (*ārthika-vidhi*).
The meaning is that there is no defect whatsoever, because the contingency of a split in the sentence does not arise.
Because its being an object of refinement is logically established.

And therefore, the meaning is that the status of being the object of a consecration (saṃskāryatā) does not necessarily result from the application (viniyoga) being delimited by the delimitor of the intended object (uddeśyatāvacchedaka), but rather also by delimitation through a property that is co-locative with it.
Because there is an absence of mastery.

For when there is a connection with an action as a subordinate element (*guṇa*), a mutual restriction is established according to the requirements through the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for that [action]. But in the present case, since the action itself is subordinate toward the object to be designated (*uddeśya*), and because the two objects to be designated are inherently primary and thus lack mutual expectancy, and since the action functions in accordance with them, how can it be that what is delimited by "cup-ness" (*grahatva*) is the same as what is delimited by "oneness" (*ekatva*)?
The meaning is that the restriction—that [the object] is delimited by "cowness" and delimited by "oneness"—is established.
[This occurs] "in accordance with the quality."
The meaning is: "in accordance with the requirement that there be no recurrence of the quality";
that is, "in accordance with the quality."
The meaning is: in accordance with the repetition of the qualities consisting in the division [of the oblation], the injunctions of various kinds, and the fourfold distribution.
He composes himself for the sake of cultivation.

In expressions such as "he makes a pot and a cloth" (*ghaṭaṃ paṭaṃ ca karoti*), since one does not observe the two—pot and cloth—to be construed with the meaning of "making" as objects (*karman*) without the word *ca*, and because there is a rule that "making" has only a single object, the same rule applies to its synonym, *bhāvanā* (efficient force). Therefore, when there are two objects, there must be a repetition of the suffix expressing the *bhāvanā*, which constitutes a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). This is the meaning.
Now, what is this "having a single action"?

It cannot mean "having a single action" (*ekakarmakatva*) or "being the locus of a single action," for such a definition would fail to apply in cases such as "the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices] are for all [purposes]" or "bring the pots."

In this regard, because there is a distinction between the actions of the livelihoods of sons and so forth and the sons and so forth who are the substrata of those actions, nor can there be a single delimiting factor for the object (karma); for if that were the case, since "paśutva" (animalhood), "putratva" (sonship), and so forth are distinct even in the phrase "for all [desires]," a single object-status would not be established. Therefore, he says: "And [the status of] a single object..."
"Having a single awakening as its object" is a qualification of the dharma;
[it means] "by that very one."
The meaning is that by means of that single word alone, all fruits are simultaneously cognized through their respective forms and respective powers.
"But the function of the word is fulfilled," it says.

In the case of the injunction, “The *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) should restrain their speech,” although there is the possibility of a double-object construction because the two properties— being the *adhvaryu* and being the sacrificer— which serve as the delimiters of the objecthood and the substratum respectively, do not fall within the scope of a single cognition, nevertheless, by means of the case-ending following the *dvandva* compound, one determines that the objecthood (and so forth) is *vyāsajyavṛtti* (resident in a composite whole), just as in the case of deityhood and the like. This is because the property of being both *adhvaryu* and sacrificer, which serves as the delimiter for the substratum in which that [objecthood] is fully instantiated (*paryāptyadhikaraṇatāvacchedaka*), does indeed fall within the scope of the single cognition produced by the *dvandva* compound.
The term "paryāpti" (sufficiency) is used for the purpose of establishing that [the atoms] constitute a single action.

Nor does it follow from this that there is an unintended implication of a desire to express a collective unity (sāhitya) conveyed by the compound, which would lead to the undesirable consequence that if, by chance, one of the two word-meanings were sublated, the other would not necessarily be enjoined;

for even if the two as qualified by their collective unity were the objects of the injunction, since there is a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of "being a means to the transcendental result" (apūrvasādhanatva), it is precisely the capacity to produce the transcendental result residing in each individually that must be indicated, and thus that consequence does not arise.
Indeed, those two do not possess the capacity to produce a single effect when combined.

Therefore, the meaning is that there is no fault because the definition functions precisely through a form understood as residing in each [individual] member; this should be examined in the Kaustubha.
"Throughout one's entire life as the basis."

The meaning is that, because the two signs (nimitta) function as instigators through their distinctness, they equally entail the contingency of multiple actions, since each necessitates its own respective result (bhāvya) which is projected by it. Thus, there is an equality in the resulting plurality of actions whose forms are those results thus projected.

Now, one might object that in a case where there are two causes, since it is accepted that they function as causes only when combined, they cannot project two separate results; to this, he says: "And just as... (yathāca).

The meaning is as follows: since *sāhitya* (concomitance) also falls within the scope of the same category [as the other two factors], it cannot function as a qualifying attribute of the occasion (*nimitta*) as before;

consequently, it would follow by implication that it is an independent occasion itself. Because this would entail the performance of multiple rites separately, the contingency of "syntactical split" (*vākyabheda*) would indeed arise—just as in the case of the rule *yasyobhayam*, etc., where both the possession of both [fires] and the affliction of the oblation (*havirārta*) are accepted as distinct occasions. This is clearly stated in the *Kaustubha*.

Therefore, where there is no contingency of implying two distinct results, there is no split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), because the thing to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) is one and the causal factor (*nimitta*) is construed precisely as a causal factor. Even in cases such as "in the afternoon on the new moon day" (*amāvāsyāyām aparāhṇe*), where although two times are intended as the objects of reference, they do not imply a plurality of rites, there too there is no split of the sentence; thus he says, "for this very reason.
And the passage beginning with "just as [regarding] the result and so forth" has already been explained.
He raises the third alternative with the word "nanu" (surely):
"just as in the case of heaven."

For, since it is established by its recitation within the context that the mantra must assist toward the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the New- and Full-Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) through some means, whatever is employed for that *darśapūrṇamāsa* *apūrva* becomes the means;
for the fruit is not employed for that *apūrva*, nor for the action that produces it.

Therefore, even in the absence of that [number], just as there is a connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, so too—insofar as the singularity is construed as an instrument within the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of cleansing—it is logical for the cup (*graha*), though it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*), to serve as the "means" (*dvāra*) merely by virtue of its connection to the cleansing; and since the singularity is accepted as defining the cup connected to that [cleansing], the syntactic connection "one should cleanse the cup with singularity" is established. This is the meaning.
Regarding "suchness" (tathātva): it refers to the state of being thus.

The meaning is that even if [the objecthood] were expressed by a second syntactical string (*tantra*), since there is no single cognition of the property— such as singularity or being a cow— which serves as the delimitor of the substratum where the objecthood is fully instantiated, the unity of the single object would be destroyed, resulting in the undesirable consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).
This is what is meant by "anuvāda" (restatement).

The meaning is as follows: either by taking the singularity with reference to the genus (*jāti*), or by taking it as already established (*prāpta*) through the singular number of each individual, the denoted meaning is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). However, in the case of the singularity of the animal (*paśu*), since it is construed as an instrument (*karaṇa*), its connection with the action occurs through that instrumental role; thus, there is no occurrence of defects such as syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
