Therefore, the intention to express [the singularity] is appropriate—this constitutes the difference between the two cases.

Now, one might object: "In the injunction ‘One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age,’ since there would be the consequence that the qualifying attribute of the person to be consecrated—namely, being eight years old—is not intended to be significant, it would follow that initiation could take place at any age whatsoever. To dispel this doubt, he says:
"And just as in this case... and so forth.

Even though the state of being eight years old is a qualifier of the subject (*uddeśya*), nevertheless, when its utility is required, one must assume an application (*viniyoga*) by means of the injunction "he should teach him"—which is a transformation of the statement "he should study"—since it is logical to intend that [age] as something to be included (*upādeya*) because it is referred to by the word *tam*.

Although, if [the age] were not intended in the initial connection with the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), it would follow that even in the subsequent injunction of application, the word *tam* would refer to the subject precisely as having an unintended qualifier; [nevertheless, this is not the case].

Nevertheless, even though it follows from the initial injunction, because there is no possibility of obtaining the state of being eight years old—just as there is none for the singularity of the cup—it cannot be a mere restatement (anuvāda). Consequently, as in the case of the rule "half within the altar" (*ardham antarvedi*), since a qualified objective is possible through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the intended meaning is established.
For in cases such as "the cup" (*graham*), where the possibility of obtaining both [the cup and its quality] exists, [the two are indeed taken together].

The meaning is that while there exists a restrictive factor— such as the *pāśanyāya* (the logic of the rope)— for applying the secondary figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) characterized by plurality to a singular [word], in that case there is no qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭoddeśa*) through figurative sense in both [words] simultaneously;
however, in the present context, since neither [of the two] is otherwise established, there is no defect whatsoever in accepting it, as has been demonstrated in the *Kaustubha*.

Thus, in the expression "he gathers grass for the fire" (*agner tṛṇāny apacinoti*), although the fire is perceived as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*) in the act of gathering via the medium of the grass because of its genitive case, nevertheless, when there is a desire to know the specific nature of that general relation, and since no other qualifier is possible, it is determined to reside in a specific relation characterized by the status of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgitva*).

Furthermore, when the expectation arises as to "who is the principal here?", since the fire possesses a purpose, it is determined to be the principal; this applies to a refinement (*saṃskāra*) intended for future use.

Because that [fire] is more important, it acquires a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) by way of avoiding the falling of a firebrand outside [the altar] caused by contact with grass; furthermore, since the genitive case expressing the relationship between property and owner is seen to be used for the owner, it is determined to signify predominance (*prādhānya*). Consequently, because the fire is understood to be predominant and thus the object of the injunction (*uddeśya*), it is logical not to intend the singularity that qualifies it. And therefore, because it is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the fire...

The reduction consisting of the distribution of grass is a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra-vidhi*) specifically for that fire whose use is immediately before me; therefore, there is no reduction of grass for the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires.
However, as for the strewing (*paristaraṇa*), it certainly applies to those two fires as well, because of the general scriptural injunction: "He strews around the fires."
Or let it be that [the fire] belongs to both of them as well.

Even if this were a fifth case (pañcamī), the Vārttikakāra maintains there is no fault, because— just as in the expression "he cuts from the middle and from the eastern half"— since the fire serves a purpose, the word is used figuratively (lakṣaṇā) to denote its primary status.

And in this view, for the sake of making the reduction have a visible purpose, Āpastamba’s Sūtra states that the strewing should be performed again and again using only the grasses that have been gathered.

According to Pūjyapāda, however, since there is no evidence for a disruption of the application (*viniyoga-bhaṅga*) when the predominance of the grasses is understood through the second [case-ending], it is simply the *tṛṇa-pratipatti* (the disposal of the grasses).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of intending to express the plurality inherent in the grasses; by the logic of the *kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa*, this would result in the removal of only three blades of grass. Consequently, the falling of the firebrand outside the circle of grasses—which would arise due to contact with the remaining blades—would be unavoidable, and thus it would be impossible for the fire to be the object of the purificatory rite (*saṃskārya*) effected by the removal of the grasses.

Therefore, since the non-intentionality of plurality cannot be established without the grass being the object of the consecration (*saṃskārya*), it is logical that the act of removal (*apacaya*) is merely a disposal-rite (*pratipattikarma*) for the grass used in the strewing (*paristaraṇa*).
Nor does this entail the removal of grass from only a single fire;

for even though the fire is subordinate as the recipient (*apādāna*) expressed by the ablative case, there arises the consequence of intending plurality, because we understand the singular number to be restated in reference to each individual portion of grass to be disposed of.
Therefore, it is stated in the Kaustubha that this is indeed a case of "acceptance as grass" (tṛṇapratipatti).

As for what the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* stated—that on this view, since even the grasses used for the *paristaraṇa* (strewing) around the fire for the sake of the previous ritual performance are disposed of (*pratipatti*) due to their depletion at the time of a subsequent performance, it is improper to regard them as a *pratipatti*—that is incorrect. This is because the statement in the *Āpastamba-sūtra*, "Having approached [the fire], he removes the grasses," speaks of the action occurring after the worship performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), in accordance with the fact that the one who performs the worship is the same one who completes the act of approaching the fire. Thus, [the *Nyāyasudhā*’s objection] is untenable.
This was rightly disregarded by the venerable teacher (Pūjyapāda).

For this very reason, since the tips of the grass blades are not utilized in the actual performance (*pratipatti*), Dhūrtasvāmī and others have stated that in the subsequent ritual applications (*uttaraprayoga*), the strewing (*paristaraṇa*) is performed with entirely different blades of grass; enough of this elaboration.
And just as there is an intention to express the accompaniment of fire (*agnisāhitya*) in the injunction for the laying of the fires (*adhāna*), so it should be understood in the *Kaustubha*.
The purpose has not been stated because it is evident.
Thus ends the seventh section concerning the singularity of the cup.
(B1) (8th Topic /) (a.3 pā.1 adhi.8) Or [it is] due to consecration.
The singular number is not intended to be significant for the cup (*graha*) either;

for, by the very force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is understood that the purpose of the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) is the removal of the Soma-drops, and thus it is understood that all Soma-vessels are the objects to be consecrated.

Furthermore, since both the cups (*graha*) and the goblets (*camasa*) are means for accomplishing the single transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the cleansing would apply to the goblets as well, just as it does to the barley grains.

When [the term *graha*] is employed with the intention of expressing the status of being a *graha*, since there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) or other such defects, even though there is unity in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice itself, there is a distinction among the various apūrvas (transcendental results) arising from those respective repetitions.

Therefore, just as in the case of the injunction "he mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk," it is logical to define [the object of the action] solely as that which is the means for producing the apūrva generated by a *graha*; consequently, there is no wiping (*saṃmārjana*) of the *camasa* cups. // 3 // 8 //
Thus ends the eighth section, concerning the intention to express the status of being a planet.
(B2) This is for the sake of clarity.
Thus ends the eighth section concerning the intention to express the status of being a planet.
(B1) (Section 9 on the Topic of the Subject Matter) (a.3 pā.1 adhi.9) Because of meaninglessness.

In the case of the statement, “The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of the *vājapeya* is seventeen cubits long,” the quality of being seventeen cubits long is enjoined by means of the genitive *śruti* with reference to the *vājapeya*, because it is not separated [from it], because it is the primary element, and because it favors the context (*prakaraṇa*), rather than with reference to the sacrificial post;
for otherwise, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would result.

Because there is a qualification by means of the *vājapeya*, and because there is a qualified objective (*viśiṣṭoddeśa*), the measurement of seventeen cubits (*saptadaśāratnitva*)—being enjoined with reference to the *vājapeya*—finds its place through the medium of the upright vessel belonging to that sacrifice. Since it is argued that the word "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) due to similarity, [we reply: in the absence of any evidence for the figurative use of the word "sacrificial post," the term "sacrificial post" indicates its own function (*svakārya*), and with reference to that function, the substance of seventeen cubits is enjoined.
It is enjoined.

And although the substance and the measurement of one cubit (*aratni*) may be obtained through extension (*atideśa*), nevertheless, because the fault of breaking the unity of syntactic force (*ekaprasaratābhaṅga*) would arise if the number were enjoined as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of those, it is accepted that they apply first; thus, it is the qualified substance itself that results from the injunction of the number, as in "those with red turbans" (*lohitoṣṇīṣāḥ*).
It is enjoined in this manner and so forth.

Since [the term "of the Vājapeya"] would be meaningless in reference to the essential nature of the sacrificial post's function, it is understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*) by means of an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being a means to the *apūrva* of the Vājapeya; thus, because the sacrificial post connected to the *apūrva* of the Vājapeya is obtained, the phrase "of the Vājapeya" is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Furthermore, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is appropriate even for an indirect relationship (*paraṃparā-sambandha*), just as one says, "this is Devadatta’s grandson."
And [factors] such as being separated are not defects when considered in relation to figurative usage. // 3.9 //
Thus ends the ninth section, concerning the pointlessness [of a subsidiary] due to its being a part thereof.

(B2) Here, since the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is primary according to the view of the predecessors (*prācīnamata*) but secondary according to our own view (*svamata*), and since we are considering the application of a śruti that is common to both the secondary and the primary, the connection with the chapter and the section (*pādādhyāyasaṃgati*) is clear and thus not explicitly shown. Instead, after first presenting the subject matter found within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Vājapeya sacrifice, [the author] states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself as follows: "saptadaśa... (seventeen...).

As for "connection by immediate sequence" (*anantarasaṅgati*): when it was previously considered that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) was intended while the meaning of the number (*vacana*) was not, a desire for knowledge arises as to which [of the two] is not intended when both meanings of the nominal stem are present. Because there is an occasion [for such inquiry], the intention or non-intention regarding one or the other is investigated; thus, it is of the nature of an "occasion" (*avasara*).

Regarding this, the authors of the *Prakāśa* have refuted the claim made by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*— that the inquiry as to whether the measurement of seventeen cubits applies to the *ṣoḍaśin* vessel or to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is merely incidental (*prāsaṅgika*) following the statement that in the preceding section the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) applies to the cups (*graha*) and not to the chalices (*camasa*)— on the grounds that it is improper to assert an incidental connection when a direct and primary connection is possible; they have instead established a direct connection.

Having established the rule regarding the relationship between internal and external factors with respect to the injunctions concerning substances and qualities— in accordance with their respective connections—

by means of an exception to the application of singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth to the action and its associated substance as stated in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, two sections have been devoted to an investigation into the specific rules and exceptions regarding the application of these principles to *saṃskāra* (preparatory acts) according to their respective connections; since such an investigation into specific cases is not possible regarding the *dravya* (substance) itself.

Regarding the quality of being seventeen cubits in length, since its status as a subsidiary to the ritual action and its application to the substance belonging to that action are established in general by the principle of the *Āruṇyādhikaraṇa*, there arises an inquiry into its specific application:

does it, as a subsidiary to the Vājapeya sacrifice, find its place in the *ṣoḍaśin* cup which is a subsidiary of that sacrifice; or rather, as a subsidiary to the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*), does it apply to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) which is a subsidiary of that sacrifice?

The venerable teachers have set aside this [objection] as improper because it lacks direct relevance; for, like the word *ekahāyanī* and others, the term *saptadaśāratni*—being a *bahuvrīhi* compound—is denotative of a substance (*dravya*). Consequently, just like the quality of redness (*āruṇya*), it cannot be subordinate to the ritual action (*kriyā*), and thus it is impossible for it to be the subject of the general inquiry (*sāmānyacintā*). Since a specific inquiry (*viśeṣacintā*) is likewise impossible here, there can be no direct connection.
As for how this term denotes a substance, that will be demonstrated later.

Therefore, in the Kaustubha, having set aside both the "contextual connection" (prasaṅga-saṅgati) and even the "direct connection" (sākṣāt-saṅgati), only the "connection by occasion" (avasara-saṅgati) has been shown.

In that context, regarding the prescription of seventeen cubits with reference to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), it is first of all impossible for the sacrificial post to be the object of reference (*uddeśya*) as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) of the bahuvrīhi compound,
because that would result in the violation of the principle of "single thrust" (*ekaprasaratābhaṅga*). Nor can it be so by virtue of being the meaning of the word *yūpa* itself.

If that were the case, the compound would be untenable because of the lack of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the meaning of the other word; furthermore, since the *aratnis* (cubits) are already established, their prescription (*vidhi*) would be untenable.

If one were to prescribe the number by referring back to the *aratnis*, then even when adding the qualification "belonging to the sacrificial post" (*yūpīyatva*) to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), there would result both a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) and a violation of the principle of single thrust (*ekaprasaratābhaṅga*).

Therefore, the substance consisting of seventeen cubits is enjoined with reference to the Vājapeya—which is established as the primary element by the genitive case expressing ownership—and thus, through its immediate connection with the primary rite, the genitive hearing (*ṣaṣṭhī-śruti*) obtains support from the requirement of the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*). Otherwise, according to the logic of the restriction of speech (*vāṅ-niyama*) at the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, it would follow that the substance serves either the purpose of the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the animal sacrifice or merely the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); consequently, since it would not be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Vājapeya, there would be the undesirable consequence of its sublation.

Furthermore, since a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result if both [the sacrificial post and the seventeen-cubit measure] were intended as qualified objects, and since one of the two must be left unexpressed, it is more appropriate to accept the expression of the term *vājapeya* as primary while leaving the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) unexpressed;
otherwise, because the connection with the *vājapeya* would already be established by the context (*prakaraṇa*), the word *vājapeya* would become redundant.

Therefore, intending to reject the view that the rule enjoins a sacrificial post specifically characterized by the measure of seventeen cubits, he establishes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) by stating: "because of the lack of intervention" (*avyavahitatvāt*).

Even though it is a prescription for a substance, it is stated that "the state of being seventeen cubits long" applies to the qualifier, with the intention that the power of the injunction transfers [to it], just as in the case of "red turban" and so forth.
This refutes the objection: "How can that be an auxiliary (aṅga) since it is set aside in the Vājapeya?"—by the words "tadīya" (belonging to that).

The meaning is as follows: although the *ṣoḍaśi* cup is the receptacle for the *rasa* (soma-juice), because of the injunction "one offers with the cups" (*grahair juhoti*), it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the act of throwing [the offering] into the fire—which is part of the sacrifice—and thus it is a direct auxiliary (*sākṣād-aṅga*) to the *Vājapeya*. Therefore, its application (*niveśa*) occurs therein by way of that [direct auxiliary status].

To indicate that its placement is specifically there—due to its unique connection with the *Vājapeya*, whereas other cup-vessels are common to many sacrifices—the term "belonging to that" (*tadīya*) is used.
"Urdhvapātra" means the *ṣoḍaśi-graha* (the sixteen-fold cup).
"Because of similarity."

Because that vessel is made of *khadira* wood and is upright, it possesses a similarity to a sacrificial post (*yūpa*); thus, the word "post" is used here in a figurative sense. For this very reason—even in the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word denoting an upright vessel—the status of being an object referring to an upright vessel is established by adopting a figurative coreferentiality in the form: "it is like a seventeen-cubit sacrificial post. As for what Somanātha stated—that because the use of *khadira* wood for a post is optional, there is no constant presence of that quality [in the case of the vessel]—this is addressed as follows: The meaning is that the word "post" is applied figuratively to the vessel by taking its similarity to a post based on its being made of *khadira* wood and its verticality. Therefore, even though there is no direct coreferentiality with a term signifying an upright vessel, the status of the subject matter as an upright vessel is established by means of figurative coreferentiality, namely: "it is similar to a sacrificial post of seventeen cubits. As for the objection raised by Somanātha—that since the use of *khadira* wood for a post is optional, there is no necessary or constant presentation of that specific quality (in the vessel)—[the response is: this is not a fault, because the word "post" is employed figuratively based on the presence of other qualities such as verticality and the like. Furthermore, the word "post" is indeed applied to the sacrificial post primarily in its literal sense; however, when it is applied to something else, it is necessarily understood in a figurative sense. Thus, there is no contradiction. Moreover, the fact that the material of the post is optional does not prevent the application of the term "post" to the vessel through figurative usage based on shared characteristics. Consequently, the conclusion remains that the injunction pertains to an upright vessel.

It was stated that because only the mere similarity to verticality—which is invariably present when the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) is used—is grasped, the application [of the term] would reside in every vessel that is merely vertical;
however, that position is incorrect, because even for that which is already present, its purpose is justified as being for the sake of restricting other things.

For this very reason, although there is an option between eleven and twelve potsherds (*kapāla*) for the *aindrāgna* offering, it is accepted—even if disregarded in the present context—that in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the twelve potsherds constitute a modification of the *aindrāgna* offering characterized by the optional twelve potsherds.
By the venerable masters.

Although it might be argued that between two [options], the non-intentional mention of the subordinate one is more appropriate, nevertheless, rather than abandoning its own primary meaning, it is more logical for even the subordinate term *yūpa* (sacrificial post) to be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already established.

Therefore, in accordance with that [restatement], one must accept the abandonment of the application (*viniyoga*) based on the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) of the genitive case— which expresses a connection with the immediately preceding principal element— and instead enjoin it solely with reference to the *yūpa*.

In this regard, since it is impossible to enjoin a substance that constitutes the meaning of the compound as a distinct referent (*anyapadārtha*) upon the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the word "yūpa" must be taken as indicating the function of the post through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Thus, when the substance of seventeen cubits is enjoined for the function of the post, even if another substance were to be introduced for that same function, nevertheless—because it is possible to incorporate the substance of seventeen cubits without contradicting the status of being a post (*yūpatva*) which is established by the archetype (*prakṛti*)—the injunction of the substance known as the "post" is successfully established; it is with this intention [that the author speaks].
He states the final conclusion: "Of the word *yūpa*..."

The meaning is that since figurative usage is impossible without coordination with another word (*parapada-sāmānādhikaraṇya*), if one were to resort to a figurative sense for the word *yūpa* by taking it to refer to the "upward-facing vessel" (*ūrdhvapātra*), there would result the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*); thus, its application to the upward-facing vessel is not established. As for the support from the context (*prakaraṇa*), he states that it is no different for me as well: "by the function of the sacrificial post" (*yūpakārya*).

Since the seventeen-cubit length is seen to be established in the archetype even without the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), its purpose being fulfilled by the tying (*niyojana*) accomplished by it or the transcendental merit (*apūrva*) of the animal sacrifice accomplished by it, it would follow that the word itself is redundant. Therefore, setting aside the rule regarding the restriction of speech (*vāṅniyama*) at the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* initiation, the term "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*)—functioning through a secondary metaphorical indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*) and aided by the context known as "qualification" (*adhikāra*)—serves as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the Vājapeya sacrifice; this is the meaning.

By this, both the position of Bhavadeva and others— who accept the word *vājapeya* as an adjective of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) in order to secure its connection with the *vājapeya* sacrifice— and the refutation of that by the authors of the *Prakāśa*, who charge it with resulting in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to the prescription of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭoddeśa*), are both discarded; for that qualification would be purposeless (*vaiyarthyāt*).

Furthermore, since according to the view of the ancients, mutual syntactic connection (*parasparānvaya*) is established in cases of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), there is no resulting split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*). By this [argument], the statement of Somanātha— that because the seventeen-cubit length as an accessory of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is not grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*) characterized by the expectancy for the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*) in the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is not prompted by the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the Vājapeya,
but rather, by the logic of the restriction of speech (*vāṅniyamanyāya*), it is prompted solely by the *apūrva* of the animal sacrifice— is refuted.

Even if [the word *yūpa*] is not grasped through the context characterized by the expectancy for the mode of being (*kathaṃbhāva*), since its status as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) is understood by the direct statement (*śruti*) of the word *yūpa* itself—assisted by the contingency of meaninglessness—it follows that it must be prompted by the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the Vājapeya sacrifice.

Now, one might object: "Since the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is not established as a subordinate element of the Vājapeya, how can there be a restatement (*anuvāda*) based on the attainment of its connection with the Vājapeya? To this, he says: "And the genitive... (*ṣaṣṭhī ca*).
And here, according to the method of the ancients, since it is impossible to enjoin the meaning of a compound upon the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) alone as the object of reference,

and because if one were to resort to an indication of a function (*kāryalakṣaṇā*), there would be the fault of *lakṣaṇā*, and furthermore, because even the injunction of a substance would result in an overly strained interpretation— being restricted solely to that which does not conflict with the nature of being a sacrificial post— and because no specific substance would be prescribed, there is no injunction of a substance with reference to that [post].

Furthermore, it appears to me that there is no fault whatsoever if one accepts that the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) functions as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), and thus prescribes a sacrificial post qualified by the attribute of being seventeen cubits long with reference to the Vājapeya sacrifice; for since such a post would not perform its original function, it cannot be introduced into the Vājapeya merely as a means or the like, yet the genitive case remains explicable even through an indirect relationship, as the post is introduced by way of being the means of tying up the animal belonging to that sacrifice.
The purpose has not been stated because it is self-evident.
Thus ends the ninth section, concerning the pointlessness [of certain injunctions] and their being subordinate members [of other rites].
— — — — — — — (B1) (10th Adhikaraṇa /) (a.3 pā.1 adhi.10) [The rule applies] when there is a quality of the agent.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the injunction "He offers while stepping forward" (*abhikrāmaṃ juhoti*) is heard in proximity to the *prayāja* offerings. Since *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) is immaterial, it cannot be syntactically connected to the *prayāja* homa which is denoted by the verb *juhoti*. Furthermore, as in the case of the quality of redness (*āruṇya*), there is no substance here that serves as a substratum for the agent, and thus no substance is mentioned through which the action could be connected. Consequently, being separated from the *prayāja*, it becomes an auxiliary to all the homas within the context.

When it is argued that [the connection] occurs through the visible effect consisting in the proximity of the agent of that [act] to the *āhavanīya* fire, the author of the *Bhāṣya* establishes the conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the [acts] are indeed subsidiary to the *prayāja* oblations; for even though not explicitly mentioned, the existence of that which is understood from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) allows for the connection with the root *hu* (to sacrifice) precisely by means of that [suffix].

The Vārttikakāra has explained this differently because, when the root *juhoti* is construed with the element ending in the suffix *ṇamul* through a relationship such as priority in time (*pūrvakālatā*), there is no lack of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); and because there is no evidence that *juhoti* refers exclusively to the *prayāja* offerings, and because this point is largely settled by the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*.

Even if there were a syntactical connection between the *juhuyāt* and the *homa*, since there is no evidence for a restriction, it must be an auxiliary to all *homas* within the context, just like the rule "the sacrificial oblations on the altar" (*vedyāṃ havīṃṣi*).
For it is untenable that a subordinate context (avāntarādhikāra) consisting of a "sandwich" (sandaṃśa) of scriptural injunctions should serve as a restrictor of the syntactical connection (vākya).
Indeed, if the word "he steps forward" (abhikrāmati) were heard within such a sandwich,
then there might indeed be its status as an auxiliary of the Prayājas by virtue of that subordinate context.
In reality, however, there is no *prakaraṇa* (context) characterized by the expectancy for a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) regarding the subsidiaries,

because there is no result [to be achieved]; otherwise, it would follow that even the *prayāja* offerings, the stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*), and so forth, would become subsidiaries of the *anuyāja* offerings and the like.

And since the requirement (ākāṅkṣā) postulated for the purpose of establishing a connection with the subsidiary parts as expressed by the text would, by its nature of grasping only that [specific part], be incapable of grasping the *abhikramaṇa* (the stepping forward), this being the prima facie view—[we reply]: because it is the very nature of productive activity (*bhāvanā*) that even the productive activities of the subsidiaries have a requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) when their objective is the benefit to the sacrifice, such a requirement certainly exists for the subsidiaries as well. It is merely obstructed—in the case of those [subsidiaries] recited in proximity—by the fact that the primary [action] possesses a fruit.
Therefore, there is no contingency of mutual dependence;

at that time, its cessation occurs either through extension (*atideśa*), by the fulfillment of what is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*), or by means of common acts such as sipping water (*ācamana*).

However, where there is a textual inclusion (*saṃdaṃśa*) of auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), the first [element] revives the expectancy for an auxiliary, while the last destroys it; it is not, as in the case of a gem (*maṇi*) and so forth, that each textual auxiliary acts as an excitant (*uttejaka*) individually,
because that would involve the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) of admitting a collection of absences of all such auxiliaries.
Likewise here, because there is no deviation [from the context],
the subsidiary nature (*aṅgatva*) of those [acts] mentioned within the verbal *saṃdaṃśa* (enclosure) is established by the stronger intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).

However, in the case at hand, since *abhikramaṇa* is enjoined as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *homa*, and the contingency of its being purposeless (*ānarthakya*) regarding the essential form of the *homa* arises, the intermediate context— consisting of the verbal *saṃdaṃśa* of subsidiaries— is taken as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being a means to the *apūrva*.
Thus, it is resorted to as the primary [act] itself, and not as a subordinate act (*aṅga*) or a context for both subordinate and primary acts, as is the case with the altar (*vedī*).

For in this instance, after beginning with "He pours together what is in the *aupabhṛt* ladle into the *juhū*," and having prescribed the "stepping forward" (*abhikramaṇa*) in the middle, there is the scriptural statement: "He sprinkles the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) with the remnant of the *prayāja*s. Therefore, that [stepping forward] is [the primary act].
Therefore, the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *prayāja* offerings.
Nor is there an absence of offering (*homa*) in the *prayājas*;

for, since the term *yajati* (he sacrifices) is determined by the usage of the elders to refer to a renunciation (*tyāga*) that has the act of throwing (*prakṣepa*) as its constituent part, it follows that an offering is obtained even for every sacrifice mentioned in the text through implication (*ākṣepa*). // 3 // 10 //
Thus ends the tenth section, the Adhikaraṇa on the Tongs.

(B2) Since it is established that [the *abhikramaṇa* and *upavyāna*] must enter as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) because otherwise they would result in meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*) and because their connection with the primary action (*kriyā*) through direct hearing (*śruta*) is impossible, the sequence of the two subsequent sections—which concern the specific details of those subsidiaries—is clearly connected. Although this inquiry ought to have been conducted immediately after the inquiry into the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) called "cleansing" (*saṃmārga*), since the *abhikramaṇa* and *upavyāna* would themselves become purificatory rites if they entered as subsidiaries of that [action], nevertheless, because an action cannot be directly connected to another action, they are connected to the action indirectly by way of the substance (*dravya*) which serves as the means for the action possessing the quality (*guṇa*). Therefore, [this inquiry follows].

Intending to show the logical connection (*saṅgati*)—namely, that this [discussion] is appropriate even after the consideration of the *guṇa* (accessory), since it is understood to be a preparation (*saṃskāra*) for the substance—he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), preceded by a demonstration of its subject matter, as follows: "In the Darśa... etc.
Because the positive concomitance (anvaya) is untenable.
The meaning is that because it lacks the status of being a *kāraka* (a factor of action), its syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is untenable.
He refutes the possibility of connecting even the action as a *kāraka* by way of delimiting the substance, stating: "and like the quality of redness (*āruṇya*)."

By the grammatical rule "the kṛt-affixes beginning with *avyaya* denote the abstract state (*bhāva*)," it is understood that because the affix *ṇamul* expresses only the abstract state due to its indeclinability (*avyayatva*), it does not denote a substance (*dravya*) consisting of a coreferential agent; thus, since the connection with an action yet to be accomplished— which serves as the justification for the restriction to substances— is established through the necessity of accounting for the co-referentiality and anteriority mentioned for *ṇamul*, there follows a syntactic relation (*anvaya*) with the substance that constitutes the agent.

The meaning is that, like the quality of redness (*āruṇya*), there is no syntactic connection with the action [of the sacrifice] because: (1) prior to the acquisition [of the substance], it is impossible for the restriction of the substance to be established; (2) since it does not delimit [the agent], it is useless for the employment of a substance that serves as the means to an action, just like a quality; and (3) the substance called "adhvaryu," which is intended as the medium, cannot serve as the exclusive medium for a specific action—unlike the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*)—because it is common to many actions. Thus, there is no syntactic connection with the action as expressed in the sentence.
By this, even the objection that the matter has already been settled by the *aruṇādhikaraṇa* (the section on the red cow) is refuted.

Now, one might object: "Even if it were an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to all oblations within the context, its status as an auxiliary would still result solely from being a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*). To this, he says: "tadīya" (belonging to that).

Based on the grammatical rule "ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca" (Pāṇini 3.4.22), which prescribes the suffix *ṇamul* for the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*), and because such repetition— which consists of recurrence— is not applicable when a rite serves as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) due to its being performed once for all (*tantratva*), whereas a sanctification (*saṃskāra*)— being for the purpose of imparting fitness for the ritual act— does not require repetition for each individual act, it must indeed be a sanctification of the agent.
And the meaning is that even he has indeed seen its form.
"Even of that which is non-appropriated."

Since the suffix *ṇamul* expresses the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvārthaka*), and because the grammatical rule "between two actions having the same agent" (*samānakartṛkayoḥ*) is intended to refer merely to the instruction regarding the sequence of actions (*saṃmārgānuśāsana*), it was stated that there is no cognition of that [sequence] through *ṇamul*. For this very reason, in the phrase "by means of the relation of priority in time, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes the relation of having the same agent (*samānakartṛtva*).

Having demonstrated the impropriety of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) formulated in the Bhāṣya by severing its connection with the verbal root *juhoti*, [the author] shows the inquiry according to the method stated by the Vārttikakāra: "That" refers to the prima facie view; he states it with the words "even though."

Although this discussion is not logically consistent as the subject matter of the *pāda*—since the *ṇamul* suffix does not denote a *kāraka* and thus cannot be a primary *śruti*; and since even the relationship with the verbal root, in the form of being a subordinate (*aṅga*), appears merely as a mode of relation (*saṃsarga-vidhayā*) and thus cannot be a secondary *śruti* like the genitive case; and since the status of being subordinate to the agent, which serves as the means [of application], is understood through *liṅga* (indicative power) rather than through *śruti*—nevertheless, [the discussion proceeds].

Since the *ṇamul* suffix cannot denote subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) when it signifies an action (*bhāva*), its connection [to the main sacrifice] is established through the figurative application of the term "direct statement" (*śrautatva*), as it is to be inferred from the direct hearing of the *ṇamul* suffix itself; this is indicated by the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even though [it exists]. The immediate [connection], however, is clearly of the nature of an occasion (*avasararūpā*), because the status of being a subsidiary to the primary act is set aside by the direct hearing of its being a subsidiary to the oblation (*homa*), and thus there arises an inquiry into its specific character. In that regard, even though its status as a subsidiary to the oblation is established, if its own essential form (*svarūpa*) were to result in meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*), then by means of the context (*prakaraṇa*) known as the "qualification of the primary act" (*pradhānādhikāra*), [its purpose is determined].

Since it is understood that the status of being a *homa* (oblation) connected to the principal *apūrva* (unseen potency) through the medium of the performer’s refinement (*saṃskāra*) constitutes the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), and since the performer— being common to both the subsidiaries and the principal— is intended as the medium such that its connection to the principal is meant to include both direct and indirect relations, [the injunction] applies to all *homas* belonging to the context. Alternatively, because there is no evidence for restricting the scope of the sentence, the reference to the subsidiaries, like the reference to the principal, serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*) by way of characterizing them as means to the *apūrva*.
Intending that [the mantra] serves the purpose of all the oblations under discussion, he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "saṃkoca" and "yadi hi."

If it were heard only as "when he steps forward" (*yadyabhikrāmati*), then, because there would be no operation of the syntactical connection (*vākya*), it would be heard as an accessory (*aṅga*) to the *prayāja*s alone; the meaning is that, due to the absence of a syntactical operation, it would thereby become an accessory only to the *prayāja*s.

If, when the primary sacrifice’s requirement for a procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*) leads to the acceptance of the *prayāja* offerings as its subsidiaries, and it is thereby understood that they have the production of a ritual benefit (*kratūpakāra*) as their objective, one were then to postulate a requirement for a procedure on the part of those *prayājas* themselves, then— by virtue of the primary sacrifice’s requirement which first arose— the *abhikramaṇa* (the stepping forward) would also result in being a subsidiary to the primary sacrifice alone, just like the *prayājas*. Even if this were the case, [the *abhikramaṇa*] would still be accepted by that [primary] requirement.
Then he states the refutation: "Otherwise..."

[Objection: But surely, because they arise with the nature of being mental realizations (*bhāvanā*), the requirement for subsidiaries (*aṅga-ākāṅkṣā*) in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth is obstructed by the primary procedure (*pradhāna-kathaṃbhāva*), which is more fundamental and operates first; thus, mutual subsidiarity is not necessary.

Furthermore, once the obstruction is removed by subsidiaries enjoined through the three means of application—direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth—that requirement is revived, and it is therefore logical that even the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward), which falls within the "sandwich" (*saṃdaṃśa*) between those subsidiaries, would be grasped by it.
To this, he says: "Based on explicit scriptural statement" (*vācanika*).

The meaning is as follows: since it is appropriate to postulate the cessation of obstacles for each [subsidiary] individually— on the grounds that such cessation must be inferred by the very means of knowledge that establishes the subject (the substrate) in order to achieve the connection with the subsidiaries prescribed by the scriptural text— it is impossible for the requirement of the *prayāja*s to be grasped, because there is no evidence for postulating that the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) is what causes the cessation of those obstacles, and thus [the *abhikramaṇa*] has not been revived [as a factor].
"By way of extended application."
The meaning is: in the Dīkṣaṇīyā, Vaimṛdha, and other such rites.
"By means of accomplishing one's own [aim]" means:
The meaning is: by means of the substances, deities, and so forth, which bring about the essential nature of the sacrifice.
"Similarly here."

Since burning is observed by fire alone even when an excitant is present as an exciter in the world, and since an obstruction is observed by the jewel alone in the second moment despite the presence of the excitant in the first and third moments, the excitant does not have "excitation" as its effect due to such deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Rather, it is postulated that the gem possesses the status of an inhibitor when characterized by the absence of an activator,
and the non-existence of that [inhibitor] serves as the auxiliary for the fire;

however, in the case at hand, since there is an absence of the initial expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), we observe the adoption of scripturally enjoined (*vācanika*) and other subsidiaries through the expectancy of the *prayāja* offerings— which are themselves obstructed from yielding their fruit— due to the presence of the fruit residing in the principal rite.

Because there is no deviation (vyabhicāra), the effect to be postulated is merely the stimulation of the obstructed expectancy— a synonym for "revival"— and not the status of being a stimulant (uttejakatā) assigned to each individual factor.

This is because it would result in the fault of excessive complexity (gaurava) if the entire set of absences of the respective sets of stimulants were included within the delimiting condition (avacchedaka) of the obstructive power (pratibandhakatā).

Moreover, since it is postulated that the initial stimulant produces stimulation, while the final one destroys that stimulation, and that the Great Context (mahāprakaraṇa) acts as an inhibitor only when distinguished by the absence of such stimulation—

and that the non-existence of this [inhibition] serves as a cooperative cause— there is no evidence for assuming that each of the intermediate requirements (ākāṅkṣā) possesses stimulant power individually. Consequently, even the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward), which falls within the intermediate context characterized by stimulated requirement, is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of that [Great Context].

Therefore, since the *adhikāra* (qualification/entitlement) of the limbs (*aṅga*)— once stimulated— is what grasps the intention (*tātparya*) characterized by being a means to the *apūrva*, and because it is impossible for that [intention] to grasp such a characterizing intention by obstructing the previously commenced primary *adhikāra* through the production of another unobstructed [result],
the meaning is that its status as being for the sake of the *prayāja*s is established according to the logic of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* restriction of speech (*vāṅniyama*).
And there is [the expression] "asti cātra" (and there is here).

After the third *prayāja* called *iḍā*, with respect to the fourth *prayāja* called *barhis*, [the text] refers to the *aupabhṛta* clarified butter from the *upabhṛt* vessel into the *juhū* because that butter serves the purpose of both the *prayājas* and the *anuyājas*; and since it is only that portion intended for the *prayājas* which is to be brought over there, the mention of the subordinate parts (*aṅga*) of the *prayājas* is established, and thus there is no contradiction.

Now, one might object: since the root *juhoti* (to sacrifice) is not heard directly in the context of the *prayāja* offerings, and because the general injunction (*anārabhyavākya*) stating "one sacrifices with what is fourfold-drawn" prescribes the fourfold-drawn portion as the means for a *homa*, it follows that the *prayājas* lack the nature of a *homa*. Therefore, how can the stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*), which is enjoined by reference to them, be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to them? For this very reason, since the injunction "one sacrifices with what is fourfold-cut" prescribes the *homa* as a purifier (*saṃskāraka*) of the fourfold-portioning in the primary sacrifices, it is more logical that the stepping forward be an auxiliary to those primary sacrifices. Anticipating this objection, the author refutes it with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
"Having the act of throwing as its constituent part."
And this will be established in detail further on, in the third [chapter].

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), because the *pratihoma* serves to purify the agent, the performance of the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) would apply by extension (*atideśa*) even to the modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *prayāja* offerings;

however, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), since that [stepping forward] is for the sake of the *prayāja* itself, it does not apply by extension. This has not been stated here because it is self-evident.
Thus ends the tenth section concerning the status of the *abhikramaṇa* as a subsidiary of the *prayāja* offerings.
— — — — — — — (B1) (11th Adhikaraṇa /) (a.3 pā.1 adhi.11) But when there is doubt...

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, after enjoining the *sāmidhenī* verses with the injunction, "One should recite fifteen *sāmidhenīs*," their verbal qualities (*vācanika-guṇa*) are prescribed. Following that are the mantras called *nivid*, beginning with "Devaidha" and so forth.
Then follow the optional (*kāmya*) arrangements of *sāmidhenīs*, such as, "One desiring stability should recite twenty-one."
Then [the text says], "He wears the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder; he thereby creates the very mark of the gods.
Then again, there are the qualities of the *sāmidhenī* verses, such as, "The recitation between [the two mantras] is for the sake of having the gods present," and so forth.
In that context, the wearing of the sacrificial cord (*upavīta*) is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the *sāmidhenī* verses.
This is because of its intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).
Nor is that intermediate context interrupted by optional rites (*kāmyakalpa*) or *nivit* mantras;
for just as the *godohana* vessel and others do not interrupt the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is likewise untenable that optional rites should interrupt it.
Furthermore, just as with the *pūṣānumantraṇa* mantra, it is untenable for the *nivid* mantra to be [an independent rite] for that same reason.

In reality, however, although the mantras—which by their indicative power (*liṅga*) reveal the fruit of the *sāmidhenī* verses, namely the kindling of the fire—do indeed belong to the *sāmidhenīs* due to the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), there is no suspicion of a break [in the context]. When the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is reached that the mantra "aganma" belongs to the sacrifice because it reveals the fruit produced by the sacrifice, [the reply is: the *upavīta* does not belong to the *sāmidhenīs* because it is separated from them by the *nivid* mantras.
And the logic of the *pūṣānumantraṇa* mantra does not apply here;

for that logic of assuming a mantra like the *pūṣānumantraṇa* belongs to a different context (*paraprakaraṇa*) only where there are many scripturally enjoined (*vācanika*) subsidiaries at a later stage.
However, in a case where there are many interruptions and the scripturally enjoined subsidiary at a later stage is few, [the principle does not apply].

In this case, since the status of the recited subsidiary (vācanikāṅga) as a constituent part is established by the principle of being taught independently (anārabhyādhītanyāya), there is no need to assume the continuation of the context (prakaraṇānuvṛtti);
otherwise, even the Viśvajit sacrifice and others would incur the status of being subsidiaries to the Darśa sacrifice.
And in the present instance, because the Nivida mantras are numerous while the recited subsequent subsidiaries are few, one does not assume the continuation of the context.

In reality, however, there is no evidence for the injunction of passages such as "one should not recite [the *ṛc*] in between" (*nāntarānūcyam*) with reference to the *sāmidhenī* verses in general; rather, they are enjoined with reference to recitation (*anuvacana*) in general.
Consequently, because there is no specific presentation of the *sāmidhenīs*, the context (*prakaraṇa*) does not continue to apply.
As for the mention at the end—"The gods, indeed, recited the *sāmidhenīs*"—and so forth, [it is merely a concluding reference].
Since that [passage] is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the *āghāra* libation, it is not a proof [of its being a subordinate element].

For this very reason—and precisely because there is no scriptural mention (*vācanika*) of the *nivid*s as subordinate elements at the end—there is no suspicion that the *nivid*s possess the status of being subordinate to the *abhidhēnī*s.

Furthermore, a suspicion that they are subordinate [to each other] based on mere proximity (*saṃnidhi*) alone is improper, because mutual subordination is logically untenable and because such a view is set aside by the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Nor does this imply an impossibility of connecting a quality with a fruit in the optional (kāmya) rites due to a lack of a substratum;

for in that case, a different recitation itself is enjoined with reference to a fruit, and because it shares the commonality of being a recitation associated with a specific number, it is understood to have the obligatory fifteen-fold recitation as its archetype (prakṛti). Consequently, since the properties of that archetype—such as the threefold repetition—and its verses are obtained [in the optional rite], it is not devoid of ritual characteristics (adharmaka).
Since the *ṛc* (verse) and the *anuvacana* (recitation) are not primary, how can there be an extended application (*atideśa*)?
For in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the required number of *ṛcs* and recitations is already established by the very fact that the text is to be read with three repetitions;

thus, the injunction "one should recite fifteen *sāmidhenīs*" would otherwise be rendered purposeless. Consequently, as there is no other way out, one must resort to the "logic of the flour" (*saktunyāya*) and set aside the original application (*viniyogabhaṅga*).

Since it is the recitation (*anuvacana*) qualified by the mantra that is the very thing to be enjoined, it is logical that the *ṛc* verses, which constitute its constituent parts, are thereby obtained. Furthermore, their status as subordinate elements (*guṇatva*) is not due to their illuminating the fruit of the recitation, but rather due to their being the generators of the recitation; this is because it is simpler [to assume the latter].

Therefore, there is neither sublation (*bādha*) nor modification (*ūha*) due to the omission of the door (*dvāra*). Since the word "after" (*anu*) expresses the immediate succession of the constituent elements that are subsidiaries of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and since such succession cannot be performed outside the sacrifice because it is dependent on another [action], its performance within the body of the sacrifice is established.

Furthermore, because the function of the original recitation (*prākṛtānuvacana*) is accomplished through the modified recitation (*vaikṛtānuvacana*) itself by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*), there is no separate performance of it.
Therefore, even in those [sacrifices], there is no continuation of the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *sāmidhenī* verses.
And if that is so, why should the *upavīta* not be a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of them?
Because they, being modified forms (*vikṛti*), have their requirements satisfied by the archetypal subsidiaries (*prākṛtāṅga*) and thus lack a [distinct] context.

Furthermore, because there is an absence of a textual statement (*vācanika*) or a syntactic connection (*aṅgasandaṃśa*), it is established by the context of the major section (*mahāprakaraṇa*) that the *upavīta* is an accessory (*aṅga*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; as a purifier of their performer, it must be performed by those performers at the commencement of every ritual application. // 11 //
Thus ends the eleventh section, concerning the fact that the *upavīta* and the *sāmidhenī* verses are not subordinate elements [of the sacrifice].
(B2) (The Principle of the Tongs):

Here, although [the example] is not directly useful for the inquiry—since it serves merely to establish the existence of a subordinate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) as the basis for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the *sāmidhenī* verses are subsidiary to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, and the refutation (*siddhānta*) that they are subsidiary to them—it is nevertheless cited together with the subject sentence: "In the *darśapūrṇamāsa*... etc.
It has been stated that because they serve as the cause for the ultimate goal of the system, [the details] belong to the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
thus, these are qualities prescribed by direct scriptural statement.
The meaning is that one recites the first verse three times and the last verse three times, and so forth.
"Recited in the interval."

"That which is chanted in the *krauñca* manner belongs to the Asuras; that which is deep (*mandra*) belongs to humans; that which is between these two belongs to the *Sadasyas*"—thus, having previously deprecated the *krauñca* and the *mandra*, the *madhyama* (middle) tone, which is intermediate between them, is established.
Furthermore, in the seventh and eighth sections of the chapter on Viśvarūpa Vaiśvāvasava, the *Sāmidhenī-brāhmaṇa* is recited;
and in the ninth section, there are the *nivid-mantras* beginning with: "The god kindled by Manu, praised by the Seers, rejoiced in by the sages, lauded by poets, and extolled by sacred hymns."

The meaning is that an inquiry is undertaken because of doubts regarding the existence of a subordinate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) and its interruption: in the tenth [section], the Brāhmaṇa text records the various optional forms of the *sāmidhenī* verses, and in the eleventh, the injunctions regarding the *upavīta* (wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder) and the qualities pertaining to the interval between it; thus, there is a doubt concerning the presence of such a subordinate context and whether it is interrupted.

Although this doubt regarding the existence and interruption of the subordinate context must necessarily be introduced for the purpose of explaining the ambiguous terms in the Sūtra, [it is addressed here].

Likewise, because of the commonality of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent, [the author]— without explicitly mentioning the immediate connection (*anantara-saṅgati*) consisting of an exception (*apavāda*) to the syntactic connection with the proximate [element] according to the Bhāṣyakāra’s view, or an exception to the intermediate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*) according to the Vārttikakāra’s view regarding the sacred thread (*upavīta*) present in the intellect—

and intending that there is no flaw even in the absence of a connection to the [specific] chapter (*pāda-saṅgati*) due to the lack of an inquiry useful for the scriptural application (*śrauta-viniyoga*), [proceeds as follows].
He states the prima facie view: "In that regard, [the rule] 'wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder'..."

In this context, regarding the doubt as to whether the so-called *upavīta*— the *brahmasūtra* consisting of nine threads, which is synonymous with the *yajñopavīta*— is what should be understood, or whether it refers to the arrangement of a cloth, the resolution will be made in the third [chapter].
This is because of the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).

And furthermore—since the *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite) such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), even though an intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) exists, the *sāmidhenī* verses have the visible effect (*dṛṣṭakārya*) of kindling the fire; thus, because their requirement for procedure is satisfied by the procedure consisting of that visible form alone, they have no need for further procedure. Moreover, even if those [rites] are subsidiary parts by virtue of explicit scriptural statement (*vacana*), how could there be subsidiariness through an intermediate context when such an intermediate context does not even exist?
This is not to be said;

for even the kindling of the fire (agnisamindhana) is to be brought about (bhāvya) because it is endowed with the status of being a means to the unseen potency (apūrva), and since the *sāmidhenī* verses produce a restricted unseen potency (*niyamādṛṣṭa*), the requirement for a Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*) is established, thereby making the existence of a subordinate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) logical— this is the meaning of the phrase "or by the *nivid* mantras."

The meaning is that, because the *nivit* mantras—by virtue of their indicative power (*liṅga*) as assisted by the context of the main section (*mahāprakaraṇa*)—serve to illuminate the kindling of the fire for Agni, just like the *sāmidhenī* verses, they cannot be subordinate to the *sāmidhenīs* for the purpose of kindling the fire;
thus, due to the intervention [of these mantras], the context of the *sāmidhenīs* is severed according to the principle of not depending on what has already been established.
This refers to the case of the *godohana* vessel and so forth.

The meaning is that, just as in the case of the *praṇayana* (carrying forward of the fire), because the context (*prakaraṇa*) continues by virtue of its serving as the basis for the *praṇayana* which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it does not interrupt the context; so too here, it is logical that there is no interruption of the context.
With the words "In reality, however," he avoids the interruption [of the ritual] by means of another method as well.

Just as the *sāmidhenī* verses, although they also serve to illuminate the kindling of the fire, are subsidiary to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices because the *sāmidhenīs* serve to illuminate the act of throwing wood into the fire for the purpose of kindling it; and just as the mantra "we have gone" (*aganma*), which serves to illuminate the accomplishment of the fruit of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, is a subsidiary of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*— so too, although the *nivid* formulas also serve to illuminate the kindling of the fire, they are [subsidiary] because they serve to illuminate the accomplishment of the kindling of the fire, which is the result of throwing fuel into the fire, as indicated by the past participle "kindled" (*iddha*) in the *nivid*.

The meaning is that because the *sāmidhenī* verses illuminate the throwing of fuel-sticks (*idhma*) and thereby manifest the accomplishment of the result, they do not constitute an auxiliary (*aṅga*) that must be depended upon; thus, it is impossible for them to act as an interrupter.

While it is possible for the manifestation of the production of a fruit to be an auxiliary (aṅga) because the fruit of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices—being accomplished through an unseen medium (adṛṣṭa)—depends upon faith, and thus its manifestation generates faith; here, however, since the state of the fire being well-kindled (samiddhatva), which is the fruit of the throwing of fuel-sticks (idhma-prakṣepa), is accomplished through a visible medium and thus does not depend upon faith, the manifestation of the production of that fruit cannot logically be an auxiliary. Therefore, [the mantra] serves the purpose of manifesting the throwing of fuel-sticks, which is the means for accomplishing the fruit manifested by the *nivid*.

Since it is impossible to preclude the fact that the *sāmidhenī* verses themselves are its constituent parts, and since there is no decisive reason (*vinigamanā*) to conclude that the interruption is caused by those [verses], the refutation of other methods stated in the passage beginning with "but in reality" (*vastutastu*) has been set aside as being obvious. Setting aside the argument that—like the *pūṣānumantraṇa* mantra—it does not cause an interruption, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words: "by the *nivid*s."
"Otherwise," means:

The meaning is that, because there exists a scriptural injunction for the *darśa* subsidiaries immediately after the injunctions for the *viśvajit* and other sacrifices, it would follow that they are subsidiaries of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* by virtue of assuming the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* context (*prakaraṇa*).
This refers to the "assumption of the continued application of the context."

Therefore, since it is impossible for the subsequent subsidiary elements (*uttarāṅga*) to be subordinate to that [central act] by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), the meaning is that—according to the principle that those studied as "unconnected" (*anārabhyādhīta*) find their place in the archetype (*prakṛti*)—the status of being a subsidiary to the *sāmidhenī* verses of the archetype is established. Furthermore, this has been stated while not yet accepting that the *upavīta* (wearing of the sacred thread) falls within the "sandwiching" (*sandaṃśa*) of the ritual procedure.
In reality, however, he states that there is no "tongs" (sandaṃśa) at all, beginning with the words "vastutastu."
Because there is no specific presentation [of the object].

Furthermore, since there would be no interruption [of the context], the general term *anūcya* (to be recited) would have to refer to a specific [recitation] due to the continuation of the context (*prakaraṇānuvṛtti*). And if it were to refer to a specific [recitation], then the continuation of the context would result from the "sandwiching" (*saṃdaṃśa*), which leads to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Thus, the meaning is that there is no presentation of the *sāmidhenī* verses by virtue of referring to a specific [recitation].
[This is stated] because [the passage in question] is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) for the *āghāra* libation.

The meaning is that since the restatement of the *sāmidhenī* verses lacks the purpose of enjoining a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), and is instead employed for the sake of praise (*stuti*), it is impossible to assume the persistence of an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) toward them.
But surely— according to the principle of the *indriyakāmādhikaraṇa*, since the qualities such as "twenty-onefold" must necessarily be connected to a fruit,

and since it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if the locus were provided by that same sentence, the locus must be provided by the context (*prakaraṇa*) alone; thus, because the context is revitalized by these optional rites for specific desires, their status as subsidiaries of the *sāmidhenī* verses is unavoidable.

And considering that in the absence of the revitalization of the context, how could the connection between the quality and the fruit be established, he raises an objection with the words: "Nor is it thus."
Therefore, because no substratum is obtained, there is no connection between the qualities and the fruit;

rather, the injunction applies to the recitation itself as distinct from the twenty-one qualities and so forth which do not enter into it. Thus, he refutes [the opponent's view] by stating that the context cannot be revived on account of that [recitation], saying "tattra" and "saṅkhyāyuktā."
The phrase "accompanied by a number" is stated in order to exclude similarity based on commonality with the *anuvākyā* verses.

Now, one might object: "In the archetypal injunction, 'There are fifteen *sāmidhenīs*, since the *ṛks* known as *sāmidhenīs*—whose status as subsidiaries is understood through the context—are objects to be refined (*saṃskārya*) by the accusative case, and since the production of a fruit [for the archetype] has been refuted in the eighth [book] via the rule of extension (*atideśa*), there is no need for a result here.

Furthermore, one might suspect that if the *sāmidhenīs* were the objects of the injunction, the qualification "fifteen" would not be intended to be significant; however, this is not the case, because that number is already established by the very recitation [of the verses] together with the rule for threefold repetition. With this intention, he raises the objection: "Nor [is it the case] that... (*na cārccām iti*).
"Endowed with threefold practice."
The meaning is that it is simply by reciting the eleven verses together with the injunction for triple repetition, as expressed by the phrase "he recites the first verse thrice.
And [it is so] by implication.
For recitation (*anuvacana*) consists of the act of utterance;
and since that [recitation] is possible only through the delimitation of the act of utterance for the purpose of manifesting the meaning, it is obtained by implication (*arthataḥ*).
This is the meaning of the phrase "as something to be enjoined" (*vidheyatvena*).
The meaning is that [the object] is to be enjoined by virtue of its being the purpose of fire and fuel as conceived through its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).

As for what has been stated here by the authors of the *Prakāśa*— that, in order to avoid conflict with the indicative power (*liṅga*) residing in the *sāmidhenī* verses, the subordinate status of the *sāmidhenīs* toward the recitation is established on the grounds that they illuminate the kindling of the fire which is the fruit of the recitation— that is somehow untenable; for in the case of a recitation intended for fruits such as stability (*pratiṣṭhā*), the *sāmidhenīs* would fail to apply due to the loss of the necessary means (*dvāra*).

To indicate that [the view] is incorrect—because it would result in the displacement (*ūha*) of terms such as "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) with respect to the attainment [of results], and because it would fail to establish the incidental fulfillment (*prasaṅga-siddhi*) of the obligatory (*nitya*) rite by means of the optional (*kāmya*) one—he explains its status as a subordinate factor (*guṇatva*) in another way: "And its being a subordinate factor... and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Does this not lead to the conclusion that other recitations (*anuvacana*), which are not included within the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, would have to be performed outside of those rituals? To this, he says: "And by the word *anu*..."

Regarding this, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* maintains that there is no performance outside the sacrifice; for, having accepted the meaning of the prefix *anu-* as "immediately following" in the injunction "Recite for Agni while being kindled" (*agnaye samidhyamānāyānubrūhi*), and since the injunction itself serves the purpose of kindling the fire for the sake of the ritual, it would follow that its application occurs outside the ritual context, which would result in the contradiction of it being a recitation (*anuvacana*). Therefore, it cannot be performed outside the sacrifice.

Pārthasārathi [argues] that because the *namaḥ pravaktre* formula is recited immediately after the *praiṣa*, and because the *sāmidhenī* verses are recited immediately after that, one must accept the sequence following the *nigada*. Since this [formula] also serves the purpose of kindling the fire—which is itself prompted by another [rite]—it does not obtain a place outside the sacrifice; thus, its status as an *anuvacana* (recitation) would be sublated if it were used externally, and therefore there is no external performance of it.

And thus, even without extracting one [of the two options], since the accomplishment of the result occurs in every way through the non-performance of the external sacrifice, it was stated that the sequence immediately following the preceding ritual act (*pūrvapadārtha*) is mentioned collectively in order to indicate the difference of opinion without having performed that [extraction].

However, in reality—because the sequence following the *praiṣa* (direction) would be obtained by the very force of the context within the meaning of the *praiṣa*, which would render the injunction for recitation (*anuvacana*) purposeless;

and because there would be the consequence of the injunction being unnecessary, as no sequence is required between two actions performed by different agents—in order to secure the status of a necessary injunction (*apekṣitavidhi*), [the sequence] is established.

It is appropriate to enjoin the immediate sequence of the *hautra* recitations themselves—having been set aside by the immediate sequence of the *praiṣas*—by means of a restorative injunction (*pratiprasava-vidhi*).

Furthermore, since the *nigadas*, like the *sāmidhenīs*, are not established as subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the *sāmidhenīs* due to their independence in serving the purpose of kindling the fire (*agnisamindhana*), it should be understood that the performance [of the *nigadas*] occurs within [the sequence] in accordance with them.
Now, although the recitation (*anuvacana*) follows immediately after the *nigada* beginning with "Homage to the speaker" (*namah pravaktre*),

nevertheless, by examining such sentences as "O five peoples, enjoy my *hautra*; may I today attain the first [portion] of speech," it is determined that this recitation is intended for the sake of all rites to be performed— or at least for the sake of the *sāmidhenī* verses alone— and thus has the purpose of praying to the speaker and others.

Since the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *sāmidhenī* verses also exists, its application outside the sacrifice is logically consistent; thus, its immediate succession [to the main act] is indeed possible. Even when there is immediate succession to the meaning of the *praiṣa* (direction), since the application of an auxiliary—in the form of making known the permission for the sake of its own result—can occur through modification (*ūha*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), immediate succession is possible even when it is performed outside the sacrifice by way of implication; therefore, there is performance outside the sacrifice.

If it is argued that [the sequence] is difficult to establish, we say no; for, by the word *anu* (after), which denotes a subsequent time, the performance of the *sāmidhenī* verses along with their ancillaries is enjoined as occurring at a time subsequent to other preceding constituent elements that are not themselves ancillaries of those verses.

Since a preceding element that has been prompted by another cannot itself be brought forward [as a primary impeller], it is impossible for the [recitation of the *sāmidhenīs*] to occur at a time subsequent to such a [primary] element.
Therefore, it should be understood from the Kaustubha that there is no occurrence of the performance of a separate external sacrifice.

As for what is stated in the Vārtika: "If there were a separate performance, then even those verses such as 'pravo vāja' which are obtained through extension (*atideśa*) would not qualify as *sāmidhenīs*, because they do not illuminate the kindling of the fire, and since the fire situated within the performance would be fruitless and thus not something to be kindled, it would be impossible for the verses to illuminate the kindling of the fire; consequently, the number twenty-one and so forth could not serve to delimit the *sāmidhenīs*."
It was stated that [the requirement] obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) would be sublated;
however, because the recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses serves the purpose of merely generating [the fire], and since the incidental kindling of the fire is assumed to be its secondary purpose,
the recitation— which has "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) as its fruit— remains an impelling factor (*prayojaka*) even in the absence of the kindling of the fire prompted by another [rite].

Since its occurrence is possible because it serves the purpose of occasionally kindling the fire, its status as a *sāmidhenī* verse is not compromised; thus, its performance outside the ritual is not a subverter [of the rule], as noted by the Venerable Teacher.
He states the result of establishing that the performance occurs within the ritual as follows: "vaikṛta... etc.

Therefore, he concludes that because the necessary substratum is obtained even for the fruits of optional rites (*kāmya*), there is no need to revive the context of the *sāmidhenī* verses; thus he says, "Therefore, even in those [optional rites]...
and "...by way of being a purifier of their performer."

And by this, it is shown that according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the *upavīta* is subordinate to the *sāmidhenī* verses, the performer must wear it at the very commencement of those verses so as not to cause distraction; whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is to be worn at the commencement of the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice itself. This is the demonstrated purpose.
Thus ends the eleventh section, concerning the fact that the wearing of the sacred thread (upavīta) is not an auxiliary element of the *sāmidhenī* verses.
