In another section concerning the *ādhāna* (the fire-consecration rite) following the *pavamāneṣṭi*, it is heard in the scripture: "The *vāraṇa* wood is fit for sacrifice; the *vaikaṅkata* wood is fit for sacrifice.

Since the *vāraṇa* and other woods mentioned there as means of sacrifice cannot be directly employed in the *ādhāna*—which is not itself a sacrifice—the conclusion reached by the author of the *Bhāṣya* is that, according to the principle of "uselessness [of the primary] leading to its inclusion in its parts" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), they must be applied specifically to the *pavamāneṣṭi*, which is a sacrifice. This is the position attained.

Since the sentence "He offers in the Āhavanīya" (yadāhavanīye juhoti), which is recited in the section on the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), establishes that the Pavamāna oblations are subsidiary to the fires (*agni*) and not subsidiary to the consecration itself, the principle of "uselessness [otherwise] leading to subsidiarity to its parts" (*anarthakyatadaṅganyāya*) is inapplicable.

Furthermore, because the Pavamāna sacrifices themselves are not present in their own form at that time, the materials such as *vāraṇa* and *vaikaṅkata* wood must be subsidiary to all archetypal sacrifices (*sarvaprakṛtiyajña*) or to all sacrifices (*sarvayajña*).

The author of the Vārttika, however, maintains that the pavamāna oblations do not have the fire-altar (*agni*) as their subordinate element by virtue of the *anārabhyavākya* (the general statement not occurring in a specific context).
This is because, by that [statement], the *āhavanīya* fire is enjoined with reference to all oblations (*sarvahoma*);
and since there is no specific presentation of the pavamāna sacrifices themselves, there is no evidence for the locative case to indicate their status as the primary locus (*prādhānya*).
Nor can another sentence be postulated within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices,
because even in its absence, it is logically established that the *vāraṇa* wood and other materials serve the purpose of all sacrifices.

Or, even if such a [sentence] were to exist in the context of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), even then it would only establish that the oblations which are subsidiary to the consecration have the *āhavanīya* fire as their locus, but not that they have the fires themselves as their primary purpose.
Because [if it were taken literally], there would be the consequence of it being merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*).

Therefore, the word *āhavanīya* occurring in that context is indeed indicative (*lakṣaka*) of fire qualified by the unique transcendental result (*apūrva*) of origination produced by the consecration (*ādhāna*);
for at that time, the primary *āhavanīya*, which consists of fire qualified by the supreme transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*), does not yet exist.
And it is not the case that, because of the mention of the oblations for the Pavamāna sacrifices, there is an absence of means to obtain the Gārhapatya and other fires;
for in that context, there is no evidence for setting aside the primary Gārhapatya and others.

Therefore, even though there is another statement, since there is no proof that the Pavamāna sacrifices are subsidiary to the fires, or even if they were subsidiary to the fire-installation (ādhāna), the fact that the Vāraṇa wood and so forth serve the purpose of all sacrifices must be established in this very manner.

In all cases where there is no inherent non-deviation from its own intended object, the entry into the context (*prakaraṇa*) is for the purpose of defining it as a means to the unseen merit (*apūrva*), as in the case of "the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn*) and so forth.

For this very reason, in such instances, the principle of "uselessness [of the whole] leading to its parts" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*) applies. However, in the present case, since the status of being a means to the *apūrva* without deviation is already established by the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) itself, there is no entry into the context for that purpose. Consequently, since the connection with the primary act (*pradhāna*) does not even arise, how could there be an application of the principle regarding its subsidiaries (*tadaṅga*)?

Even if this were the case, if the vessels were mentioned in the proximity of the Pavamāna-iṣṭis, then— since a restatement (anuvāda) applies to what is proximate when possible, as in the case of "one should sacrifice with rice" (vrīhibhir yajeta)— it would have as its scope only the primary sacrifice (prakṛta).
But this is not the case either.
Since the Pavamāna sacrifices are located in another section [of the ritual manual],
the Vāraṇa and other vessels are intended for all sacrifices.

The purpose [of this discussion] is that, following the Pavamāneṣṭis, if the vessels are destroyed, there arises a need for new ones for the sake of the Darśa and other sacrifices; according to the Siddhānta, these must be made of Vāraṇa wood and so forth. // 3 // 12 //
Thus ends the twelfth section, concerning the fact that the horse-sacrifice is for the purpose of all sacrifices.
(B2) He provides an example of the subject sentence: "in the case of the fire-consecration."

The meaning of the term *yajñāvacara* is "an instrument for the performance of sacrifice," based on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that it is that by which one proceeds (*avacaryate*) or performs (*anuṣṭhīyate*) the sacrifice. In this context, since there is a cognition of non-difference—namely, that "that by which one performs in the sacrifice is the *vāraṇa* (elephant-apple tree)"—the injunction prescribes the species of *vāraṇa* and *vaikaṅkata* with reference to the sacrifice, by way of delimiting the sacrificial vessels that serve as its instruments. Therefore, in cases such as the *juhū* ladle where another species is enjoined, [the rule] does not apply.
Even in the case of the mortar, pestle, and so forth, there is no contradiction with that injunction;

for there too, by virtue of the exclusion (paryudāsa) contained in the supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa), "But one should not offer with this," the prohibition is effected through vessels that serve as implements other than the oblation (homa) known as "depositing" which is an auxiliary of the sacrifice;

and likewise, by the force of the supplementary statement recorded in the *Adhikaraṇamālā*, "One should indeed offer with this," it is effected through vessels that serve as implements for the oblation of depositing which is an auxiliary of the sacrifice.
Regarding the phrase "the placement of the *vaikaṅkata* [wood]," the venerable Pūjyapāda states in the *Kaustubha* that it refers to the *vaikaṅkata* wood being used for the purpose of all vessels.

However, in the *Nyāyasudhā*, it is stated that the *vaikaṅkata* serves the function of all vessels; thus, there is a distinction. He himself will clarify the purpose of the phrase "in another location" (*pradeśāntare*).

In that context, since the measurement of seventeen *aratnis*—which is understood as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *Vājapeya* sacrifice—is impossible there, it applies to the animal sacrifices (*paśuyāga*) which are subordinate to it.

By that same reasoning, since it is established that the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) and *upavyāna* (tying the sacred thread over the left shoulder) involve the agent who is a constituent part of the ritual action, there arises an inquiry into the specific distinction regarding the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that agent, which serves as a subordinate part of a particular ritual. Consequently, the principle of "uselessness [of the primary] and its subordination to that" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), which had previously reached its conclusion in that context, applies here as well.

Even according to the view of the Vārttikakāra, although the *pavamāneṣṭis* are auxiliary to the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), they lack the nature of a sacrifice (*yajña*); therefore, for those [rites] recited within the context of the *ādhāna*, [the aforementioned principle holds].

In the opinion of the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), the introduction of the vessels (*pātra*) into those [verses] is an exception (*apavāda*). However, according to the author of the *Vārttika*, it is a contextual application (*prāsaṅgika*). He does not explicitly state the immediate connection (*anantara-saṅgati*), nor the connection with the chapter (*pāda-saṅgati*)—which consists in an inquiry into the application of figurative Vedic texts (*gauṇa-śruti*)—nor the doubt itself, as these are obvious; instead, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) directly with the words "In that case" (*tatra*).

When the contingency of meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*) arises regarding the nature of the sacrifice, and when entry into the context (*prakaraṇa*) is required for the purpose of characterizing it as a means to the *apūrva*,

then— since the installation (*ādhāna*), which is the means to the *apūrva* under discussion, is not itself a sacrifice and thus cannot be included [directly] within the sacrifice— the contingency of meaninglessness arises even with respect to that installation.

Consequently, because the *Pavamāneṣṭis*, which are its constituent parts (*aṅga*), possess the status of being subsidiaries (*aṅgatva*), they alone [are connected] by way of their relationship as contributing to the *apūrva* under discussion.
The injunction regarding the elephant and others is made by referring to them through the word "sacrifice" (yajña).

Although there is no specific qualifying authority that brings the Pavamāneṣṭis to mind because they are recited in another section, nevertheless, by means of the authority pertaining to the primary rite itself—and since that authority is not sublated in its primary aspect—it brings to mind the Pavamāneṣṭis as related to it; thus, this is not a case of the maxim of "uselessness [of the primary] leading to its subsidiary."
The meaning is that there is a contradiction if [the scripture] has that as its purpose.

Since the sentence "one offers in the Āhavanīya," being studied as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), prescribes the Āhavanīya fire as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), there is no evidence for interpreting the locative case as having the sense of the accusative. Therefore, even if one were to somehow assume its primacy and conceive of the Pavamāna oblations as subordinate to it, this would lead to the undesirable consequence that other sacrifices such as the Viśvajit would also become subordinate to it, thereby rendering them fruitless. Thus, although by that [injunction] their status as subordinate parts of the fire-sacrifice (*agni*) is not established;

Nevertheless, because of the author of the Bhāṣya’s writing in the section on the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), he infers the existence of another sentence and establishes its established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the passage beginning with "in the section on the *ādhāna*."

And by that assumed sentence, there is no injunction of the *āhavanīya* fire as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the oblation (*homa*) by way of being its locus (*adhikaraṇatā*), because the *āhavanīya* itself is not yet established [at this stage].

Therefore, just as in the case of "the cows should be kept in that house," one must accept that the locative case here expresses predominance (*prādhānya*). Consequently, based on the sentence, there is the cognition of the fire's status as a subordinate element common to all oblations, such as the *pūrṇāhuti*.

The meaning is that, because it would contradict the context (*prakaraṇa*), these [offerings] are subsidiary to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration); thus, since they possess equal primacy with the *ādhāna*, the principle of "uselessness [leading to inclusion] in its subsidiary" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*) does not apply here.
By this, the objection—"How can the *pavamāna-havis* offerings be included as subsidiaries when the fire is already occupied by the scripturally enjoined *ādhāna*?"—is refuted;
for even this [principle of context] is capable of establishing that [subsidiarity] through the force of the principle of "prevention by uselessness" (*ānarthakya-pratihata-nyāya*).
"Consisting of all constituent elements."

In the eleventh [book], because of the hearing of the word "sacrifice" in the statement, "He yokes with five; the sacrifice is fivefold," the Commentator will establish as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the yoking of Agni—enjoined by the sentence, "I yoke Agni with power and ghee"—is for the sake of the primary vessel.
Following that, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* establishes here as well that the word "sacrifice" denotes only the primary sacrifice; it is with this intention [that the following is stated].

Having stated that the term *yajña* (sacrifice)—which is a synonym for the root *yajati*—functions as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of all primary rituals (*pradhāna*), there is no evidence for postulating an additional power for the word *yajña*. Therefore, since it is improper to restrict the scope of the word *yajña* in the sentence "All this indeed... and in the sentence "This seventeen-fold Prajāpati is dependent upon the sacrifice," just as [it is improper to restrict it] in those other passages, it must refer to the entirety of sacrifice, common to both the primary and the subordinate rites.

It should be understood that another alternative view has been stated—namely, that it serves as an auxiliary to all sacrifices (sarvayajñāṅgatva)—according to the manner explained by Kaustubha, namely, that this is "proper" (yuktam).
"Even in the absence of that."
The assumption [of such a connection] is improper because it serves merely to exclude the elephants and so forth from being auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the Pavamāna-oblation;
for even without making that assumption, by means of the exclusion itself, they would—according to the method to be explained—result in being for the sake of other sacrifices. This is the meaning.
"It is indeed established" (*siddhir eva*).

The particle *eva* (only) is used precisely to indicate that otherwise, the status of the *āhavanīya* as the locus [of the oblation] could not be established by the sentence taught as an *anārabhyādhīta* (independent injunction).

Even though there is a sublation of the primary *āhavanīya* as the locus— which would otherwise apply to the archetypal *homa*s that are parts of the *pavamāneṣṭi*s by means of extended application (*atideśa*)—
it is still possible, given the circumstances, for the locus to be fire characterized by being produced specifically through the act of *ādhāna* (consecration), as observed in the archetype.
Since there is no evidence to sublate it, the attainment of having the *āhavanīya* fire as the locus for the aforementioned [acts] is possible.

In the same way, the attainment of having the *gārhapatya* and *anvāhāryapacana* fires as loci for the aforementioned acts—such as the cooking of oblations, the offering of flour-residue (*piṣṭalepa*), and the offering of parched grains (*phalīkaraṇa*)—which are auxiliary to the *pavamāneṣṭi*, must be established.

To indicate that, in accordance with that [possibility], there is no necessity for enjoining the *āhavanīya* as the locus, it was stated: "only those which are auxiliary to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration)."

The sense is that since these [entities] are non-ordinary (aprākṛta), the aforementioned method does not apply to them as their substratum; therefore, this very [method] must be resorted to in order to achieve that application.

And thus, when it is established through the context (*prakaraṇa*) that the Pavamāna-iṣṭis are subsidiary to the fire-installation (*ādhāna*), one might ask: "How is it that the maxim of 'uselessness [of the primary] leading to its being a subsidiary' (*anarthakyatadaṅganyāya*) does not apply here? To this doubt, the answer is as follows: according to the method set forth in the *Nyāyasudhā* and the *Vārtika*, the term "sacrifice" (*yajña*) applies only to the principal sacrifices; since the Pavamāna-iṣṭis, being merely subsidiaries, lack the status of a "sacrifice," the prohibition of the *vāraṇa* wood and other such items—enjoined with reference to a "sacrifice"—cannot find application therein. This is the intended meaning.
Considering even the possible solution to be untenable according to the reasoning set forth previously regarding the Kaustubha, and setting that aside, he proposes another solution:
"Even though the Vāraṇa tree and others are auxiliary to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration)..."
It is precisely for the sake of all sacrifices.
“This seventeenfold Prajāpati indeed follows along in the sacrifice. The meaning is that, just as the seventeen syllables designated as Prajāpati—
being enjoined with reference to the sacrifice in general— are for the sake of all sacrifices because they are enjoined in that form, so too this [sāman] is for the sake of all sacrifices,
and not merely for the sake of the archetype (prakṛti) alone.

And thus, since the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is untenable due to the application of the principle that "what is purposeless is not a part of that" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), it is improper to state the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of a different section (*adhikaraṇa*) for the sake of refuting it; furthermore, because its placement outside the context would result in its being established elsewhere—just like the *puṣānumantraṇa* mantra—and because there would be no point in establishing it here, there arises the suspicion that the restatement of the sūtra is redundant. [This refers to] the *nivid*s...

Anticipating the objection that there can be no interruption of the context of the *sāmidhenī* verses because they are subordinate to them, and intending to provide a resolution by showing the meaningfulness of the present discussion as a supplement to the preceding section, he states the remaining purpose: "The purpose," etc.

The meaning is that, although it is possible to perform the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa and other rites in the interim by using those very vessels—since they are held until the end for the purpose of burning them as a disposal method (pratipatti) once their function as *pavamāna-havis* has ended—and thus there would be parsimony in material usage (*upādāna-lāghava*), nevertheless, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), if those vessels should be destroyed by chance, one must employ materials from unspecified trees for the sake of the Darśa and other rites.
However, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the requirement is that they must be made of the specific materials such as *vāraṇa* wood; this is the practical application (*prayojana*).
Thus ends the twelfth section concerning the fact that the sacrificial post and other elements serve the purpose of all sacrifices.
— — — — — — — (B1) (Thirteenth Topic / [A.3 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 13]) And mutually.

In the sequence of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, the *liṅga* (indicative power) and *krama* (sequence) of the *vārtraghnī* and *vṛdhanvatī* mantras—which are heard [in the text]—are set aside by the two sentences, "The *vārtraghnī* verses are recited at the full moon sacrifice; the *vṛdhanvatī* verses at the new moon sacrifice," which establish their status as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the primary rites (*pradhāna*).

Since it is accepted that even the *liṅga* residing in a mantra may be set aside by a sentence residing in the *Brāhmaṇa*, as in the passage beginning with "Even if [the offering] is for another deity," this being the case, [we reply: because sublation (*bādha*) is improper when an interpretation without sublation is possible, there is no sublation.
It is a subordinate factor of the primary rite;
for it is not possible for a mantra dedicated to Soma to be free from conflict with its indicative power (liṅga),
since Soma lacks the status of being a deity [in this context].
Furthermore, because even the status of being a substratum (*adhiṣṭhānatva*) is impossible on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).

In reality, however, since this sentence achieves its purpose through the mere establishment of a restrictive rule (*vyavasthā*), it does not convey that [the *vārtraghni* verses] are subsidiary to the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*).

As for the restriction, it is a temporal one, such as "the two *ājyabhāga* offerings performed on the full moon day are those characterized by the *vārtraghni* verses," and so forth; these specific details should be consulted in the *Kaustubha*. (3/13)
Thus ends the thirteenth section concerning the status of the *vārtraghnī* verses as auxiliary elements of the Full Moon sacrifice.

(B1) Having previously stated that the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside by the sentence (*vākya*), and because the sublation of order (*krama*) follows as a consequence of that, [the author] here provides the immediate connection (*anantara-saṅgati*) by means of an exception (*apavāda*). Without explicitly stating the connection to the chapter (*pāda-saṅgati*) or the doubt— since these are clear— due to the consideration of the application of figurative direct statement (*gauṇa-śruti-viniyoga*) through the indication of the sense of the accusative case (*dvitīyārtha-lakṣaṇā*) by the locative case (*saptamī*) in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the prima facie position after first demonstrating the subject matter (*viṣaya*).
This is the sequence for the portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga).
“Agni shall strike down the Vṛtras”—this is the first *vārtraghnī* verse.
“O Soma, you are the lord of the virtuous”—this is the second *vārtraghnī*, belonging to Soma.
“Agni with the ancient hymn”—this is the first *vṛdhanvatī* verse, belonging to Agni.

The meaning is that in the *hautraka* section [of the Veda], following the sequence of the *prayāja* formulas, four mantras are heard as the *anuvākyās* for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings to Agni and Soma, beginning with “*soma gīrbhis tvā vayam*” and “*dvitīyā vṛdhanvatī*. Among them,
the distinction is that the first two are called *vārtraghnī* because they contain the word *vṛtrahan*, while the latter two are called *vṛdhanvatī* because they contain the root *vṛdh*.

Since there is no evidence in the words of the learned (the *Mīmāṃsāsūtras*) to indicate that these are separate rites, and since it is impossible for these two sentences to enjoin mantras in those very [rites],

yet such an application is possible in the principal rites such as the Āgneya, the author— intending to show that this is not redundant with the *Paurṇamāsī* section because of the arising of a further doubt regarding their purpose being a restriction (*vyavasthā*)— establishes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words: "The indicative power (*liṅga*) and the order (*krama*)."

In that case, since it is impossible for the sequence [of the two ājyabhāgas] to be sublated by a temporal restriction established through their performance according to the introductory [textual order], a restriction must be stated by means of an indication (lakṣaṇā) referring to the ājyabhāgas that are subsidiary to the principal rites occurring at the times of the full moon and the new moon. And such an indication is improper precisely because it would entail the fault of *lakṣaṇā*.

Therefore, since it is observed elsewhere that the words "full moon" (paurṇamāsī) and "new moon" (amāvāsyā) refer to the Āgneya and other sacrifices either through direct denotation (śakti) or through conventional metaphorical indication (nirūḍhalakṣaṇā), here too one must somehow resort to the locative case as signifying predominance;
thus, the meaning is that it is logical that [the Āgneya and others] are indeed subordinate to it (the sacrifice).

Now, one might object: "Even if it is appropriate for a sentence to sublate a weak order, it is not proper for it to sublate a powerful indicative mark (liṅga). To this, he says: "And it is accepted... and so forth.

The meaning is that, although the *manotā* mantra would— according to the principle to be explained in the section on relative strength (*balābala*)— attain the status of being an auxiliary to the *savanīya* animal sacrifice by virtue of its indicative mark (*liṅga*) of having Agni as its deity, a sublation (*bādha*) is nevertheless appropriate here,

just like the sublation to be explained later regarding the passage in the Brāhmaṇa which states, "Even if the animal belongs to another deity," thereby establishing its status as an auxiliary to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice. Thus, a sublation occurs in this case as well.
Because of the absence of the state of being a deity.

The meaning is that, although Agni and Soma are the deities on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), there is no deity-status for Soma alone. For here, even though Soma lacks deity-status on the full moon day, there is no contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) because it is possible for the two mantras—one illuminating Agni and one illuminating Soma—to be combined (*samuccaya*) so as to illuminate the joint deity Agni-Soma; this is because in the injunction "he recites the *puronuvākyā*," the accusative case is taken as indicating the instrumental sense, thereby [establishing] the singularity of the *anuvākyā* to be employed.

The meaning is that, because [the number] is intended to be significant—as in the case of the Pitṛyajña sacrifice—and because there is no injunction stating "there are two invitatory verses (anuvākyā) each," it is impossible for two invitatory verses to occur in a single ritual action.

And here, the authors of the *Prakāśa*, by means of the second position stated in the *Śāstradīpikā*, demonstrate a lack of reliance on both types of restrictive rules (*vyavasthā*), indicating that the restriction based on action (*karmakṛta-vyavasthā*)—which was established by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* after refuting the restriction based on time (*kālakṛta-vyavasthā*)—is improper; this is shown in the phrase "and the restriction" (*vyavasthā ca*).

When there is no injunction with multiple subjects, and the contingency of mentioning multiple things to be enjoined without restriction has arisen, the meaning of the term *vyavasthāpada* (the word of restriction) is the injunction of one thing in relation to another.
Although the view that the restriction is established by the verbal suffix (*kṛt*) was not favored, its mention at the end indicates that it alone is logical.

This should be seen and demonstrated in the *Kaustubha* under the section on the Full Moon sacrifice (*Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*), where I have already explained it; it is not elaborated here for fear of prolixity.

As for the point raised here by the authors of the *Prakāśa*— namely, that since the two *ājyabhāga* offerings have no direct connection with time, it would be untenable to establish a fixed rule such that "at the time of the full moon, the two *ājyabhāgas* are those with [the verses] containing *vārtraghna*, and at the time of the new moon, the two *ājyabhāgas* are those with [the verses] containing *vṛdhanvatī*"— and that if the rule were established through time, then according to the sentence "ya iṣṭyā," when performing a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *darśa* sacrifice on the full moon day...

Since the *vārtraghnī* verses would apply at the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) sacrifice due to its connection with the full moon (*pūrṇamāsa*), and the *vṛdhanvatī* verses would apply during the performance of the modified (*vikṛti*) rite, there would arise the contingency of a structural discrepancy (*vairūpya*) regarding the principle of acting according to the archetype (*prakṛtivadbhāva*). Consequently, in the *Vārtika*, the mention of "time" within the scope of the final conclusion (*siddhāntakoṭi*) refers to the connection of that [time] as it pertains to the time characterized by the primary act, and does not refer to the specific forms of "full moon" or "new moon. This is stated in refuting the objection raised by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* regarding the restriction based on time, concerning the modified time of the ritual.

Just as in the case of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, because of the prescription of the time for its constituent parts by means of the designation "Full Moon" (paurṇamāsī), there arises the application of the original Full Moon-time constituent parts when that modification is prescribed at the New Moon time— which takes the place of the Full Moon— so too does the application of the Vārtraghni verse likewise arise.

However, the *vṛdhanvatī* verses do not apply there either by direct instruction (*upadeśa*), because they have already fulfilled their purpose in the archetype (*prakṛti*); nor by extension (*atideśa*), because that [archetype] lacks the status of being a model for the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice.

Furthermore, the attempt to resolve the difficulty by arguing that because the two *ājyabhāga* offerings have a direct connection with time, and because even in the scriptural text (*śruti*) there exists a direct relationship in the form of a container-and-contained relation (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*), their connection with time is established—that is incorrect.

This is because, under the view that the restriction is determined by time, one must necessarily accept a connection either as the two times of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and new moon (*amāvāsyā*) being the conditions (*nimitta*), or else as the two *ājyabhāgas* belonging to those respective times being the objects of reference (*uddeśya*). And such [a connection] does not exist in the case of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
Because the absence of an impelling cause (prayojaka) makes the application of the *vārtraghni* and other such [mantras] difficult to establish;

for this very reason, in those subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) where the time of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and so forth is obtained as a subordinate element, their performance is obstructed by another modified injunction regarding the time (*vaikṛta-kāla-vidhi*).

Therefore, even in the absence of that [primary time], since it is improper to let the primary rite (*pradhāna*) lapse merely out of regard for the time belonging to the subsidiary, it is not difficult to perform them at other times that take the place of that [original] time.
For it is not possible for the *bhedana-homa* (the oblation for a broken vessel) to occur in the absence of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

Furthermore, as for what was stated beginning with "whatever [else]... that too is incorrect, because even an implied relationship of container and contained (*ādhāra-ādheya-bhāva*) between the two *ājyabhāga* offerings performed on the *pratipad* day cannot possibly exist.
Therefore, even if the principal rites are performed on the *pratipad*, their status as the substratum might somehow be established through the medium of the commencement of their own performance.
In this case, even that [connection] with the two Ājyabhāga offerings is possible;

therefore, the fact that the full-moon time (*paurṇamāsī-kālatva*) applies to the subsidiaries cannot be established directly, but must be understood as being mediated by the commencement of the performance of their own primary rites.
Furthermore, it is incorrect to maintain that the temporal distinction is justified solely by the fact of having such a full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) as its time;

for if that were the case, since only the *ājyabhāga* offerings—which are subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of the primary rite (*pradhāna*) occurring at the time of the full moon—would logically be the objects of reference, a temporal distinction would be untenable. Thus, this attempt at a refutation is improper.

As for what Somanātha said—that because these two are rules of distribution (*vyavasthā-vidhi*), and since such a rule is rooted in the prior absence of a fixed distribution, upon considering that... [the text continues].

It has been stated that since it is established that [the mantra] functions by way of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, when a mantra is prescribed with reference to time, there is no possibility of *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication) or of two distinct qualifications being intended; therefore, a restriction based on time is indeed appropriate.

That too is because, in the absence of the occurrence of non-restriction regarding that which is delimited by the delimiting factor of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), there is simply the determination that it is a restrictive injunction (*vyavasthāvidhi*).

Since it is initially impossible [to establish the connection], because the status of being mediated by the *ājyabhāga* offerings cannot be obtained, because figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is necessary, and because the previously mentioned objections remain unrefuted, this [interpretation] is even more improper; thus it was disregarded by the Venerable Master—enough said.
Thus ends the thirteenth section concerning the status of the *vātraghni* and other mantras as subsidiaries of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
— — — — — — — (B1) (14th Topic /) (a.3 pā.1 adhi.14) Immediate Succession.
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard: "He washes his hands; he spreads the grass-bundle (ulaparājī).
Likewise, in the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "He clenches his fists, restrains his speech, and announces the initiated one.
Among these, the washing of the hands is for the purpose of purifying the hands.
The clenching of the fists and the restraint of speech are for the purpose of fixing the mind;
therefore, it is beyond doubt that all three are intended for the rite about to be performed.

In this context, because of the immediate sequence and the syntactic unity, the rite to be performed consists precisely of the spreading of the *ulaparāji* grass and the announcement of the consecration (*dīkṣitāvedana*).

Since [the action] has already been reached, immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) is unavoidable; therefore, it is impossible for it to grasp [the subsequent act] as its subsidiary (*aṅga*). Even if it were to grasp it, such a claim would be sublated by the context (*prakaraṇa*). Furthermore, as in the expression "Look, the deer runs," there is an absence of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); thus, in the absence of a connection with words such as *yad*, it is impossible for two finite verbs to form a single sentence. Consequently, this [act of] hand-washing, which is a refinement of the agent, belongs—as a subsidiary to the subsequent act—equally to both the primary and the subsidiary rites, on account of the context. This is the case with the washing of the hands.
However, the acts of clenching the fists and maintaining silence are subsidiary only to the objects that precede the opening of the fingers and the release of speech.
Thus ends the fourteenth section concerning the washing of the hands and so forth, [establishing] that these are subsidiary to all parts of the context.

(B2) Since the recitation verses (*anuvākyās*) would otherwise result in meaninglessness if they were merely subordinate to the principal [sacrifice], and since the restriction of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings—which are themselves subsidiaries of that sacrifice—is established according to their sequence, the principle of "meaninglessness and its subsidiaries" (*anarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), which was set aside in the *Vāraṇādhikaraṇa*, is here revived. Consequently, because a counter-exception is made here to the restriction obtained through sequence, there is an immediate connection (*anantara-saṅgati*) based on this exception. Likewise, regarding those things understood from the second case ending as being for the purpose of purifying the hand, the fist, or speech—

Because of proximity (*sannidhāna*), there is the characterization of being a means to the *apūrva* by way of [substances] such as *ulapa* grass and clarified butter; or alternatively, because that [characterization] occurs by way of all constituent elements (*padārtha*). Having thus established the connection with the section (*pāda-saṅgati*) through this investigation—which consists of reflecting on the application of the Vedic injunction (*śruti-viniyoga*)—and without explicitly stating it since it is clear, he cites the subject sentence: "In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices... (*darśapūrṇamāsayoḥ*).

The washing of the hands (*hastāvanejana*), which consists of rinsing the hands with the second [mantra], serves to purify the hands through the visible means of removing impurities; thus, by way of its aspect as an agent (*kartṛtva-aṃśa*), it is a purifier of the agent.

Even though there was already a previous purification, nevertheless, since there are multiple mantras, there is no contradiction in allowing for another purification, just as there is room for further strengthening of the memory.

Therefore, because the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that which is about to be employed is more significant, the sequence of performance occurs at the very beginning—since it is required as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the preceding ritual act even though it contradicts the order of the textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) by virtue of the order of purpose (*arthakrama*). By this [argument], the view of the *Prakāśakāras* who claim that the washing of the hands (*hastāvanejana*) functions as an aid through an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭavidhayā*) is refuted; for when a visible purpose is possible, it is improper to postulate an unseen one.
He causes [them] to hear.
According to Dhūrtasvāmin, the term *ulapa* refers to fragrant, hard grasses such as *uśīra* that are fit for being cut upright; this is followed by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*.
However, based on Halāyudha’s statement, “*Ulapā* are said to be *balvajā*,” the *Prakāśakāras* maintain that *ulapas* are *balbajas*.

In either case, because they have the appearance of lines—another synonym for which is *rājī*—the act of spreading them before the previously prepared altar (*pūrva-vedi*) constitutes the *ulaparājistaraṇa* (the spreading of the *ulapa*-grass lines).
"Clenched fists," it is said.

When the sacrificer performs the clenching of the fists and the restraint of speech, the Adhvaryu priest performs the announcement of the initiated one (*dīkṣitāvedana*) by reciting three times in a low voice, "This sacrificer has been initiated. Then, although there is no dispute regarding these [fists and silence], which have been consecrated by the washing and other rites, being the means for accomplishing the subsequent ritual acts, the point of deliberation is this: are only those subsequent acts mentioned immediately following [the announcement] to be performed due to proximity (*sannidhāna*), or rather all of them?
This is the meaning.
It is precisely of the nature of an announcement.

Although the relationship of principal and subordinate (aṅgāṅgibhāva) is not possible because they have different agents, nevertheless, since the sacrificer is the agent even in the Adhvaryu ritual by virtue of being the instigator, or alternatively, because that [subordination] is possible through the postulation of its utility in the knowledge of the state of consecration (dīkṣitatva)— which resides in the sacrificer and constitutes the fruit of that [action]— this is the meaning.
That is, it serves as a subordinate element to the meaning of its own subsequent word.

By this, the argument of the *Nyāyasudhākṛt*— who, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that washing the hands serves to remove dirt, concludes that because it is unsuitable for the subsequent ritual acts following the making of the *piṇḍas* (which cause flour-dust to adhere), it is an auxiliary only to those acts preceding it— is refuted. For although this washing, which occurs prior to the [making of the] *piṇḍas*, does not remove the dust adhering to the flour at that specific moment, it is nonetheless established as serving all purposes by effecting the constant absence of such dirt during every ritual act.
The mention of "for the sake of purifying the agent" is for the purpose of establishing that [the act] serves all purposes.

Consequently, because it purifies the agent, and because the agent is for the sake of both the primary and subsidiary rites, the meaning is that it serves all purposes, just like the *upavyāna* (wearing of the sacred thread).

As for what has been stated here by the commentators— that just as the washing of the hands is a refinement of the agent (*kartṛsaṃskāra*), so too are the clenching of the fists and the restraint of speech, since they serve the purpose of focusing the mind;

and just as their utility lies in the recollection of the previously understood items belonging to that time, so too does it lie in the recollection of all the primary and subsidiary elements (*aṅga-pradhāna*) that are to be performed.

It has been stated that "utility through that" means there is utility even for the primary act— which is to be performed at a time subsequent to the emission of speech and the movement of the fingers— along with its subsidiary parts,

but not by virtue of occurring prior to them; otherwise, since it would lack the status of being a subsidiary to the primary act, there would be no application [of the rule] by way of context (*prakaraṇa*).
To indicate that this is incorrect, he says: "By the act of clenching the fist."

Since the clenching of the fists and the restraint of speech, which precede the *visarga*, serve the purpose of mental concentration by means of ceasing the fickleness of the hands and tongue respectively, they are understood—by virtue of their inherent fitness—to have the purpose of apprehending the object-matter [of the *visarga*] itself; consequently, it is perceived that the subsequent apprehension of the object-matter must be produced by a distinct effort and a distinct mental concentration. Thus, even though these acts are purificatory (*saṃskāraka*) of the agent, they are subsidiary only to the object-matter occurring prior to the *visarga*, on the basis of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) consisting of their functional fitness.
The position stated in the *Nyāyasudhā* alone is correct.

The meaning is that even if there is no status as being for the sake of the primary rite (*pradhāna*) occurring subsequent to it, its application to the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) is established by the principle of "uselessness [of the main] leading to [its application to] its parts" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*). Thus, even in the absence of the operation of the context (*prakaraṇa*) regarding its being for the sake of the subsidiaries, there is no harm. By this, the intention is that the statement in the *Vārtika*—that the clenching of the fists and so forth are for the sake of both the primary and its subsidiaries, and that their application is determined by the context—is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhavāda*).

The purpose [of this discussion] is that the washing of the hands, which is forgotten at its own time, should not be performed in the first half of the month after the spreading of the *ulapa* grass altar.
Likewise, in the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, there is an omission of the washing of the hands due to the omission of the *ulapa* grass altar, which is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*).

However, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), because it is an auxiliary to the subsequent [rites] and because in the *Gṛhamedhīya* it is an auxiliary to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, it must indeed be performed; this has not been stated here as it is self-evident.
Thus ends the fourteenth section concerning the washing of the hands and so forth being subsidiary to all parts of the context.
— — — — — — — (B1) (15th Adhikaraṇa /) (A.3 Pā.1 Adhi.15) But the remainder...

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, regarding the injunction "one divides the offering to Agni into four parts," the fact of being an offering whose deity is Agni is not the limiting factor for the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*); for if one were to refer to a qualified entity, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Rather, it is simply the status of being an offering (*haviṣṭva*) as conveyed by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).
In some way, the status of being an oblation (*haviṣṭva*) is connected to fire;
furthermore, a connection with fire exists even in the case of the *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice] and others.

Alternatively, because of the restrictive conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) by the statement, "He divides the *puroḍāśa* into four parts," that [division] applies only to the *puroḍāśa* that is connected to fire.
Having bowed, [the author says] "even of the clarified butter" (ājyasyāpi). Or,

even if there were some intention to express the status of being a deity (devatātva) [for the butter] as well, nevertheless, in the case of an offering to two deities (dvidevatya), Agni still certainly possesses the status of being a deity.

Because the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix heard at the end of the *dvandva* compound is connected with each member individually, it follows that the division into four parts applies to all of them. However, since the suffix—being most commonly used in the sense of "divinity" (*devatātva*)—cannot possibly indicate a mere relationship, there is no intention to express a connection with Agni. Thus, [the division does not apply to all].
Furthermore, deityhood does not reside individually in each member of a dual-deity (dvidevatya) offering.

This is because, through a *dvandva* compound prescribed with the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), the accompaniment (*sāhitya*) is intended; thus, deityhood—which is an indivisible, pervasive attribute (*avyāsajyavṛtty-akhaṇḍopādhi*)—is accepted as belonging only to the two deities in combination.

For this very reason, the common maxim "at the end of a *dvandva*" and so forth should be understood to apply only to cases where the accompaniment is not intended to be the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*).

Therefore, a taddhita suffix produced from the word *agni* alone is not capable of expressing the deity-status of that which is dependent on something else, because that would result in a contradiction of its own expressive capacity (*sāmarthya*).
As for the claim that the fact of having Agni as the deity is not intended to be expressed—

That is not so; for if that were the case, the mere fact of being the substance under discussion would not denote the means of the *apūrva*, since that [status] is not expressed by the deity-designating suffix (*taddhita*). Nor does it denote the status of being an oblation (*haviṣṭva*).
For the state of being intent upon that [the deity] is untenable without the cognition that the word denotes the deity.
Indeed, the traditional rule (smṛti) does not restrict the taddhita suffix to denote the deity only when the oblation (havis) is the object denoted;
for even when that [oblation] is denoted, there exists the taddhita suffix expressing a general relationship.
Therefore, it is the very status of being a deity (devatātva), as first understood, that serves as the delimiting factor of the objective (uddeśyatāvacchedaka).

Since this [status] is dependent upon a correlative (anuyogin) and a counter-correlative (pratiyogin), the status of being an oblation (haviṣṭva) dedicated to Agni as its deity is established—through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā)—as the delimiting factor of the objective, according to the principle of the "Havirārti" [passage], just as in the case of the expression "the sacrificial grass within the altar" (aradham antarvedi).
And by means of this, there is a restriction (upasaṃhāra) of the general statement, "He divides the cake into four parts."
Therefore, the division into four parts applies only to the cake dedicated to Agni. // 15 //
Thus ends the fifteenth section, concerning the conclusion.
Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* composed by the venerable Khaṇḍadeva.

(B2) Without explicitly stating the immediate connection (*saṅgati*) and the doubt (*saṃśaya*), since they are clear, [the author] states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) after first indicating the subject matter, by way of an exception (*apavāda*) to the universal applicability mentioned in the preceding section:
"He says 'darśa...
[ending with] "...because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)."

The meaning is as follows: since, according to the method stated in the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*, the connection of Agni’s status as a deity with the *bhāvanā* through the relation of being a factor (*kāraka*) is grammatically established, whereas its connection with the substance (*dravya*) would result in the fault of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to an unestablished connection; therefore, here, because the referent of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is understood as the object of the injunction (*uddeśya*) by virtue of the accusative case-ending, and because that [referent] has the sense of a pronoun, it refers back to what is present in its own sentence in the absence of such a thing. Consequently, since it is understood that the object of the injunction is merely the oblation (*havis*) under discussion, the qualifying attribute consisting of "being related to Agni" is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*).
The state of being an oblation (*haviṣṭva*) is the delimitor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*).

Alternatively, in order to avoid restricting the substance, by accepting that the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) has the general sense of relation, since fire lacks the status of a grammatical factor (*kāraka*), it follows that there is a rule of syntactic connection even with respect to the substance; thus, because the qualification is intended to be expressed, the state of being an oblation related to Agni [is the delimitor].
The delimiting factor of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) must be stated.

Since the fact of being pervaded by such a form of the delimiting factor of the object of reference is uniform everywhere, the author sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), intending that in the first position the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*) would apply to all sacrificial oblations (*havir-mātra*) common to both the subsidiaries and the primary rite, while in the second position it would apply commonly to all clarified butter (*ājya*) connected with the fire: "But rather... (*api tu*).
And it exists.

The meaning is that since the connection with Agni is understood as having the nature of being the substratum for the deityhood determined by the oblation, and since that [connection] exists in the Agnīṣomīya, Aindrāgna, and other sacrifices as well.

Since the word has abundant usage when there is an intention to express the substance qualified by divinity, and because of the grammatical rule (anuśāsana), it is more appropriate to assume its denotative power (*śakti*) resides solely in the substance as qualified by divinity. Otherwise, if it were to signify a general relationship, one would have to resort to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). To avoid this, even if one accepts that "having Agni as the deity" (*agnidevatāka*)—characterized by being an oblation (*haviṣṭva*)—serves as the delimiting factor for the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), the author states "let it be so" (*astu vā*) to establish the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by another means.
Because of the individual connection [of each].

Just as in the case of "Bring the jar and the cloth" (*ghaṭapaṭāv ānaya*), where the status of being the object (*karmatva*) applies to each individually because the case-ending is heard at the end of the *dvandva* compound, so too here: since the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is heard at the end [of the compound], and since the state of being the object of the deity to whom the gift is made—which consists in being the recipient of that which is being abandoned—cannot possibly be distributed [over multiple deities], one must accept that the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) applies to each [deity] individually; thus, it exists even in a sacrifice for two deities (*dvidevatya*).
The meaning is that the division into four parts must indeed be obtained.
"An indivisible limiting adjunct."

The meaning is that, because the status of being a deity—likewise consisting of an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*)—is distributed [over both members] just like the agency of the husband and wife, there is no contradiction.

However, in the case of "the pot and the cloth" (*ghaṭapaṭau*), since those two are the objects of reference (*uddeśya*), their conjunction is not intended to be expressed; therefore, it is logical that the status of being the object (*karmatva*) applies to each one individually. To establish this distinction, he says: "For this very reason."
"Of that" means:
The meaning is that, according to the traditional rule "the *iṣṭi* [suffix] is used for *sūkta* and *havis*," the suffix does not denote the mere substance (*dravya*) itself.
It is being restrained.
The meaning is that by this [method], one would understand from the very outset that the focus is on the oblation (*havis*).

Therefore, because the *taddhita* suffix denoting a deity establishes a rule that the *sūkta* or the oblation must be expressed, it is logical that the divinity—which is the basis of reliance and is understood first—serves as the indicator of being the means to the *apūrva*.
Thus, he states "therefore" (*ataḥ*) to show that the divinity possesses the status of being the delimitor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) as it appears in cognition.

Now, one might object: even so, since that [prohibition] would apply to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice as well—on the basis of the Śatapatha Śruti passage to be cited later and the statement of Kātyāyana, "Or both, because there is no distinction"—how can it be established that it pertains exclusively to the Āgneya? To this, he states the restrictive rule: "And by that... (tena ca).

The statement from the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, “Having divided that into four parts, he places the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*),” by referring to the sacrificial cake with the word “that,” effectively maintains an injunction for the fourfold division of the sacrificial cake in general.

If one does not accept such a restrictive application (*upasaṃhāra*), then even though it belongs to a different recension (*śākhā*), since the fourfold division of the sacrificial cake as prescribed by the direct scriptural statement cannot be entirely sublated, the result would be an option (*vikalpa*).

If one were to assume a restrictive application (upasaṃhāra) by means of the term *āgneya* itself through a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the general category of sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), there would result the fault of indicating a referent not delimited by the delimitor of the primary denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

Therefore, the restrictive application occurs through the term *puroḍāśa* itself, by means of a secondary indication that restricts it solely to those cakes dedicated to Agni (*āgneya*) as delimited by their own primary denotative capacity.
Therefore it has been said: "A general rule that is unclear should be restricted by means of a specific one."
Thus [it is said].

And therefore, since the general rule does not operate first, it follows that the restriction—which is a specific variety of *parisaṅkhyā*—is actually a contraction (*upasaṃhāra*) of the scope of the general statement to that alone; thus, because the Vedic text itself refers only to the *Āgneya* sacrifice, Kātyāyana’s statement is invalid as a source of authority because it merely presents a reason. This is the meaning.
Nor should it be argued: "In the Śatapatha passage, since the bhāvanā of making [the cake] into six parts— qualified by the time subsequent to the fourfold division—

is enjoined as an auxiliary to the consumption (bhakṣa), how can the fourfold division, being restated merely as a temporal qualifier, possess the status of a general rule (sāmānyavidhi) with respect to that matter in the absence of an injunction for it?"— this objection cannot be maintained.

Since it belongs to another recension (*śākhāntarīya*), for those belonging to that recension, its injunction is established by accepting a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) based on the assumption of a result consisting of an exalted prosperity (*abhyudayaśiraskatva*).

By this, the following is also refuted: even if the general rule remains meaningful when there is a mutual combination (*parasparopasaṃhāra*), the general rule would be rendered useless if only one of the two were combined; [this objection is refuted] because the general rule retains its purpose by having the aforementioned result of exalted prosperity.
The same should be understood regarding the combination of two statements belonging to a single school (ekaśākhīya).

By this [it is shown that], although the lack of clarity—consisting in the requirement for a specific mode of performance—is impossible in the case of the *puroḍāśa* statement, here, because the placing upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is enjoined, there arises the understanding that the fourfold division is a restatement (*anuvāda*). And since such a restatement depends on how [the action] has already been established [by other means], [the injunction of placing upon the grass serves as the basis for the restatement].

Furthermore, Somanātha’s argument— that because the statement regarding the Āgneya sacrifice pertains to a specific case, the general statement is established as a restrictive application (*upasaṃhāra*) by being restricted to that specific instance— is refuted.

Even though [the disposal] is already established as a specific instance, since it is possible for it to be an injunction by virtue of being the disposal for all *puroḍāśa* offerings, it cannot be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Therefore, because it would be illogical for it to terminate in a specific [instance], as soon as its status as an injunction begins,
it must be stated that its nature is that of a concluding summary (*upasaṃhāra*), whose fruit is the prevention [of the disposal] common to all.

In this regard, the intention is as follows: since the possibility of "indistinctness"—defined as the capacity for connection with specific particulars due to the lack of determination of those particulars—exists in a general statement, while the possibility of "distinctness"—defined as the absence of that [indistinctness]—exists in a specific statement, it was stated by the venerable teachers that a general statement does not effect a restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) to a specific case, because that would entail a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) in what is not delimited by the delimitor of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*). This is the underlying meaning.
He concludes the established tenet with the words: "Therefore..."
The purpose has not been stated because it is obvious.
Thus ends the fifteenth section, on the conclusion [of the ritual].
Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāṭṭadīpikāprabhāvalī*, composed by Śambhubhaṭṭa, the ornament of the learned, a disciple of the venerable Khaṇḍadeva.
